articles.title: Land mine casualties soar in Syria, two years after war
articles.summary: Nearly 1,000 children are among those killed or injured by explosives left over from the conflict, figures show.

blocks.text: Eleven-year-old Alaa was tending her family's goats with her siblings in a field behind their home in Umm Khuzaym, north-west Syria, on Sunday when there was a flash and a deafening bang.
"Then we heard people screaming," Alaa's father, Walid Mohammed Al-Ghafar, told the BBC.
Walid ran outside to find his daughter lying face down, killed, and her 10-year-old brother, Mahmoud, seriously injured.
Unwittingly, the children had triggered a landmine.

The incident and others this week bring to nearly 1,000 the number of children killed or injured by explosive ordnance in Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, according to the UN Mine Action Service (Unmas).
The village is one of many where families have returned to homes and farmland that were once on the front lines of Syria's 13-year civil war.
Alaa's father said demining teams had visited several times to clear the fields. He and other residents believed it was safe for farmers and children to move around.
But mines and other explosives can lie far beyond former battle lines, making it difficult to establish which areas are safe.

"Remnants of war from today's conflicts are often very widely and broadly scattered, often without patterns, which makes it extremely difficult to do clearance," Katrin Atkins, research lead at Landmine Monitor, a global mine monitoring initiative, told the BBC.
The dangers are reflected in a sharp rise in casualties across Syria.

A total of 1,602 people were killed or injured by landmines and explosive remnants of war in 2025 alone, an increase of more than 50% on the previous year, according to the Landmine Monitor report, published by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines on Tuesday.
Only Myanmar, with 1,891 casualties, recorded more.
The report attributes the rise in Syria partly to the large-scale return of refugees and internally displaced people following Assad's overthrow.

"When you look at population movement, a couple of months later you see an increase of incidents in these areas, because that's exactly where people go and start to use the fields again," Atkins said.

More than 60% of casualties recorded by the world's largest landmine clearance charity, the Halo Trust, involve farming, agriculture or shepherding, according to its Syria programme manager, Simon Jackson.
"They're not going to wait for the government or for organisations like us to come and tell them that everything is safe and clear," he told the BBC. "People are taking risks out of desperation."
Since Assad's fall on 8 December 2024, Unmas has recorded at least 1,556 incidents in Syria involving explosive ordnance.
They have caused 2,701 casualties: 935 people killed and 1,766 injured. Children account for 995 of those victims, or about 37%.
But the toll is likely to be higher, with experts estimating that overall casualties could be under-reported by 25-50%.
For many of those who survive, the consequences are devastating and permanent.

Majid Abdul Rahman, 27, was travelling in a car in the Ghouta region on the outskirts of Damascus in March 2025 when it struck an explosive device. The vehicle filled with smoke and he felt a pain in his leg.
More than a year later, Majid has difficulty walking and has been unable to return to work, leaving him struggling to provide for his family.
The danger has continued into this month, with at least 20 people killed and more than 40 injured by explosive ordnance in November.

In one of the worst recorded incidents, an explosion in a school courtyard in Hasakah on 4 November killed a 12-year-old and injured 19 others. And on Monday, a 13-year-old boy was killed when an unexploded cluster munition detonated in southern Daraa province.

The threat is also holding back Syria's economic recovery. Contaminated farmland cannot be safely cultivated, while people collecting scrap metal or trying to salvage materials from abandoned areas also risk triggering explosions.
The Syrian Ministry of Defence says since the end of 2024 its teams have found and dealt with more than 315,000 mines and unexploded munitions.
But no nationwide survey has established how much land remains contaminated, making it difficult to assess the full scale of the problem.
"We're in a bit of a black hole," Atkins said.
And with the extent of contamination still largely unknown, the war continues to claim victims two years after it ended.
Additional reporting by Lana Antaki in Damascus

articles.title: U2 announces 2027 shows in Toronto, Vancouver as part of world tour
articles.summary: U2 announced the first Canadian dates in its world tour on Tuesday, in support of the new album Carnaval de Luz.

image.caption: Bono, left, and The Edge, right, are shown performing during U2's surprise performance at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles on Nov. 14. (Chris Pizzello/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
U2 announced the first Canadian dates in its world tour on Tuesday, in support of the new album Carnaval de Luz.
Band has not played in Canada since 2018

The Irish superstars will be hitting Canadian cities for the first time in about a decade in 2027, with shows Sept. 7 and Sept. 9 at Rogers Stadium in Toronto and Oct. 18 at BC Place in Vancouver. Stephen Wilson Jr. is scheduled to open for the band in Toronto, with The War on Drugs announced as the opening act in Vancouver.
The band earlier announced dates in Latin America beginning in February to launch the tour, dubbed the Greatest Show on Earth tour.

U2 last played in Canada in 2017-18. The band has an extensive history in the country, with Toronto, Montreal and Ottawa some of the first shows the band ever played outside Europe, in 1980-81 while touring their debut album Boy.
Carnaval de Luz, released on Nov. 13, is the band's 16th studio album.

While the band reworked old favourites for 2023's Songs of Surrender, it's the band's first original collection of songs in nine years. Singles released from the new album have included The Greatest Show on Earth, Street of Dreams and Silencio.

"There will be loud guitars, deep bass, some ecstatic rhythms," singer Bono promised in a statement announcing the album, which was again produced with their frequent collaborator Garret (Jacknife) Lee.
The last track on the album is Torn, a duet with Dolly Parton, who died in August.
The band performed Silencio, along with their classic 1984 song Pride (In the Name of Love), at a surprise appearance earlier this month at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame ceremony in Los Angeles.

In addition to the tour, Bono, guitarist The Edge, bassist Adam Clayton and drummer Larry Mullen Jr. will be in the spotlight in 2027 as recipients of the MusiCares persons of the year, the annual honour given during the Grammy Awards weekend in Los Angeles in February.

U2 has supported many causes since forming 50 years ago in Dublin, including global health, disaster response, addiction recovery, mental health and access to music education. MusiCares honoured Bono individually in 2003.
Bono also received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in early 2025 from U.S. President Joe Biden, in recognition of his humanitarian efforts.
With files from the Associated Press

articles.title: Pip assessments are ‘not fit for purpose’, Timms tells MPs as he unveils his review – UK politics live
articles.summary: Social security minister has been overseeing review designed to ‘rehumanise’ the system but Tories say it will lead to higher spending and fewer checks

blocks.text: Timms gives statement to MPs on his Pip review, setting out its three key conclusions
In the Commons, Stephen Timms is now delivering his statement on Pip.
He says Pip provides “vital support to deaf and disabled people and people with long term health conditions”. It was introduced 13 years ago, but has not been reviewed since then.

He says it was co-produced by himself, his two co-chair and 12 other members of a steering group. Almost all of those 12 people had “lived experience of disability or long term ill health”. Every member – including Timms himself – had just one vote, he says.
Timms says:

double quotation mark The review is clear that Pip remains a vital source of support, but it finds that the system is failing in three fundamental respects. First of all, the assessment is not fit for purpose. It doesn’t consider people’s needs, their aspirations, their barriers, or their extra costs. It’s just about what somebody cannot do. Many people find it adversarial and dehumanising. It struggles to reflect fluctuating and cumulative conditions properly, and it too often leaves people fearing that work, health, treatment or greater independence will count against them. Far from supporting independence, it can be a barrier to it. Second, awards do not consistently enable the right contribution toward the additional costs that people face. The areas of extra cost survey reviewed by the steering group showed that Pip does not always target the highest levels of support on those with the most severe needs. The future system should make the basis for support clearer, with decisions reflecting individual circumstances better. And third, the system’s offers offers too little scope for personalised solutions. The review recommends that cash should remain central, but that people should have the choice to access practical services as part of the overall support that they receive. That would allow the system to respond more flexibly to individual needs.

blocks.text: Steve Darling, the Lib Dem work and pensions secretary, praised Timms for working well with disabled people on the report. But it said it was interesting to note that Timms’ approach to young people was different from Alan Milburn’s. He urged the government to “get a grip on that”, and clarify its intentions.
IFS says proposals in Timms review for short-term changes to Pip would lead to 'likely increase' in spending

The Institute for Fiscal Studies thinktank has released its response to the Timms report. One point it makes is that the recommendations for short-term changes to Pip would probably lead to higher spending on the benefit.
Eduin Latimer, a senior research economist at the IFS, said:

double quotation markIn the short run, and while Pip continues in its current form, the Timms review recommends a range of changes to the application process, including making more of it available online, a fast-track process for those with severe disabilities, and providing an advocacy service to help applicants. Many of these proposals are intended to reduce the burden on applicants and make the process of applying easier. This has obvious benefits for applicants, but evidence from past reforms tells us it would likely increase the number of claimants – and hence spending.
In response to Whately, Timms said she was wrong to suggest that he was just proposing to tinker with the system. He was proposing a “fundamental new approach”, he said.
Tories claim Burnham has created welfare 'mess', with Timms and Milburn reports making recommendations 'poles apart'
Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, criticised the review for not proposing cuts to welfare spending in her response to Timms.
And she rejected his claim that his review overlapped with Milburn’s. She said:

double quotation markAlan Milburn also proposed changes to the disability benefit system, based on the plans we have set out shifting from cash to support for milder conditions and reducing the amount spent in total on sickness benefits. Two landmark reviews commissioned by the government landing one week apart, saying completely different things. The minister has tried to make out they fit together, that they have much in common, but pull the other one. They may have similar diagnoses, but their proposals are poles apart. What a mess. Which side is the prime minister going to pick? Team Milburn or Team Timms? Or will he freeze in the headlights and avoid the argument? Refuse to choose and create a two-tier system with one rule for under-25s and another for everyone else? This is no joke – £200bn, that’s what the working age welfare bill will cost taxpayers by the end of this parliament. But two and a half years after they’ve come into power, after two supposedly landmark reviews, they are no closer to doing anything about it to fix welfare, tackle soaring costs and get the benefits bill down.
Timms claims his report and Milburn's report have 'much in common' in their diagnoses
Timms said the government would consider the recommendations alongside the recommendations in the Milburn report.

double quotation markThe two reviews had different remits, but their diagnoses have much in common. Both find a fragmented system that asked people to prove what they cannot do, rather than understand what they could do with the right support. Both identify the worry that participation, treatment, or improvement could put somebody’s financial security at risk, and both argue for support that is more personalised, more joined up and more responsive to people’s lives. So, taken together, the two reviews share ambition for a system that offers security for those with the most severe needs.
Timms said the government did want to bring the benefits bill down, “but not through crude cuts that push people into hardship and increase costs elsewhere in the system”.
Timms says government accepting two of review's recommendations now, and others being considered
Timms says further work is needed on the way ahead.

double quotation markSupport should correspond more closely to genuine additional costs and needs. Cumulative and fluctuating impacts should be recognised properly, and the highest support should reflect the most severe needs. A good deal of further work is needed. The government will now undertake this work and set out its plans in next year’s white paper.
The report includes multiple recommendations. Timms says the government will consider them in full.
But the government can announce it is confirming two of them, he says.

double quotation markFirst, the people with serious well evidence conditions whose effects on daily life are clear should have access to a fast-track route without an unnecessary full assessment. That should include a distinct and rapid route for people at the end of life, as at present. But others should benefit from a fast-track as well. And second, that people whose health conditions are lifelong or degenerative, where there’s clear evidence that their functional needs are unlikely to improve, should not face repeated award reviews.
Timms says final decisions about future Pip eligibility rules will be matter for government and MPs
Timms says his review concluded “full system reform” was needed.

double quotation markThe review reaches the view that we need a full system reform, not just some adjustment of the forms or descriptors. It doesn’t prescribe a final set of eligibility rules because it recognises that decisions about eligibility criteria should sit with the elected government accountable to this house. But it does suggest principles on which those decisions should be made.
But the Green party has welcomed the Timms review. This is from the Green MP Siân Berry.

double quotation markThe long-awaited Timms review has clearly found the current situation to be dehumanising, harmful and counterproductive. And I agree the whole system should be made more responsive, specific and dependable to support equality and respect disabled people’s human rights. The rhetoric of insult and blame must end. It is so important for the government to recognise Pip is not an out of work benefit, to be chopped away and replaced by work support and that there should be no arbitrary age discrimination. I urge Stephen Timms to remind Alan Milburn of this.
Tories dismiss Timms review as 'complete farce', saying it will lead to more spending and fewer checks
Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, has described the Timms review as “a complete farce”. In a response, she said:

double quotation markThis review is a complete farce. After Labour abandoned welfare reform last year, all that is left is a review which will mean more spending, fewer checks, and a complete absence of substance. Labour’s flagship review into sickness benefits has failed. Labour will never cut welfare because they are the welfare party, and their leftwing backbenchers will never let them. The Conservatives will review the entire Pip system, remove eligibility for low-level mental health Pip claims, rapidly assess hundreds of thousands of additional claims and get Britain working again.

articles.title: World Chess Championship 2026 Game 1: Gukesh Dommaraju v Javokhir Sindarov – live
articles.summary:
• Youngest title match in chess history starts Tuesday

  • Sindarov, Gukesh open with Berlin defense of Ruy Lopez

blocks.text: Everything you need to know about the World Chess Championship

India’s Gukesh Dommaraju is defending the world chess championship against fast-rising Uzbek grandmaster Javokhir Sindarov in the youngest title match in the competition’s 140-year history. The best-of-14-games contest is scheduled to take place from 24 November to 12 December at the Fondation Martin Bodmer outside Geneva, with an overall prize fund of $2.5m (£1.9m).

items: Game 1 starts at 3pm in Geneva, 2pm in London, 9am in New York and 7.30pm in India
Sindarov will have the white pieces for Game 1 and make the first move
Gukesh and Sindarov are both 20 years old, making this the youngest matchup in world championship’s 140-year history
Read the Guardian’s comprehensive watch guide for the Gukesh v Sindarov showdown
Go move by move through 22 of the most famous games in world championship history

blocks.text: Key events

items: 1h agoGame 1 is under way!
2h agoHow do Gukesh and Sindarov match up?
2h agoThe format
2h agoPreamble
3h agoEverything you need to know about the World Chess Championship

blocks.text: And finally Gukesh makes his move! After a think of more than 15 minutes, the world champion has opted for 13 ... Bd7, bringing his last minor piece into play. The bishop also shields the black king from a potential check along the d-file, giving Gukesh greater flexibility in repositioning his king and coordinating his rooks. He’s more than 35 minutes behind the challenger on time, though.
Gukesh is in another deep think as Javokhir leaves the board for the nearby lounge chair inside the cramped playing hall.

“Now I understand what Javokhir was playing for,” English grandmaster David Howell says on the Chess.com broadcast. “I would have expected this opening from two older players, not maybe two 20-year-olds. But now I understand he’s trying to bait Gukesh. He’s trying to tempt him into some line where he has a deep, deep idea. Yeah, it’s very provocative.”

blocks.caption: Sindarov looks on as Gukesh ponders his response to 13 Ne4. Photograph: Chess.com

blocks.text: Gukesh has developed his dark-squared bishop and Sindarov has centralized his queenside knight (12 ... Be7 13 Ne4). The pace of play has slowed considerably as the players begin to grapple with the strategic subtleties of the Berlin. Both Stockfish and the Sesse supercomputer assess the position as dead even (0.00).

blocks.caption: Gukesh studies the position during Tuesday’s opening game of the world chess championship. Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters

blocks.text: An email from the always welcome Gary Naylor, who sees parallels between the world chess championship and another of Europe’s great endurance events:

double quotation markGiven the location, the schedule, the fact that each leader has a team supporting him and, more than anything, the stamina required, this feels like the Tour de France. I suppose players have the ability to make stages – games – hard or easy by their strategies too. Any sign of lycra?

No lycra to report, Gary, but there’s certainly something to the analogy. The ability to conserve energy over a three-week campaign, knowing when to attack and when to settle for a quiet day, is an underrated component of world championship matchplay.
Gukesh has been mulling his response to 12 Be3 for more than 10 minutes, after spending about eight minutes on his previous move.

“He still knows the position, but he is taking time to make sure he makes the right moves,” Russian grandmaster Peter Svidler says on the official Fide broadcast. “But Gukesh is already down almost 18 minutes on the clock. Considering he’s playing one of the most topical openings of the past 25 years, that’s some time expenditure.”
Gukesh has brought his knight to g6, putting pressure on the advanced white pawn on e5, and Sindarov has continued his development by bringing his bishop into play (11 ... Ng6 12 Be3).

Gukesh has returned his king to its original square and rerouted his knight (9 Rd1+ Ke8 10 Nc3 Ne7 11 h3). Sindarov’s last move prevents black’s light-squared bishop from coming to g4 and pinning the knight on f3, while giving his own king some breathing room.

“I think it’s important to highlight for our viewers that black is not playing for a draw,” the Hungarian grandmaster Judit Polgár says on Chess.com’s broadcast. “Black is just deciding to go into an endgame or a middlegame without queens, where it seems like only white has a slight edge. Black has doubled pawns on c6 and c7, black has the bishop pair, but basically black can go b6, develop the pieces properly.”

blocks.caption: The position after 10 Nc3. Photograph: Fide

blocks.text: We’re heading straight into the famous Berlin endgame (4 O-O Nxe4 5 d4 Nd6 6 Bxc6 dxc6 7 dxe5 Nf5 8 Qxd8+ Kxd8). The queens are off the board after only eight moves, leaving white with a kingside pawn majority and black with the bishop pair but doubled c-pawns and a king that has forfeited the right to castle.

Don’t mistake the early exchange of queens for a lack of ambition. The resulting position is deceptively rich in strategic possibilities and has been the subject of decades of analysis at the highest level. Gukesh has continued with 9 Rd1+, and both players are still moving quickly.
Game 1 is under way!
The players have shaken hands and we’re off! We have a Berlin defense of the Ruy Lopez (1 e4 e5 2 Nf3 Nc6 3 Bb5 Nf6), one of the most thoroughly analyzed openings in modern chess.

The Berlin famously helped Vladimir Kramnik dethrone Garry Kasparov in their 2000 world title match in London and has been a staple of elite chess ever since, earning a reputation as one of black’s most reliable weapons against 1 e4.

We’re eight minutes to the scheduled first move, but American grandmaster Maurice Ashley has started with his introduction of the players to the playing hall. Gukesh enters first and takes his seat behind the black pieces. Sindarov, playing as white after Sunday’s drawing of lots, enters second.

blocks.caption: Fide president Timur Turlov makes the ceremonial first move for white in Tuesday’s opening game of the world chess championship between Javokhir Sindarov and Gukesh Dommaraju near Geneva. Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters

blocks.text: If you’re looking for some pre-match reading, the Guardian spoke exclusively with Javokhir Sindarov on Sunday about his meteoric rise, his love of Lionel Messi, his plans to play GTA VI once the match is over and why chess’s happy warrior believes there’s more to life than the game. A taste:

double quotation mark“I’m the guy who can’t play games just for fun,” Sindarov tells the Guardian less than 48 hours before Tuesday’s world championship opener in Geneva, smiling at the absurdity of it. “If I play something, I always try to learn, trying to become better.” That means poring over Counter-Strike tactics and watching YouTube tutorials before joining in with his mates. There is, it appears, no such thing as a casual game in Sindarov’s world, much less a friendly. “I always like to beat my friends,” he says. “I watch some video lessons and then come and beat them after some tournaments. I think the best thing is to beat your friends in some game.” It is a revealing admission from a young man who has acquired a reputation for being uncommonly relaxed at the chess board. While many of the world’s elite players seem to carry the weight of every position on their shoulders – the viral clip of Sergey Karjakin agonizing for 25 minutes over a move during the 2016 world title match remains a cult classic in chess circles – Sindarov frequently gives off the impression of someone who is simply enjoying himself. The easygoing mien of the sport’s happy warrior is a quality that has caught his opponent’s attention. “One thing I learned from Sindarov is that he seems to be so happy while playing chess,” Gukesh Dommaraju, the reigning world champion, said in an interview published last week.

We’ve gone through the 140-year history of the world championship and chosen 22 of the most memorable games. You can go move by move through each of them here. It’s the perfect timesuck in the final run-up to today’s first move.

double quotation markFrom the middle of the 16th century, there have come down to us the names of chess players who have been widely regarded as the strongest of their time. The earliest of these was the Spanish priest Ruy López de Segura, after whom one of the most popular openings of modern times is named. Others who followed include the Calabrese Gioachino Greco, François-André Danican Philidor, Louis-Charles Mahé de La Bourdonnais, Alexander McDonnell, Howard Staunton, Adolf Anderssen, Mikhail Chigorin and Paul Morphy, each of whom are lionized for their contributions to the development of theory and strategy as well as their dominance over their board during their respective eras. But not until Wilhelm Steinitz and Johannes Zukertort sat down in a small room at 80 Fifth Avenue in New York City on the afternoon of 11 January 1886 did a formal competition to determine the best player on the planet come to pass. Their first-to-10-wins encounter was held in three US cities over the next 78 days for a prize fund of $4,000. Since then, the world chess championship has provided the stage for countless unforgettable contests showcasing the precision, imagination and brilliance of the royal game at the highest level.

The legitimacy of the world championship, of course, remains a subject of lively debate. The absence of Magnus Carlsen continues to cast a long shadow over the sport’s showcase event. The 35-year-old Norwegian has held the world No 1 ranking for more than 15 consecutive years and was widely regarded as the game’s strongest player even before he defeated Vishy Anand for the world title in 2013. He only strengthened his claim as the greatest player of any era in 2021, when he crushed Ian Nepomniachtchi in Dubai in his fourth successful defense of the crown.

But Carlsen declined to defend his title for a fifth time in 2023, citing a lack of motivation to endure the months-long grind of preparation that championship matches demand. Only twice before had the chain of succession that stretches back to Wilhelm Steinitz in 1886 been broken: when Alexander Alekhine died as champion in 1946 and when Bobby Fischer forfeited the title in 1975.

blocks.caption: Norway’s Magnus Carlsen has held the world No 1 ranking for more than 15 consecutive years. Photograph: Yu Chun Christopher Wong/Eurasia Sport Images/Getty Images

blocks.text: Ding Liren went on to defeat Nepomniachtchi for the vacant title before losing it to Gukesh Dommaraju in Singapore the following year. Now Gukesh faces Sindarov in a match between two 20-year-olds ranked No 26 and No 4 in the world respectively, while the planet’s top-ranked player remains on the sidelines – at a time when his No 1 ranking is looking more vulnerable than any time in anyone’s memory. The generational stakes are undeniable, but the question that has dogged the championship since Carlsen walked away remains unresolved: can the winner truly claim to be the best chess player in the world?
How do Gukesh and Sindarov match up?

For two elite players born in the same general part of the world barely six months apart, their competitive history is remarkably sparse: just three encounters in classical chess. Sindarov holds a 2½-½ advantage with two wins and one draw in their lifetime head-to-head, which dates back to their first encounter as tweens at the Moscow Open in 2018. Their most recent meeting happened in January at the prestigious Tata Steel tournament in Wijk aan Zee, where a tense positional struggle gave way to a wild, time-scrambled endgame before the pair settled for a draw after 78 moves. Sindarov also holds a 2-1 edge in their three rapid and blitz contests this year.
Allow content provided by a third party?

This article includes content hosted on lichess.org. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Gukesh’s form has largely gone off the rails since reaching the summit 23 months ago in Singapore. After making it to No 3 in the world with a peak rating of 2794, the Indian suffered a prolonged run of disappointing results, including a joint-last finish at March’s Prague Chess Festival and last-place showings at Norway Chess and the Chennai Grand Masters. He subsequently withdrew from the classical portion of the Grand Chess Tour and had tumbled to No 32 in the rankings by September, when his live rating briefly dipped below the 2700 barrier for the first time in four years, although his performances improved at that month’s Chess Olympiad.

Many of the world’s top grandmasters have expressed deep pessimism about Gukesh’s chances in Geneva due to his lengthy slump and Sindarov’s sustained upward tick. So too have the bookmakers, who have installed the Uzbek as a clear frontrunner at roughly 1-3 odds despite Gukesh being the champion. Carlsen has described Sindarov as “a pretty significant favorite”, citing the Indian’s tendency to take excessive risks. “His evaluations are way too optimistic,” the world No 1 said recently. “That makes him take way more chances than he should. I think especially now his confidence hasn’t been too high, he just tries to do a little bit too much.”

Yet one factor in Gukesh’s favor is his firsthand experience in the cauldron of a world championship match, where the intense psychological and physical rigors of facing the same opponent for weeks on end can be as punishing as the chess itself. Caruana, the world No 3 and former world title challenger who pushed Carlsen to the brink in 2018, has cautioned against writing off the champion despite his struggles. “The kind of ability he had – or has, whatever you want to say – it doesn’t disappear overnight,” Caruana said in September. “So, in my opinion, it can reverse at any moment.”

blocks.caption: Javokhir Sindarov, left, and Gukesh Dommaraju stand on the podium during Sunday’s world chess championship opening ceremony at the United Nations’ European headquarters in Geneva. Photograph: Salvatore Di Nolfi/EPA

blocks.text: The format

Here’s a review of the format for the world championship match. Gukesh and Sindarov will play up to 14 classical games with each player awarded one point for a win and a half-point for a draw. Whoever reaches seven and a half points first will be declared the champion (and no dead rubbers will be played).

The time control for each game is 120 minutes per side for the first 40 moves, then 30 minutes for the remainder of the game, with a 30-second increment per move starting with move 41. That means games can stretch beyond seven hours, testing both players’ concentration and endurance. Players are not permitted to agree to a draw before black’s 40th move, a rule designed to discourage short, uneventful games. A draw claim before then is only allowed in the case of threefold repetition or stalemate, subject to approval by the chief arbiter or deputy arbiter.

If the score is level after 14 games, a series of tiebreaks will be played on 12 December, starting with four rapid games at 15 minutes per player plus 10 seconds per move. If still tied, the players will contest two games at 10 minutes plus five seconds, followed if necessary by two blitz games at three minutes plus two seconds. Further single blitz games will be played until a winner emerges. Three of the past five world championship matches have been deadlocked after the classical portion and required tiebreaks: 2016, 2018 and 2023.
The complete official regulations can be found here.

blocks.caption: Gukesh Dommaraju speaks with chess presenter Charlize van Zyl during Sunday’s media day at the United Nations’ European headquarters in Geneva. Photograph: Michał Walusza/Fide

blocks.text: Preamble

Hello and welcome to Geneva for day one of the World Chess Championship. Over the next three weeks, India’s defending champion Gukesh Dommaraju and Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan will compete in a scheduled best-of-14-games match for the sport’s most prestigious title and a share of a $2.5m prize fund. The setting is the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, an affluent suburb overlooking Lake Geneva, where the two 20-year-olds will make history as the youngest pairing ever to contest a world championship match in the competition’s 140-year history.

Gukesh became the youngest undisputed world chess champion in history when he defeated China’s Ding Liren in Singapore in December 2024, aged just 18, shattering the record held by Garry Kasparov, who was 22 when he dethroned Anatoly Karpov in 1985. An aggressive player known for creating sharp, tactically complex positions aimed at unsettling opponents, the Chennai-born grandmaster has struggled badly for form since winning the crown, sliding from a career-high No 3 to No 26 in the world rankings and raising questions over his chances of retaining the title in his first defense.

blocks.caption: A tram bearing promotional artwork for the world chess championship in Geneva. Photograph: Maurizio Giuliani/Fide

blocks.text: Sindarov, meanwhile, has emerged as one of the most formidable talents of a new generation of Uzbek grandmasters. Born in Tashkent, he became a grandmaster at 12 years and 10 months, the second-youngest in history at the time, and secured his place in Geneva by winning the eight-man Candidates tournament earlier this year. A fearless, resourceful player in a rich vein of form, he enters his first world championship match ranked fourth in the world, up from No 25 last year and a remarkable 22 places above the reigning champion, and with a favorable head-to-head record against Gukesh in classical chess.

We’re roughly 80 minutes away from the ceremonial opening moves. Fide president Timur Turlov will do the honors for white, with five-time world champion and Fide deputy president Viswanathan Anand moving for black. Plenty more to come between now and then.

articles.title: Gaza issues meningitis epidemic alert after steep rise in cases
articles.summary:
Health ministry records 272 new infections in October, more than eight times the normal monthly rate

Gaza’s health ministry has issued an epidemic alert after a sharp rise in meningitis…

blocks.text: Gaza’s health ministry has issued an epidemic alert after a sharp rise in meningitis infections, with more than 270 new cases reported in October.
Dr Nidal Ghoneim, a senior official at the ministry, said the spread of the disease posed a threat to the lives of hundreds of thousands of people, including children.

Health organisations attribute the rise in infections to the destruction of infrastructure, overcrowded shelters and the contamination of drinking water with sewage – a crisis made worse by winter flooding and restrictions on humanitarian aid. Much of Gaza’s drinking water previously came from desalination plants and three Israeli-controlled pipelines, which were cut off at the start of the war and have only partially reopened.

Ghoneim told a news conference that 272 meningitis infections had been reported in the territory in October, more than eight times the normal monthly rate of 30 to 50 cases. Fifteen Palestinians have died of meningitis since the beginning of this year, he said.

blocks.caption: A doctor examines a child suffering from meningitis at al-Rantisi children’s hospital in Gaza City. Photograph: Omar Ashtawy/HL/Getty Images

blocks.text: “We hold the [Israeli] occupation fully and directly responsible for the epidemic outbreak due to its prevention of the entry of maintenance spare parts, sterilisation materials and fuel,” the health ministry said.

The UN’s humanitarian agency (Ocha) had previously reported 413 suspected cases of meningitis in Gaza between 27 September and 31 October, including 294 viral and 119 bacterial cases. About 68% were recorded in Gaza City.
Ocha said the increase in cases could be attributed to crowded tents and schools, the deterioration of shelter and sanitation conditions and exposure to unsafe water.
Gaza’s water crisis is severe. Before the war, 80% of the territory’s supply came from an aquifer that is now contaminated by seawater and wastewater, making it unfit for human consumption.

For many, this means a stark choice between drinking an extra cup of water or saving it to wash their hands and prevent disease. Acute diarrhoea is among the leading causes of illness in the territory. About 15,000 cubic metres a day of untreated waste seeps into the groundwater from soak-away pits, particularly in the informal camps in al-Mawasi.
The World Health Organization said in September that microbial contamination in water samples had risen from less than 6% in January to nearly 20% in August.

In addition to disease outbreaks and shortages of drinking water and basic necessities, Palestinians continue to face attacks and ceasefire violations by the Israeli military, which has intensified its strikes in recent days.

Soldiers crossed into Hamas-controlled central Gaza last Wednesday in the first ground operation across the “yellow line” boundary since a fragile ceasefire was agreed in October last year, forcing dozens of displaced Palestinians to flee their tents.
Four people were killed and seven wounded in Gaza over the past 24 hours, according to the health ministry, bringing the death toll since the ceasefire took effect to 1,679.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and more than 176,000 wounded since the beginning of the war in October 2023, according to Gaza’s health authorities.

articles.title: EU enlargement: Why do some EU member states use their vetoes to block the accession of certain candidate countries?
articles.summary: Individual EU member states use their veto powers to block candidate countries in the accession process — often for reasons of domestic politics. DW takes a look at some cases and examines what's…

image.caption: Will the European Union soon have 28 members or more? Or will some member states block the accession of certain candidate countries?Image: Nicolas Economou/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: It's been quite a while since the EU's last enlargement: Croatia was the last country to join the bloc back in 2013.

If everything goes according to plan, another enlargement might soon be on the cards: Montenegro, with a population of just 620,000, could complete accession negotiations in the coming months and join the European Union in early 2028.

But no sooner had EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos made this announcement in October than news emerged that Croatia might veto Montenegro's accession unless the country meets a series of Croatian demands.
EU politicians and MEPs were dismayed.

This is not the first time that something like this has happened: The veto rights that member states have on many EU matters have increasingly been used by individual countries in recent years as a means of blackmail and a political weapon, paralyzing the EU in the process.

blocks.caption: EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said in October that Montenegro could become a member of the European Union in 2028Image: Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: DW takes a look at some of the most significant cases, the background to them and what are — in some instances — the serious political consequences of them.
Montenegro: Croatia's eight demands
Montenegro is the most advanced EU candidate country, with a potential accession date of 2028. It has already provisionally closed several of the EU's 33 negotiating chapters.
As of November 23, however, Croatia is blocking the closure of three chapters that have already been negotiated.

Zagreb is demanding, among other things, compensation for former prisoners held in Montenegrin camps during the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s, clarification of the fate of Croatians who have been missing since that time, and more rigorous prosecution of war crimes.

There are also disputes over the precise maritime boundary between the two countries. In addition, Croatia is demanding payment of about €2.4 billion (about $2.6 billion) for assets that belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army, the army of the former Yugoslavia to which both countries belonged before its breakup in the early 1990s.

blocks.caption: Croatia is calling, among other things, for the return of the training ship Jadran, which used to belong to the Yugoslav Royal Navy and was based in Split (now Croatia) before the Yugoslav warsImage: Martin Vas/Depositphotos/IMAGO

blocks.text: Montenegro has already responded to some of Croatia's demands, including those concerning compensation for former prisoners. Others, such as the one relating to the assets of the Yugoslav People's Army, are disputed.

It is clear that Croatia's list of demands is also driven by domestic politics. No government in Zagreb can afford to appear compliant on issues relating to the Croatian War of Independence (1991–95).

Moreover, moderate conservative Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic, who is regularly accused in Croatia of being too pro-EU, can use the dispute to portray himself as a staunch defender of national interests.
Ukraine: Hungarian domestic politics in the name of a minority
After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the EU in June 2022 granted Ukraine and the Republic of Moldova EU candidate status through an accelerated procedure as a gesture of solidarity.
Many EU member states have reservations about Ukraine joining the bloc quickly. Nevertheless, only Hungary, under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, adopted an obstructive stance.

Ostensibly, Hungary's obstruction was about getting Ukraine to improve the rights of the Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia in western Ukraine. Ultimately, however, Orban used the matter for domestic political purposes and as an election campaign issue, portraying Ukraine as a "mafia state."

blocks.caption: A poster for a petition organized by the previous Hungarian government against EU financial aid for Ukraine in March. The slogan reads 'Let's not let Zelenskyy have the last laugh'Image: Denes Erdos/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In an effort to appeal to widespread anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Hungary, the country's new prime minister, Peter Magyar, has also adopted a tough stance on Ukraine.

Nevertheless, Magyar's government lifted several temporary blocks on the opening of new negotiating chapters, among other things after the Ukrainian parliament passed a law in early October strengthening the educational rights of national minorities.
North Macedonia: The never-ending blockade
No EU candidate country has suffered as much or as long from veto politics as North Macedonia: It was granted EU candidate status in 2005 but only began accession negotiations in July 2022.

Greece blocked the start of negotiations for 13 years because it objected to the name "Republic of Macedonia," as the country was previously known, and accused its neighbor of laying territorial claims to the region of Macedonia in northern Greece.
The dispute was settled in 2018 through a compromise that saw the country change its name to the Republic of North Macedonia the following year.
But just as the path to accession negotiations seemed clear, Bulgaria blocked the opening of talks in November 2020.
Bulgaria regards the Macedonian language as a dialect of Bulgarian and disputes the existence of a distinct Macedonian nation.

blocks.caption: A protest in Skopje, the capital of North Macedonia, against making any concessions to Bulgaria in 2022Image: Petr Stojanovski/DW

blocks.text: Here, too, domestic Bulgarian politics is ultimately a factor.
Former Bulgarian President and current Prime Minister Rumen Radev, for example, fueled the escalation with North Macedonia to enhance his political profile.
Serbia: Croatia is not the only country obstructing progress
Although Serbia has been negotiating EU accession since 2014, little progress has been made.
In July, when the country was still led by President Aleksandar Vucic, no less than eight EU member states — including Croatia — opposed opening further negotiating chapters with Serbia.
While the main reservations relate to democratic shortcomings, deficiencies in the rule of law and corruption in Serbia, Croatia also has its own disputes with its eastern neighbor.
These concern the 1991–95 war, including missing persons, war crimes, minority rights and differing interpretations of history. Relations are also strained by nationalist rhetoric on both sides.
EU enlargement: Montenegro on track to join bloc by 2028
Whether the election victory of the Student List in Belgrade in late October after almost two years of anti-government, anti-corruption protests will change this situation is impossible to say.
Albania: Greece threatens to use minority rights as leverage
The EU opened accession negotiations with Albania, which has been an EU candidate since 2014, in July 2022.

Albania could become the bloc's next new member after Montenegro. However, Greece has repeatedly threatened (most recently in June) to block the accession process unless the rights of the Greek minority, particularly relating to property rights, are adequately protected.
An end to the veto system?
In light of all this, Brussels has long been debating a reform of the accession process and the EU veto system.

In early October, the European Commission proposed that decisions to open negotiations with candidate countries be made by qualified majority rather than unanimously. It also proposed that new EU members would be required to give up the right to veto decisions in certain policy areas altogether for a specified period.
The problem with these proposed reforms is that they would themselves have to be adopted unanimously. In other words, any member state could veto the reform.

articles.title: BBC’s preschool shows to be made available in CBeebies hub on Netflix
articles.summary:
Teletubbies, Numberblocks and Hey Duggee among 24 shows to be trialled on world’s biggest streaming service

Teletubbies, Numberblocks and Hey Duggee are among a host of the BBC’s preschool…

blocks.text: Teletubbies, Numberblocks and Hey Duggee are among a host of the BBC’s preschool shows to be made available on Netflix, as the broadcaster battles to arrest a generational shift away from its programming.

In an unprecedented six-month trial, a dedicated CBeebies hub will be set up on the world’s biggest streaming service, with a substantial selection of 24 shows to choose from. It will include some of the BBC’s best-known titles and characters.
BBC executives said the deal was a “win-win”, allowing the corporation to reach more families and handing Netflix a windfall of quality children’s programming.

It marks the BBC’s latest deal with an “off-platform” provider, having already announced plans to make content designed for YouTube. The shows will be available on Netflix globally apart from in China, New Zealand and South Africa.

While parents and children still report appreciating the BBC’s children’s content, a huge shift to global streaming and digital platforms means gen alpha – people born between 2010 and 2025 – are simply not as reliant on the broadcaster as previous generations.

Having a clearly branded home on Netflix will help ensure viewers continue to associate the programming with the BBC, which has lost 2.7 million payers of the £180 annual licence fee since the beginning of the decade.
When the streaming giant has previously snapped up international rights to hit BBC shows, such as The Bodyguard and Peaky Blinders, it has branded the content as a “Netflix Original”.
However, the educationally focused BBC content will now sit alongside some Netflix kids’ content, such as CoComelon, which has come in for criticism over its fast-pacing leading to overstimulation.

With linear broadcast television reaching just a third of children aged four to 15 in an average week last year, down from 54% in 2022, traditional broadcasters are seeking deals to increase the reach of their shows as viewing habits move to streaming.

Meanwhile, the BBC’s iPlayer has been falling behind. More than 90% of children aged three to 16 say they like the services offered by YouTube, Netflix and Disney. Only 65% of child users say they like using the iPlayer.

The CBeebies deal also helps Netflix, which is itself under pressure from its rival Disney, which has a younger audience, and YouTube. Children in the UK aged four to 15 watch the most YouTube of any age group at home across all devices, averaging 61 minutes a day.
Children are now heading to YouTube from the moment they turn on the television. Netflix is close behind, though BBC One remains in the top five of first TV destinations.
The new Netflix deal will also strengthen the argument that anyone watching a streaming service should pay the BBC’s licence fee.

That proposal is expected to be announced by the government later this year, amid growing concerns that the BBC’s current licence fee model will soon mean the broadcaster is unsustainable without radically reducing its output and remit.
after newsletter promotion
The CBeebies hub will be trialled on Netflix for six months from the start of December. Some CBeebies shows have previously featured on the streamer, but the trial marks an unprecedented expansion.

Patricia Hidalgo, the director of BBC children and education, who has previously raised concerns about the lack of culturally relevant content reaching young children, said it was an opportunity to increase “the amount of content that is homegrown and telling British stories to British children”.
The BBC is now engaging in more deals with streamers and digital services, as it seeks to increase commercial income and remain relevant as audiences fragment.

Hidalgo said the trial would provide a “taster” to Netflix subscribers and would be assessed after six months to see if it was helping the BBC reach new audiences and whether they understood it was BBC content.

Anne Mensah, the head of content for Netflix in the UK, said CBeebies held a “special and unrivalled place in the hearts of UK families and we are delighted to bring that love to all our Netflix homes in the UK and beyond”.
Last month, Channel 4 struck a deal to make a range of its programmes, as well as its flagship channel, available on Disney+ in the UK and Ireland from next year.

The deal goes signifcantly further than a partnership struck by ITV and Disney+ last year in which the two companies agreed to share a selection of shows, including Mr Bates vs The Post Office and Lucasfilm’s Andor, on their respective streaming services.

articles.title: China’s media hails Huang’s Nvidia return as it warns over ‘witch-hunts’
articles.summary: State-owned media outlet says reports about CEO’s affair with alleged Chinese spy were ‘malicious’

blocks.text: Chinese media have reacted with glee to the dramatic reinstatement of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of Nvidia, with one commentary warning against future “witch-hunts”.

An article published on Tuesday in the state-run outlet the Global Times said US media reports about Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset were “malicious” and “negatively impacted American public perception of China”.

Huang was reinstated to the US artificial intelligence company on Tuesday, weeks after he was ousted by the board after allegations that he had three affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with employees. But the Nvidia board reinstated him after an intervention from Donald Trump.

The Global Times warned that future “political witch-hunts” against companies and individuals accused of links to Chinese intelligence could take the form of investigations and congressional hearings.
“Certain American media outlets and politicians turned the episode into a Hollywood-style spectacle, complete with gossip, conspiracy theories, and political maneuvering [sic],” it said.
In another article, the influential blogger Niu Tanqin wrote that Huang’s return indicated that the “so-called female spy allegations are complete nonsense”.
Niu also said that China would be flattered by Donald Trump’s suggestion, made in an interview with CNBC, that Huang could be poached by China.
The US president said on Monday that Xi Jinping, China’s leader, described Huang as a “brilliant man” in their recent meeting in Shenzhen, a city in southern China.

Trump said that, despite the national security concerns surrounding Huang’s affair with the alleged China spy Alice Huang – no relation – “the bigger threat would be losing the brainpower of somebody like Jensen”.

Nvidia produces the world’s most advanced semiconductors, which underpin the artificial intelligence sector. US export controls have blocked Nvidia from shipping its most sophisticated models to China in a bid to slow down the country’s AI development. Huang has pushed for looser regulations, arguing that it is better to keep China dependent on US technology rather than spur Chinese innovation.

Trump said he had personally intervened with the Nvidia board, which had previously ruled out reinstating Huang. “I spoke to them, let me put it that way,” Trump told CNBC on Monday. “And I convinced them … I made the deal.”
Huang’s comeback caused Nvidia’s shares to soar on Monday, adding almost $1tn (£763bn) in market value to the company which props up much of the US stock markets.
after newsletter promotion

Senator Tom Cotton, the Republican chair of the intelligence committee, said: “I have warned the administration from the start about communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access. “The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it’s not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back,” he said.
China’s foreign ministry declined to comment on Huang’s reinstatement. The government has consistently denied the espionage allegations, calling them “slander and defamation”.

Several accounts on Chinese social media shared memes and AI-generated videos showing Huang in various revenge scenarios. In one video, shared by an influential blogger, with more than 1.1 million followers, Huang is reimagined in the Arnold Schwarzenegger movie The Terminator, in the famous “I’ll be back” scene.

In another video, Huang is reimagined as Jack Nicholson’s murderous Jack Torrance in the 1980 horror film The Shining. Huang is shown using an axe to destroy a locked bathroom door, terrorising an AI-generated Colette Kress, who was Nvidia’s interim boss, who is cowering behind it. The video ends with an AI-generated “Here’s Jensen!” channelling Nicholson’s famous line, “Here’s Johnny!”, from the movie.
Analysts believe that the saga also demonstrated to Beijing how power works in the US.

“The lesson Chinese policymakers are likely drawing is neither subtle nor complicated: Donald Trump remains the most influential political figure in America and, in many respects, the most consequential variable in the trajectory of US-China relations,” wrote George Chen, a partner at The Asia Group, a consultancy, in a post on Substack.

articles.title: CAS reinstates Senegal as 2025 AFCON champions
articles.summary: The Court of Arbitration for Sport has reinstated Senegal as 2025 AFCON champions, overturning a CAF decision that stripped them of the title. Morocco, previously declared winners, are confirmed…

image.caption: Senegal won the trophy on the field, but Morocco were awarded the trophy after a CAF review of the events of the finalImage: Sebastien Bozon/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Just over eight months after Senegal were stripped of their 2025 African Cup of Nations (AFCON) title, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has announced that Senegal's appeal has been upheld, reinstating them as 2025 AFCON winners. Morocco, who had been declared champions after a Confederation of African Football (CAF) review, has now been confirmed as runners-up.

"The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF, in French)," the CAS statement read.

"The decision rendered by the CAF Appeal Board is set aside and the decision by the CAF Disciplinary Board is reinstated. Consequently, the result obtained at the end of the AFCON 2025 final is confirmed."

The statement continued that it felt "the Referee's decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority" and that his "decision was covered by the ‘field of play’ doctrine."
The decision comes after a closed-doors hearing at CAS' headquarters in Lausanne in early October.

Before the verdict was delivered, Morocco captain Achraf Hakimi posted a message on Instagram saying he would disagree with Senegal being stripped of the title because "its players fought so hard to win."

"I respect the authorities responsible for football, but I firmly believe that what happens on the pitch should be the most important thing of all. Senegal won that Africa Cup of Nations final through their performance, their determination, and the effort of every player, just as every player represents his country. They fought for that title, and no one can erase what those players achieved on the pitch," Hakimi wrote.
"African football needs unity, fairness, and credibility. We cannot keep building our game if decisions like these leave players and fans questioning everything."
An infamous AFCON final

The final was played on January 18, with Senegal winning 1-0 after extra-time. However, the game was thrown into confusion when many Senegal players walked off the pitch following the referee's decision to award Morocco a penalty in the final minutes. Around 15 minutes later, and after furious Senegalese fans had attempted a pitch invasion, the players did return. Morocco's Brahim Diaz inexplicably missed the penalty, sending the game into extra time, which is when Senegal scored the eventual winner.
Just 10 days afterwards, the CAF issued fines worth more than $1 million (€835,000) and banned players from both teams.

Two months later, and after the Senegal team had paraded the trophy to their fans, CAF declared that Senegal had "forfeited" the final by leaving the pitch. CAF then overturned the result, awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory and the title. The Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) denounced the CAF decision and took the case to CAS.
The aftermath had rumbled on for months, with many believing it damaging for African football as a whole.
"If you look at it critically, the value of African football will definitely go down with this," Collins Okinyo, a former CAF media consultant, told DW after the result had been overturned in March.
Why African football is changing the World Cup forever
Impact on future World Cup host
The ruling brings an end to a saga that had cast a cloud over a well-organized tournament in Morocco.

The country is emerging as a major football hub in Africa. Already confirmed as a co-host for the World Cup in 2030, Morocco also hosted the 2026 Women's AFCON and has been hosting the U17 Women's World Cup annually since 2025 and is set to do so until 2029. It is further rumored that the Morocco, along with fellow 2030 World Cup hosts Spain and Portugal, is keen to host the next Club World Cup in 2029 as a form of preparation ahead of the big event in 2030.

Although it has made significant advances in sports infrastructure, not everyone is happy about Morocco's push into the football world. In 2025, there were major protests by Gen Z questioning the country's priorities in light of struggling health and education systems.

articles.title: Meta launches Muse in UK – the AI agent that can do your Christmas shopping
articles.summary: Users can give agents tasks such as booking travel or buying presents, but glitches have been reported

blocks.text: Want to avoid the Christmas shopping hordes? Then let your AI agent do the shopping for you. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta is launching its Muse AI assistant in the UK and is encouraging users to let it loose on your apps – and the high street.

Muse has been a hit in the US and is ranked first and second respectively on Google and Apple’s free app stores, having been downloaded millions of times. However, UK regulators have said they are keeping a close eye on the launch over privacy and consumer protection requirements.

Muse can be used as an app or directly within Meta’s WhatsApp messaging platform. Meta invites users to give their assistant a name, a look and a personality, so they can talk to it as well as assign it tasks such as sending an email, booking travel or buying festive presents.
“From doing the Christmas shopping and searching for a cheaper energy deal, to sorting the school calendar … Muse can get it done for you,” Meta said.

The company acknowledged that handing control of your day-to-day digital life to an AI agent was “an act of trust”. Muse cannot make a purchase or send an email without your permission and will only be connected to apps that you let it join.

The app has no visibility into people’s passwords or payment methods, Meta said, and it does not share your conversations with advertisers. It will ask for your approval before making a purchase or sending an email, while a separate “security agent” checks Muse’s actions against the permissions you’ve granted.

“Think of it as a helping hand for the jobs that pile up, like chasing a refund, renewing car insurance or keeping on top of the school calendar,” Meta said. “To get those jobs done, you can connect Muse to the apps you already use, from your email and calendar to the retailer apps you shop on.”

Meta said it had signed deals with an array of British businesses – including Marks & Spencer, Currys, Sainsbury’s and easyJet – allowing Muse to navigate their websites more easily and to access their apps. If a company does not offer a “connector” app that Muse can visit, the agent will access their website instead.

The Information Commission’s Office and the Competition and Markets Authority said they had been in talks with Meta ahead of the launch about its responsibility to comply with UK laws. The ICO, the UK’s data protection watchdog, said on Tuesday that Meta had committed to a “voluntary monitoring and reporting scheme” with the regulator, while the CMA said talks with Meta had resulted in changes to make the app’s terms and conditions “fairer”.
“We will be closely monitoring this and if we have concerns we will not hesitate to act to protect UK consumers,” said Sarah Cardell, the CMA chief executive.

Reuters reported last week that Meta employees had raised concerns about the app’s performance, including one staff member receiving a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal, an encrypted messaging app. In another example reported by Reuters, Muse delivered a message with random bank account balances in it.
after newsletter promotion

Meta said internal testing was vital for product development and allowed the company to implement safety and privacy protection before releasing anything publicly. It is understood the majority of problems flagged by Reuters related to a bug that has been fixed.

Muse is powered by Muse Spark, Meta’s first model from the company’s “super intelligence” AI lab. In a social media post on Sunday, Meta’s chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang, raised the possibility of humanity losing control over AI systems that are able to improve themselves autonomously.
“It is … hard to imagine a world where humanity maintains control with super intelligence that is 1000x smarter and more capable than humans in every field,” he wrote.

Responding to reports that AI had cracked one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics – the Riemann hypothesis – Wang said the tech industry needed to make progress in the “extremely urgent” areas of AI safety, security and alignment. Alignment refers to ensuring an AI system adheres to human goals and values.

articles.title: Why Iran's medicine supply chain is failing
articles.summary: Pharmacies in Iran are closing, hospital deliveries have stalled and patients are rationing doses or turning to black markets.

image.caption: Iran has faced medicine shortages for years. But the current war is making things worse [FILE 2018]Image: Kyodo News/IMAGO

blocks.text: Ahmad,* 67, visited nearly 20 Tehran pharmacies for the antipsychotic drug chlorpromazine, but left empty-handed.
"When a patient has to go to this many pharmacies just to find an essential drug, you really have to ask who is responsible for supplying medicine," he told DW.

Mitra,* a 37-year-old Tehran resident with diabetes , spent days hunting for insulin. "These are not drugs I can postpone taking or simply give up," she said. "My life depends on regular access to this insulin."
Their ordeal reflects a wider crisis across Iran's health care system.

Along with Tehran residents, DW spoke with an official at Iran's Food and Drug Administration (IFDA) and pharmacy workers in Tehran, Rasht and Mahabad. The interviews were conducted anonymously or using pseudonyms as speaking with foreign media remains dangerous in Iran.
Iran's broken drug supply chain
The official said that Iran's falling currency, along with price controls, has drained domestic drugmaker profits, while unpaid hospital debts have delayed deliveries.
"Add our own hospitals' heavy unpaid debts to distributors, and you can see why distribution has ground to a halt and companies are no longer supplying hospitals," the official said.

"Unless the Plan and Budget Organization makes our currency allocation realistic, banks step in with loans for drugmakers and insurers settle their debts, the Health Ministry's hands will remain tied and this disaster cannot be stopped," the official warned.

blocks.caption: Some patients are being forced to ration supplies [FILE 2024] Image: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: IFDA spokesman Mohammad Hashemi told Iran's semi-official ILNA news agency on November 9 that fewer than 40 of roughly 700 essential drugs faced supply difficulties. However, pharmacists told DW about how difficult it can be to get drugs on shelves.

A pharmacy manager in Tehran said insurance payments are often delayed by months, while drug prices continue to climb. Another pharmacist in the northwestern Mahabad region said distributors demand cash upfront for scarce items.
The insurance delays and shifting rules have pushed some pharmacies to drop contracts or refuse costly insured drugs.

The pharmacist in Mahabad, who prefers to be called Leili,* said that general pharmacies can lack about 40 items, and larger specialty pharmacies stocking chemotherapy and complex treatments can lack over 100, including psychiatric and Parkinson's drugs, and insulin vials.

"Many drugs can no longer be found in the official supply chain at all, such as nimodipine tablets [used to treat certain strokes] or hospital injectable antibiotics that have no substitutes," she said.
Turning to low-quality, black market medicine

As common items like cold medication become scarcer or more expensive, some people are turning to home remedies, she said. She added that for essential medicines like insulin, chronic patients are using smaller doses to preserve supply.
Many of those unable to pay are middle-class customers whom pharmacists cannot easily refer to charities, she said, with elderly and psychiatric patients among the hardest hit.
Leili warned that lower quality seen in some reverse-engineered domestic drugs presents a high risk for cancer, transplant and autoimmune patients.

She added that some families are forced to turn to street markets usually located outside of clinics, which lack cold-chain controls and sell counterfeit medicines or drugs with altered expiration dates.
Another pharmacy manager who asked to be called Khadiv* said scarce medicines can fetch up to 10 times their official price.
Sanctions and blockades
Amid the current conflict with the US, Khadiv said US sanctions, along with border disruptions and the US maritime blockade in the Strait of Hormuz inflate import costs.

In a statement, the US State Department told DW its sanctions follow international law to deny Tehran funds for "destabilizing behavior," stressing the measures allow "broad authorizations and exceptions" for food, medicine and medical devices. It pointed to what it called Iran's "corrupt ruling elite" for not properly allocating resources.

Iranian officials, however, reject that claim. In late summer, Health Minister Mohammad Reza Zafarghandi called US exemption claims "a big lie," saying banking, insurance, flight and shipping sanctions block imports.
Earlier this fall, the IFDA's raw materials chief cited currency, banking, customs and shipping hurdles as the main bottleneck.
DW emailed the Iranian Embassy's media office in Berlin for comment but received no reply.

"Seeing so many people unable to afford their medicine or reach medical centers leaves me with a sense of guilt and helplessness," Khadiv said, adding that lack of access can even lead to patient deaths.
For patients like Ahmad and Mitra, the standoff offers no relief, and every day, the gap between official assurances and what is actually on pharmacy shelves grows harder to ignore.
*Names changed for safety reasons.
When sanctions threaten people's health

articles.title: Democrats hit out at Nvidia and Trump over Huang’s return – US politics live
articles.summary: Possible presidential hopeful Ruben Gallego warns of a ‘bad lesson for corporate America’ while Ro Khanna says ‘rules should apply to everyone’

blocks.text: Democrats criticise Nvidia after Trump's intervention sees CEO Huang resinstated
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO sends a message “that the national security of this country is not as important as your relationship with president Trump”, Democratic senator Ruben Gallego said.

Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993, was ousted by the board after allegations that he had three affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with employees. But the Nvidia board reinstated him after an intervention from the US president.

“We also have to figure out how corporate America doesn’t take a bad lesson from this, and thinks that somehow it’s OK for them to evade national security for the purposes of just selling more,” Gallego, an Arizona Democrat considering a White House campaign, said.

Meanwhile, California representative Ro Khanna wrote on social media that “rules should apply to everyone”, noting: “The rich + powerful, like Jensen, do not get to evade export controls or accountability just because it props up the stock price.”
Huang returned to the company’s HQ in Santa Clara, California, on Monday and received a hero’s welcome, with crowds of employees chanting “Jensen, Jensen, Jensen!”
Donald Trump made up to $15m on his holdings of Nvidia stock after the US chipmaker’s share price soared on the surprise return of Huang.
His return as CEO came despite Huang being subject to several government and internal investigations, shareholder lawsuits and accusations that he’s a national security threat.

Nvidia is one of the most valuable businesses in the world, worth about $4tn, and the entire AI ecosphere relies on it. The company engineers advanced chips used to train AI models and power tech firms such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google.
In other developments:

items: Mike Huckabee, the US ⁠ambassador to Israel, ⁠has cast doubt ​on whether Washington would end its $3.8bn in annual military aid to Israel by the end of this year, as promised by Trump on the day ⁠of this month’s midterm elections. In his surprise announcement as voters headed to the polls on 3 November, Trump said he had made a deal with prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu several months earlier ⁠to stop providing Israel with about $4bn in annual US funding.

Speaking at the US Department of Justice, Trump railed against the commutations of death row inmates’ sentences by California’s governor, Gavin Newsom. Newsom responded by criticizing Trump for “selling” pardons and for demanding the execution of five wrongfully convicted young New Yorkers of color in 1989.

Jimmy Gomez will resign from Congress after a House ethics report released on Monday found “substantial evidence” that the California Democrat had “engaged in sexual misconduct”, including by “making unwelcome sexual advances and sexual contact toward a House staffer”. The 19-page report from the House ethics committee found that Gomez “made unwanted sexual advances” toward a House staffer on two occasions, “including an incident in which he made sexual contact with her and another in which he was ‘forceful’ with her in his congressional office”.
