blocks.text: US preparing to raise tariffs on China and dozens of other countries – report

The US is preparing to raise tariffs on China and dozens of other countries that the Trump administration argues are harming American companies by supporting their own domestic industrial production, the Wall Street Journal reports (paywall) this morning, citing people familiar with the plans.

Per the Journal’s report: “US trade representative Jamieson Greer as soon as this week is expected to unveil the results of a monthslong tariff investigation into the industrial subsidies of China, the European Union and 14 other nations, said the people, who warned the timing could change.

“Greer has said those subsidies and other governmental supports have created excess industrial capacity in the targeted economies, allowing their firms to flood global markets with cheaper goods, undermining US producers.”

As we noted earlier, Nvidia’s freshly reinstated CEO, Jensen Huang, will appear on Capitol Hill next week, where skeptical lawmakers from both parties will grill him over his ties to a woman that some in the intelligence community have said was a spy for China. Huang will also sit for transcribed interviews with the Senate banking committee and House foreign affairs committee, as well as the select committee on the Chinese Communist party and the House intelligence committee. (Here’s our Shrai Popat’s report).

Massachusetts Democrat Elizabeth Warren, the incoming Senate banking chair, has told Politico Playbook: “President Trump insisting that the company should rehire him does not get Mr. Huang or Nvidia off the hook.”
Asked whether Huang’s return changes the investigation, Warren replied without hesitation: “Yes, and not to Nvidia’s benefit.”

“All the excuses of ‘I don’t know what Nvidia is doing now because I’m not there’ will be denied to Mr. Huang,” Warren said, “and Nvidia’s ability to separate itself from a CEO that is under serious investigation over whether [he] has participated in an international scandal of monumental proportions will also have disappeared.”
Huang and Nvidia “together makes very clear the need for a serious, independent investigation”, Warren added.
Three bipartisan bills are ready to go, she outlined:
double quotation markDon’t sell these chips to China. Don’t sell the equipment to make these chips to China, and every chip that leaves the United States should have a tracker on it.

Huang “will have to answer Republican and Democratic members of the Banking Committee”, Warren said, “on why he actively lobbied to send Nvidia’s chips to China and whether Nvidia’s chips have been smuggled to fuel China’s military”. She added: “I’ll be pressing for that. But I won’t be the only one.”
Iran’s chief negotiator and parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf reiterated on Tuesday that Tehran would not hold talks with the United States until Iran’s seven conditions are met.

“Our position remains what we have previously stated: There will be no actions or negotiations until Iran’s seven conditions are met,” Iran’s chief negotiator said in a report carried by the IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency.
He also warned:
double quotation markFurthermore, we are prepared to respond decisively to any hostile moves by the enemy and, should the enemy commit a miscalculation, to shift the geography of the conflict.
Tehran’s conditions include sanctions relief, lifting the US naval blockade of Iranian ports, releasing seized Iranian assets, ending hostilities on all fronts and formally declaring the war over.

It comes as the naval arm of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard said three oil tankers were struck naval mines in strait of Hormuz because they were “in violation of regulations” regarding passage through the waterway.
The Guard’s navy said in a post on Telegram on Monday that the strait “is not a place to test unauthorized routes or to disregard maritime warnings”.
It said the tankers were “engulfed in flames” after hitting the mines despite being under US aerial escort.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said on Tuesday that all three vessels continued their transits and all crew were accounted for.

Donald Trump will take part in a Medal of Freedom ceremony in the Oval Office at 11am ET this morning, it’s closed to press but we’ll let you know if it opens up. Then at 2pm he and the first lady will participate in the Thanksgiving turkey pardoning at the White House, this year featuring turkeys Freedom and Feather. The president will then do a print interview before departing for Palm Beach, where he’ll spend Thanksgiving.

blocks.caption: Rachel Leingang

blocks.text: Rachel Leingang

Juliana Stratton, the incoming Democratic senator from Illinois, said she would support significantly reforming or abolishing the filibuster in order to allow Congress to deliver on the promises they made American voters.

The filibuster means that most successful legislation in the Senate must have 60 supporters instead of a simple majority. Eliminating that requirement is one of several reforms Democrats can act on after they won an unexpected 56-44 majority in the next US Senate, their largest majority in nearly two decades.

Stratton, currently the Illinois lieutenant governor, was a professional mediator before she entered politics. For two decades, she ran a dispute resolution firm, bringing people who did not agree together to find ways to solve problems.

The experience will serve her well in a divided government, she told the Guardian. She welcomes Republicans who want to stand up to Trump and “have a real spine” to work with and Democrats in the US Senate.

“We cannot go in kind of waffling on, ‘Well, we’ll see what we can do, it’s going to be hard.’ That’s the same kind of thing that really turned so many voters off this election cycle – people going in, telling them how hard everything is and that there’s so many hurdles,” Stratton said. “Sure, there are hurdles, but we were elected to do hard things.”
House Democrat expands investigation into Donald Trump Jr's investment firm

A top House Democrat is broadening his investigation into Donald Trump Jr’s venture capital fund 1789 Capital by demanding records from four companies that secured an investment before benefiting from lucrative federal contracts or policies, AP reports.

Representative Jamie Raskin, the ranking member of the House judiciary committee and the panel’s incoming chair, sent letters on Monday evening to the defense contractor Hadrian Automation, vape maker Juul Labs, prediction market platform Polymarket and the online firearms seller GrabAGun.

The Maryland congressman requested that each firm send him two years’ worth of communications with 1789 Capital and other select documents, saying the materials would help him investigate whether president Donald Trump’s eldest son used insider information to orchestrate or anticipate government actions that boosted the companies and his own finances.
US envoy 'not certain' military aid to Israel will end this year as Trump promised

Mike Huckabee, the US ⁠ambassador to Israel, ⁠has cast doubt ​on whether Washington would end its $3.8bn in annual military aid to Israel by the end of this year, as promised by Donald Trump on the day ⁠of this month’s midterm elections.

In his surprise announcement as voters headed to the polls on 3 November, Trump said he had made a deal with prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu several months earlier ⁠to stop providing Israel with about $4bn in annual US funding.
Trump said Israel no longer needed US funds, and ​the issue had been used as a “bad talking point” by ‌his leftwing critics, Reuters reported.
The election that ‌day subsequently saw Democrats, including many who publicly oppose military funding for Israel, win control of both houses of Congress ‌from Trump’s Republicans.

Trump did not provide details or explain how the funding would be halted. The US has a longstanding agreement with Israel, known as a memorandum of understanding, to provide it with $3.8bn a year until 2028 to fund purchases of American-made military equipment.
Congress to grill Jensen Huang over ties with China and Trump’s intervention

blocks.caption: Shrai Popat

blocks.text: Shrai Popat

Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia’s chief executive is “exhibit A” of the “political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration’s big tech and AI policy”, Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland Democrat vying to become the next Senate majority leader, told reporters Monday.

Van Hollen said he intends to focus on Huang’s “efforts to increase and accelerate the export of high-end chips to China, how he’s been accomplishing that, how he’s been getting his way with the administration” when the reinstalled Nvidia CEO appears before the Senate banking committee on 3 December.

It will be one of several appearances on Capitol Hill next week where skeptical lawmakers from both parties will grill Huang over his ties to a woman that some in the intelligence community have said was a spy for China. Huang will also sit for transcribed interviews with the House foreign affairs committee, as well as the select committee on the Chinese Communist party and the House intelligence committee.

“It’s completely hypocritical for the Trump administration, on the one hand, to say the reason we have to take all the brakes off AI development here at home is because China will leap ahead if we don’t,” Van Hollen said. “When in fact, it’s the Trump administration that’s helping China leap ahead.”

Nvidia’s board reinstated Huang after Donald Trump intervened on the executive’s behalf, assuring company leadership that he did not pose a national security risk despite questions surrounding his relationship with Alice Huang, a tech executive of no relation who has been accused of acting as a Chinese asset and routing advanced chips to Beijing via her data center company, Megaspeed.

In an interview with CNBC on Monday, the US president defended his involvement in Huang’s reinstatement, arguing it would be a “bigger threat” for Nvidia to lose Huang’s “brain power” in the AI race. Trump also confirmed that he had provided the board with assurances regarding any national security concerns.
“I spoke to them, let me put it that way. And I convinced them,” Trump said.

articles.title: Mamdani says Nvidia drama shows stock market is overly dependent on AI
articles.summary:
New York City mayor notes ‘massive impact’ on working Americans’ lives when Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO

Zohran Mamdani,…

blocks.text: Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, on Monday weighed in on the corporate turbulence surrounding Nvidia and the chipmaker’s chief executive officer, Jensen Huang, saying he does not think working Americans “signed up for their pensions being tied to the question of … Huang’s fidelity to his marriage”.

The mayor said Huang “had a massive impact”, with Nvidia’s share price dropping dramatically when Huang stepped down as the company’s CEO on 12 November after a reported extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
But on Monday, after he was reinstated after Donald Trump intervened, the California-based company’s value bounced back by 31.5%.

Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori Huang – who have been married since 1985 and have combined assets of about $160bn – have made no statement about their marriage in the wake of the reported affair. But at a news conference on Monday after Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia’s CEO, Mamdani took the opportunity to make a point about wealth.

“We’re speaking about a divorce settlement that has been rumored to be around $81bn,” he said. “That would be the cost of providing universal childcare for every three- and four-year-old in the United States of America for an entire year.”

Alluding to Louis Brandeis, the late US supreme court justice who was at the forefront of an antitrust movement, Mamdani continued: “A lot of this just brings to mind what Justice Brandeis said quite some time ago, which is: We can have democracy. We can have great wealth concentrated in the hands of a few. We cannot have both.”

Mamdani also made a point about the stock market. He said that market was “disproportionately dependent” on stocks related to the artificial intelligence boom powered by Nvidia’s chips. “It cannot help but give you a sense of concern about just how much this technology is now dominant,” he said.

“I do not think that working people across the country signed up for their pensions being tied to the question of Jensen Huang’s fidelity to his marriage,” Mamdani said. “And yet, for many days, that had a massive impact.”

The two-week Nvidia rollercoaster has created some awkward bedfellows around private enterprise and government control. In his inaugural speech at the beginning of the year, Mamadani, a democratic socialist, explicitly advocated for “collectivism” and expansive government intervention in the economy.

Mamdani’s comments on Monday came amid an ambiguous relationship that the mayor fosters with the financial epicenter that is New York City’s Wall Street. Wall Street’s revenue supports Mamdani’s progressive agenda for the city.
Like Mamdani, Trump was among a number of US politicians to weigh in on the fallout of Huang’s reported affair, including whether it was a national security risk.

The president told the Wall Street Journal in an interview published on Monday that he liked getting involved in companies and pointed to the government taking a 10% stake in chipmaker Intel. “If I can help a company that’s got some problems,” Trump said, “I do it.”

Questions surrounded Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), a tech executive who has been accused of acting as a Chinese asset and routing advanced chips to Beijing through her datacenter company, Megaspeed.

US export controls prohibit the sale of advanced AI chips to China. But the Trump administration’s national intelligence director, Jay Clayton, said he suspected China was able to obtain Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips.

articles.title: Colombia: Car bomb attack injures at least 23
articles.summary: The explosion in Villavicencio coincides with the tenth anniversary of a peace accord with FARC guerrillas, casting doubt on Colombia's peace process.

image.caption: A car bomb exploded near the Meta Governor's Office in VillavicencioImage: Mario Toro/AFP

blocks.text: At least 23 people were injured in Colombia on Monday night when a car bomb tore through the central city of Villavicencio, local authorities confirmed on Tuesday.

The explosion occurred at approximately 9:30 p.m. (3:30 a.m. CET Tuesday) in front of the headquarters of the regional government of Meta province and caused severe structural damage to nearby buildings.
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella confirmed the incident and said no deaths had been reported "so far."
Reporters for the AFP news agency said the blast knocked out power across parts of the city center, leaving damaged cars lining nearby streets and ripping open shopfronts.
"The doors were bent in, the windows shattered, some display cases inside broken," said local resident Johan Perez, who owns a hat shop. "We are alive by a miracle."

The Spanish EFE news agency reported that a well-known local restaurant was completely destroyed and suggested that the structural integrity of the government building itself may have been compromised, raising concerns that it could collapse.
Who is behind Villavicencio blast?
The attack has not been publicly claimed by any group but it came on the eve of the 10th anniversary of Colombia's landmark peace accord with FARC guerrillas.
The agreement persuaded the FARC, once Latin America's largest guerrilla army, to lay down its weapons after more than half a century of conflict.
Shortly before Monday's blast, President De la Espriella had denounced the peace accord as a "false peace."

According to the local Caracol radio station, investigators' initial theories point to a FARC commander known as "Antonio Medina" who leads the dissidents' 28th and 39th fronts, known as the "Amazonas Bloc."
Colombia has a new right-wing president
De La Espriella blames 'narco-terrorists'
President De La Espriella, who took office in August and has launched a United States-backed military offensive against armed groups and drug traffickers, blamed "narco-terrorists" for the attack.
"I warn the narco-terrorists responsible: you will answer for every drop of blood you have spilled and every business and property you have destroyed," he wrote on social media.
"We will deploy the full power of the state to hunt you down, dismantle your organizations and take you out." De La Espriella added.
The incident marks the latest violent resurgence of a conflict that has shaken Colombia, the world's largest cocaine-producing nation, over the past two years.
Between January and November, authorities recorded 358 drone strikes, more than one a day, according to a Defense Ministry document obtained by AFP.
Last year, a presidential candidate was assassinated on the campaign trail.

British police said Tuesday that two men have been arrested over a suspected burglary at the Royal Family's Sandringham Estate.
It follows reports that the home of Prince William and Princess Catherine on the vast royal estate was broken into on Monday.

Police said that officers were called Monday evening to reported "suspicious activity" at the address. After a search involving police dogs, drones and a helicopter, two men were arrested on suspicion of burglary and trespassing.
They were being held in custody Tuesday and hadn't been charged.
Police said that "the property was unoccupied at the time of the incident."

Anmer Hall, which has 10 bedrooms, was a wedding present to the couple from the late Queen Elizabeth. William and Kate have used the house at Sandringham Estate in Norfolk, about 170 kilometres north of London, as a country residence on weekends and holidays.
The couple and their three children spend most of their time at Forest Lodge in Windsor, west of London, which they have described as their "forever home."
Previous security incidents
Intruders have breached royal properties several times over the years.

In October 2024, burglars broke into the Windsor Castle estate west of London and stole a pickup truck and a quad bike from a farm building. King Charles and Queen Camilla weren't at Windsor Castle at the time.
A police officer is shown on a church lane Tuesday following a robbery in Anmer, Norfolk. (Martin Pope/Getty Images)

Three years earlier, a man armed with a crossbow was detained on the castle grounds. Jaswant Singh Chail was later sentenced to nine years in prison after admitting he had been encouraged by a chatbot to kill Queen Elizabeth.

In 1982, intruder Michael Fagan managed to sneak into the Queen's private chambers while she was in bed. Elizabeth spent 10 minutes chatting with the burglar before raising the alarm when he asked for a cigarette.
Fagan was sent to a psychiatric hospital, then released and was later jailed for unrelated criminal offences.

items: When Aline Chrétien discovered an intruder at 24 Sussex Drive

blocks.text: As well, there was a security incident earlier this year at Sandringham when Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, the former prince, was allegedly threatened by a masked man while walking his dogs.

A court case for the 39-year-old man who was charged in connection with the incident is ongoing. Andrew, who was stripped of his royal titles and removed from his longtime Windsor Castle residence, now lives at Marsh Farms on the Sandringham estate.

Anmer Hall, a Georgian country house, is shown in 1973. Built in 1802, the property became part of the Royal Family's Sandringham Estate in 1898. (Leonard Burt/Central Press/Hulton Archive/Getty Image)
The latest incident came as William visited Prime ‌Minister Andy Burnham at the British leader's office at 10 Downing Street.

While the British royals often mingle with political leaders and government ministers at formal occasions, visits to Downing Street, ​the official residence of British leaders since 1735, are less frequent.
The pair were said to have met for about an hour, discussing issues like homelessness.
With files from CBC News

articles.title: Sotto raises concerns over LGBT content in Grade 1 books
articles.summary: Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente “Tito” Sotto III on Tuesday raised concerns regarding content related to lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) people supposedly being mentioned in books…

blocks.text: Published November 24, 2026 10:15pm

Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente “Tito” Sotto III on Tuesday raised concerns regarding content related to lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) people supposedly being mentioned in books for Grade 1 students.
This was brought up during the Senate plenary deliberations on the proposed P915.49 billion budget of the Department of Education (DepEd) and its attached agencies for fiscal year 2027.
During the session, Sotto flashed a photo of a Grade 1 textbook supposedly promoting an LGBT agenda.

“Some of us are concerned because masyado maaga ito para sa mga kabataan, sa elementary (it’s too early for those in elementary to be exposed to this). This debate has been going on for quite a while. We have people, I understand, advocating for both sides; you know, it's understandable. We have many friends on that particular side,” he said.
“But DepEd has to draw a line. Hindi ba masyadong mababaw ang pang-unawa ng mga elementarya para ituro kaagad ito nang ganito,” he added.
(But the DepEd has to draw a line. Isn’t the level of understanding of elementary students too limited for this to be taught to them so soon?)
Sotto said that he has nothing against the ideologies of the LGBT, but he is simply asking if lessons on LGBT should really be taught in schools.
He called on the DepEd to instead focus on subjects teaching kids respect and kindness to others, and how to prevent them from using illegal drugs.
He also suggested that the agency come up with books concentrating on anti-bullying, financial literacy, mental wellness, as well as improving learners’ reading capabilities.
“You know, siguro dapat doon ang concentrate talaga ng DepEd (DepEd should concentrate on these)--to build student resilience, emotional awareness, and mindful exercises,” Sotto said.

“Palagay ko ‘yun ang mas magandang pag-aksyahan natin ng mga libro kesa sa ganito na controversial ano because merong mga Catholic groups, Christian groups, even Muslim groups that are not in favor of having this in the elementary,” he continued.

(I think that’s a better way to use books instead of touching on controversial topics because there are Catholic groups, Christian groups, even Muslim groups that are not in favor of having this in the elementary.)

Budget sponsor Senator Bam Aquino, in response, said that topics on mental health awareness, GMRC, financial literacy, and anti-drug abuse are already being tackled in the schools at different grade levels.
“I'm sure the Secretary, upon your interpellation today, will check again the proper grade levels for these topics, Mr. President,” Aquino said.
Education Secretary Sonny Angara is in the session hall during the deliberations on DepEd’s proposed 2027 budget. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Mortgage delinquency rate up 31% in third quarter: Equifax report
articles.summary: Equifax Canada's third-quarter consumer credit trends report says the national 90-plus day mortgage delinquency rate — defined as missed payments three months in a row — reached 0.32 per cent, the…

image.caption: Houses are pictured in Vancouver on April 4, 2024. Mortgage delinquencies are on the rise in Canada, especially in B.C. and Ontario. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: Business

Equifax Canada's third-quarter consumer credit trends report says the national 90-plus day mortgage delinquency rate — defined as missed payments three months in a row — reached 0.32 per cent, the highest since the credit agency started tracking the metric in 2013.
Mainly pushed higher by missed payments in Ontario and B.C.
A new report suggests there's growing stress among homeowners, with some struggling to keep up with monthly mortgage payments as interest rates rise again.
That's up 31.1 per cent year-over-year, mainly pushed higher by missed mortgage payments in Ontario and British Columbia.
"That's the highest we've seen, particularly for Ontario. And it's still going up," Rebecca Oakes, Equifax Canada's vice-president of advanced analytics, said in an interview.
"That's the biggest concern for us."
The Equifax data echoes the findings of a recent TD report, which showed Ontario's mortgage arrears have nearly tripled from pre-pandemic levels to approach their 2008 financial crisis peak.
"This reflects elevated mortgage balances and greater sensitivity to borrowing costs," wrote TD economist Maria Solovieva in the report published last week.
What the new 2.5% interest rate means for Canadians

Growing pressure on households comes as the Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 2.5 per cent last month for the first time in more than three years, amid concerns that higher energy prices could spill into broader inflation.
The move prompted the big banks to raise their prime rates, which are used to set interest rates on a range of loans including variable-rate mortgages.
Equifax estimates about 1.4 million Canadians have a variable-rate mortgage out of a total 9.1 million homeowners.

Another 1.3 million consumers also have a home equity line of credit balance of more than $50,000. Every quarter-point rate hike adds roughly $860 million a year in interest on variable-rate mortgages, the company estimates.

items: Higher mortgage costs set to depress already 'bleak' housing market

blocks.text: Oakes suspects mortgage delinquencies will continue to rise in the coming months, depending on changes to interest rates.
"If interest rates stay relatively flat from this point on, I'd expect to see it ease off in the middle of next year," she said.
But if more hikes come in, "it's just going to put additional pressure."

The central bank is expected to make its last rate decision of the year on Dec. 9. Financial market odds for a quarter-point rate hike sat at 63 per cent as of Monday afternoon, according to LSEG Data & Analytics.
Oakes says first-time homebuyers and younger Canadians may bear the brunt of rising rates because they tend to carry a higher-balance mortgage.
Still, she says mortgage delinquencies overall are less than one per cent.
Buyers or renters: Who ends up richer?
"It's quite small, you know, from that standpoint, but of course it knocks on to other types of credit, like credit cards, auto loans," Oakes said.
"That's where those individuals miss the payments first rather than on the mortgage itself."
Credit card balances reached $136.2 billion in the third quarter, up 4.82 per cent from a year earlier, the Equifax data showed.
Overall, total Canadian consumer debt was $2.74 trillion in the third quarter, up 4.68 per cent from a year ago.

articles.title: Heat waves are getting so bad that even this cactus can't survive
articles.summary: Despite evolving for millennia to thrive in the blazing Sonoran Desert, the iconic saguaro cactus is struggling to survive escalating heat waves.

image.caption: Desert Botanical Garden lab manager Ali Schuessler gathers data on saguaro cacti at South Mountain Park and Preserve in Phoenix, Ariz., on July 14, 2026. (Rebecca Noble/Reuters)

blocks.text: Science
Despite evolving for millennia to thrive in the blazing Sonoran Desert, the iconic saguaro cactus is struggling to survive escalating heat waves.
Nighttime temperatures mess with cactus's key adaptation, hotter El Niños kill baby cacti
The cactus seen in countless Hollywood westerns and on Arizona licence plates can tower 40 feet (12 metres) or higher and live 150 years or more.

Before 2020, about one to two per cent of saguaro cacti died each year, according to researchers at the Desert Botanical Garden in Phoenix, one of the hottest zones in saguaro country. But as stretches of extreme heat buffeted Arizona, the mortality rate in the city that researchers attribute just to heat rose to four per cent in 2021. And then to seven per cent in 2023.
The heat-related death rate has since recovered, said the Botanical Garden’s research director Kevin Hultine, but only to four per cent, leaving him worried about the viability of the iconic cactus.

Heat waves were once relatively small, intermittent episodes 6 ½ decades ago. With climate change, they've grown into supersized, long-lasting and globe-spanning weather events that Reuters has dubbed "heat storms."
A dead saguaro cactus lays near a healthy one at South Mountain Park and Preserve in Phoenix on July 20, 2026. (Rebecca Noble/Reuters)

The sustained heat can enfeeble the cactus in many ways — by damaging its skin, which can impair the plant’s food production and expose it to infection, or by evaporating away its water, causing it to sag and collapse.
Among the changes of recent decades is that nocturnal heat storms now often blanket the desert.

The saguaro and other cacti and succulents evolved to conduct a critical photosynthesis step not in the dangerous heat of the day but in the protective cool of the night. At daybreak, the saguaro’s tough outer skin tightens its pores, known as stomata, massively restricting evaporation during the hot day.

But with its pores constricted, the saguaro can absorb hardly any carbon dioxide, hindering its ability to generate nutrients. So, it waits for ​sundown. As temperatures fall at night, the cactus opens its microscopic pores, taking deep drafts of vital carbon dioxide.

Then, enzymes transform the carbon dioxide into a form that the cactus can store until sunrise. At dawn, different enzymes release the stored CO2, allowing the rest of the photosynthesis process to turn it into food.
But there’s a catch. Nocturnal heat can disrupt the work of the nighttime enzymes.
Effectively, a hot night can deprive the saguaro of its daily bread.
A close-up of the ribs of a dead saguaro cactus at South Mountain Park and Preserve in Phoenix, Ariz., on July 20, 2026. (Rebecca Noble/Reuters)
What’s more, hot nights can also evaporate more of the saguaro’s internal water.

It’s the damage from such intense heat that researcher Ali Schuessler studies on the saguaro that grow not far away on South Mountain Park and Preserve, a hilly area overlooking the city. If the temperatures stay hot enough for long enough, saguaros can lose much of their internal water to evaporation. The saguaro needs its internal water to stay rigid, so too much water loss can cause the cactus to buckle and ⁠topple.

"I’ll never forget how shocked I was the first time one of them fell over, and our horticulture team was cutting it up and feeling the inside of the plant, and how hot it was," she recalled. The saguaro was as hot as "your tea or your coffee."
'A relic'
The saguaro’s fate is likely to unfold across decades, because it is a slow species. It grows slowly; it can live as long as 200 years, though 150 is more common; and it reproduces very slowly.

While an adult saguaro can hold a thousand gallons of water, a ​year-old saguaro is only about a quarter inch tall (two-thirds of a centimetre). This means the summer heat can kill it by simply drying it out.
How these illegal, endangered cacti ended up at Montreal’s Botanical Garden
In the northern Sonoran Desert, El Niño often provides something critical for baby saguaros: plentiful winter rains that allow the cactus to soak up enough water to survive the brutal summer.

But the last El Niño to bring along a cactus baby boom was a "super" El Niño in 1982-83. Since then, says research director Hultine, El Niños have often sent heavy rains, but they have also been accompanied by more heat storms and heat waves.
Schuessler fears for the saguaro’s long-term viability: "Even if these guys can exist out on the landscape for a long period of time, ⁠if they can’t reproduce, then they’re done for."
Today, another super El Niño to rival the one from the 1980s has formed over the Pacific. But because of the increasing heat storms and heat waves, Hultine is not hopeful.
The area’s saguaros, he says, are "effectively a relic."

articles.title: Chinese police contacted members of WeChat group after they discussed Melbourne vigil for HungryPanda rider
articles.summary:
Several members of the group chat set up after the alleged murder of Feng Jianming say they or their parents were called by police from their home towns in China

  • Get our

blocks.text: Chinese police have contacted several people who were part of a WeChat group that discussed attending a Melbourne vigil for Feng Jianming, the HungryPanda food delivery rider allegedly murdered earlier this month.

At least three members of the group set up after Feng’s death said they were contacted, raising concerns that Chinese authorities may have been alerted to discussions about the protest activity either automatically or manually by the Chinese-owned messaging and social app.
Feng was allegedly stabbed to death near Queen Victoria market on the evening of Friday 6 November after he and another rider confronted a man who was allegedly tampering with their bikes.

Angry members of the WeChat group set up in the immediate aftermath volunteered to host a vigil for the 49-year-old rider at the State Library of Victoria the following day, amid broader concerns about the treatment of riders by the company.

The group’s chat history, seen by the Guardian, shows that by Wednesday at least three members had told the group their parents or themselves had been called by police officers from their home towns in China asking about their involvement with the vigil. The group, which by then had more than 400 members, was disbanded the following day after participants expressed fears about the police calls.
Members of the chat group declined to speak on the record, citing safety concerns.
HungryPanda, founded in the UK, targets the Chinese expatriate market in 10 countries. In Australia, it operates in nine cities, including Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Adelaide.

The Melbourne incident mirrored an event in February when HungryPanda riders in Sydney were contacted by police from China after a WeChat discussion about a proposed strike over wages on lunar new year’s eve.
More than half the WeChat group’s 155 members left and the strike was abandoned after the calls from police, which were first reported by the ABC.
Joy Wang, a former HungryPanda rider who was in the February group chat, said she received four police calls from her home town in Henan province.
Wang said the police seemed unaware the protest was in Sydney. When she explained this, they threatened her with reprisals if she went back to China, she said.
“They said, ‘You better not attend the protest, or we could go after you when you return to China’,” Wang said.

Jack*, who quit HungryPanda two years ago and now runs his own business in eastern China, said he joined the February WeChat group to show support to his former colleagues. He received three calls from police in his home town and was told not to take part in the strike.

blocks.caption: HungryPanda food delivery rider Feng Jianming was allegedly stabbed to death after he and another rider confronted a man who was allegedly tampering with their bikes. Photograph: PR IMAGE/Supplied by Go Fund Me

blocks.text: Jack then quit the group chat. “I’m currently in China, there are things I need to consider,” he said.

Kitty Lu, global spokeswoman for HungryPanda, said the company had no responsibility for riders being contacted by Chinese police. The company was privately owned and independently operated, with funding from private and institutional investors in Europe and North America, she said.
Wang said the group members in Australia who were called by police had registered with WeChat under their Chinese mobile numbers.
She believed the use of keywords such as “strike” in the chat may have been the trigger for the messages to be transmitted to the Chinese authorities.

Jeffrey Knockel, a senior research fellow at the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab, agreed. He and his colleagues studied a 2016 wage protest in Jiangsu province and found the phrase “industrial strike across the city” in the organisers’ group chat activated an automated mechanism on WeChat.

He suggested something similar may have happened in the Australian cases. Knockel also argued that WeChat may have flagged the group chat to a Chinese government organisation that would have then traced the riders’ details on China’s family registration system, known as hukou, and instructed local police to contact them.

WeChat has previously stated that the data of foreign users is stored in Singapore, beyond the reach of Chinese authorities, but Knockel said that if one member of a group registered their account with a Chinese number, the whole chat could be monitored by Chinese authorities.
after newsletter promotion
WeChat did not respond to a request for comment.

Kevin Slaten, who leads the China Dissent Monitor at the US-based thinktank Freedom House, also thought the February calls might have been triggered by WeChat, given a rise in the number of labour disputes over wages in China during 2025 and early 2026.
“[The Chinese authorities may have] just assumed that these workers were in this wave of wage protests … not knowing initially that they weren’t physically located in China,” Slaten said.

But as the security apparatus was under direction to pay special attention to wage protests, the police may have persisted in warning riders to halt their action, even after learning they were overseas, he said.

The executive director of China Labor Watch, Qiang Li, has documented several cases of Chinese workers abroad being contacted by Chinese authorities after using WeChat to discuss industrial action. However, these workers were usually working for projects by China’s state companies.
Li said Chinese police had “overreacted” in the HungryPanda case but it was still alarming for Australia.

“Today we see these riders being called by Chinese police,” he said. “We could then see cases of anyone who uses WeChat, including Australian enforcement officials, their families, or anyone related to China, to be surveilled through this system.”

The home affairs department said it could not comment on operational matters but a spokesperson said it was “unacceptable for any foreign government to target members of our community to prevent individuals exercising their fundamental rights and freedoms in Australia”.

blocks.caption: A memorial for Feng Jianming in Melbourne earlier this month. Photograph: Jay Kogler/AAP

blocks.text: “Acts of harassment, assault, unwanted surveillance, intimidation, coercion or other threatening behaviour may constitute criminal offences.”
The opposition home affairs spokesman, Jonathon Duniam, called on the government to do more to address the potential use of WeChat for surveillance.

“The Coalition has raised serious concerns about WeChat’s links to the Chinese Communist party, its censorship practices and its potential use for surveillance, yet the Albanese government has not done enough to address these risks or ensure proper transparency and accountability from the platform,” he said.

In 2023, a Senate inquiry into foreign interference recommended banning WeChat on government devices and establishing a national security technology office to monitor “high-risk” social media groups, including WeChat.
The government said only that it “noted” these recommendations.
The Chinese embassy in Canberra declined to comment on the HungryPanda allegations.

articles.title: Guardian Essential poll: Albanese’s disapproval rating hits highest level as problems mount for Labor
articles.summary:
Australians also turn against AI datacentres, with nearly half saying they don’t want one near their home

  • Get our

blocks.text: Anthony Albanese’s approval ratings have nosedived in the latest Guardian Essential poll, with the prime minister reaching his highest level of disapproval after his net popularity plummeted 10 points in just a month.

Australians have also turned strongly against AI datacentres, with nearly half of the country saying they don’t want one near their home. Women, older people and One Nation and Greens supporters are among the most likely to reject living near a datacentre.

This month’s Guardian Essential poll, of 1,087 people taken last week, found a tightening political horse race amid mounting political problems for the Labor government. Labor and One Nation remain deadlocked, both with a primary vote of 26%, each having registered a slight dip since both last month recorded 28%. The Coalition’s fortunes have improved slightly, moving to 25%, up from last month’s 23%, while the Greens are on 13%.

The biggest shift in November’s poll is a sudden collapse in the approval ratings for the prime minister. Just 32% of Australians approved of his job performance, down from 38% last month, while simultaneously 60% of people disapproved of Albanese, up from last month’s 56%.
That’s a net approval rating of minus-28, a 10-point fall since October.

Albanese’s approval rating has never been lower, and his disapproval rating has never been higher, since becoming prime minister. Even after ferocious criticism and scrutiny of the government after the Bondi terror shooting last December, Albanese recorded a 39% approval and 53% disapproval in January.

The collapse in Albanese’s personal ratings comes as cost-of-living pressures continue to bite the government, with scrutiny on Labor’s spending priorities and economic record amid high petrol prices and rising interest rates. Albanese has also come under personal attack from opponents over budget decisions, comments on podcasts and grants funding. The poll was taken last week, while Albanese was overseas at the Cop31 climate conference and international summits in Asia.

blocks.caption: Was the Quad meeting at Asean summit a foreign policy success for Australia? – video

blocks.text: “No one wins popularity points on the global stage, particularly when living costs are high. But worse for the PM was his proximity to the dysfunction that global affairs has become, with Cop collapsing and then playing second fiddle at Yalta 2.0,” said Peter Lewis, the chair of Essential Media.
“A chance for a break and a reset can’t come fast enough for him.”
The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, recorded a 35% approval and 42% disapproval, which has remained largely unchanged for several months.
Essential also probed Australians’ views on datacentres, finding a significant negative shift in sentiment around the AI factories.
after newsletter promotion
Following a major rise in opposition to datacentres at the American midterm elections, Essential found only 23% of Australians would support having one near their home, with 48% against.

That compares to 28% in favour and 37% opposed in July, the last time Essential asked this question. In just four months, Australians’ support for living near a datacentre has swung 16% to the negative.

“The deterioration in support for datacentres follows successful community campaigns against local developments, as well as a string of AI-related job cuts. The datacentre becomes an avatar for all the unresolved issues around the regulation and scale of this technology,” Lewis said.

Asked for their major concerns about datacentres, the most commonly cited worry was around impacts on energy demand and electricity prices (61% of people), local water supply (54%) and impact on the environment (39%). Some 38% of people voiced general worries about the growth of AI.

Broken down by demographic, women (55% oppose) were much less likely than men (40% oppose) to support living near a datacentre. Views get more negative as Australians get older, with 57% of over-55s against living near one, compared to 37% of 18-34s and 47% of 35-54s.
Greens (59% oppose) and One Nation (53% oppose) supporters were far more negative on datacentres than Labor and Liberal voters (both 42% oppose).

articles.title: The Nvidia case is just the latest episode of Trump disregarding intelligence
articles.summary:
Trump’s reaction to sensitive information that contradicts his worldview mirrors his conduct towards war with Iran

Donald Trump’s unwillingness to heed warnings of suspected Chinese…

blocks.text: Donald Trump’s unwillingness to heed warnings of suspected Chinese penetration of the tech giant Nvidia follows a pattern of the US president ignoring sensitive intelligence that contradicts his world view.

Trump disregarded repeated information that the company’s co-founder, Jensen Huang, was having an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy that threatened to undermine Washington’s geo-strategically vital goal of pipping China for global supremacy in the artificial intelligence race.

The woman, Alice Huang – no blood relation of Jensen – was also responsible for buying $4.8bn worth of Nvidia’s highly sensitive AI chips in her capacity as head of a Singapore-based technology company, Megaspeed. The chips were then diverted to China, despite US export restrictions forbidding such sales to a country Washington regards as a key strategic adversary.

The president was inactive even after Marco Rubio, the secretary of state and national security – and one of the administration’s renowned “China hawks” – repackaged the intelligence into a classified report last May warning of the geopolitical risks posed by the relationship.

“It’s clear that the White House was warned, had adequate opportunities to take action against what was an emerging and then eventually very clear chip diversion network that was emerging under Megaspeed and other Southeast Asian offshore data farms – and it just failed to act,” said Julia Curlee, a former Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) officer who specialized in the Middle East and China and also worked on the White House national security council during Trump’s first presidency.
“It’s the latest episode of the president ignoring or not believing the intelligence that’s being provided to him.”
Despite the intelligence concerns raised by his conduct, Huang was reinstated as Nvidia’s chief executive on Monday following pressure from the White House and the company’s shareholders.

Trump’s behaviour over the Nvidia affairs mirrors his conduct towards the war with Iran, Curlee argues, where he pressed ahead with military actions despite being forewarned of potential complications.

Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran contradicted advice that the country’s Islamic regime had the resilience to withstand attempts to topple it and was likely to retaliate by closing the strait of Hormuz – predictions that were subsequently borne out.

Trump’s dismissal of intelligence warnings in both cases recalls his comments at a 2018 summit with Vladimir Putin when he openly sided the Russian president over US intelligence agencies, who had assessed that Russia had interfered in the 2016 presidential election.

His indifference to intelligence work and the professionals who perform it appears to surpass that of previous administrations, even those who were accused of deliberately politicizing the practice – an accusation leveled at George W Bush following the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

“There are other administrations that have ignored or or tried to politicize intelligence but I think the Trump administration stands alone in how little it seems to regard the intelligence analysis prepared to help the president make decisions,” said Curlee.

“The best example of this is the run-up to the war in Iran, where the administration just truly shut out the warnings which have been there and were provided for many years about what the Iranians would do in the case of a war.”

Trump’s administration has also fired agents for providing intelligence assessments at odds with the president’s own statements. Last year, Lt Gen Jeffrey Kruse, the head of the defense intelligence agency, was dismissed over a report that contradicted Trump’s claim that Iran’s nuclear sites had been “obliterated” by US strikes carried out in June 2025.

“What makes them really different from, say, the Bush administration, is that even that administration did not publicly fire officers when they didn’t provide information the president wanted to hear,” said Curlee, who also served on the White House national security council under Trump and Joe Biden.
“I feel pretty strongly that the fault of the Iran war lies at this refusal to listen to the intelligence community.”

Curlee said the Chinese acquisition of the Nvidia chips compared in strategic significance to the case of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, a US couple who were executed after being convicted of passing on atomic secrets to the Soviet Union in the early years of the cold war. That made official indifference to the intelligence discovery all the more remarkable, she argued.

“This is a technology at the heart of the strategic competition with our primary competitor in the world, and at an industrial scale, they managed to divert chips from our leading hardware company,” she said.

“It’s a terrible thing that’s occurred and we can’t undo that. But uncovering it and stopping it was done at least over a year ago. If the policymaker then refuses to do their to do their job, there’s nothing the intelligence community can do about that.”
The administration’s stance has drawn further scrutiny by deciding not to provide a “defensive briefing” to Jensen Huang about the discovery.

“Before public accusations and scandals, it used to be accepted practice for someone to pull the American target aside for a man-to-man chat – to tell him to think with the head between his shoulders,” said Fulton Armstrong, a former CIA analyst specializing in Latin America who also has experience in Taiwan.

“The chat might even include discussion of feeding the foreigner some disinformation. It seems that four years of Trump first presidency, four years of do-nothingism with Biden, and now almost two years of Trump II have so deeply changed the intel community that practical solutions are no longer allowed.”
No explanation has been provided for the failure to warn Huang – thus allowing him to continue his relationship with Alice Huang. He was also allowed to maintain his already close access to Trump.

Curlee said it was a “policy decision [rather than] an intelligence decision.” She added “It is to me a very unusual suspect decision to let something like this go on for as long as it apparently did, without at minimum protecting this US citizen, who is the object of of a Chinese spy operation.”

Fevered speculation has swirled over whether Alice Huang may have been part of a “honey trap” operation set by China’s intelligence services to lure Jensen Huang into a close business relationship that would entice him into vast amounts of Nvidia’s coveted chips to a company which would them to pass them to China, subverting American law.

China’s sprawling Ministry of State Security [MSS] is believed to use the technique, which most western intelligence agencies publicly insist they do not use, on the grounds that is unethical and potentially counterproductive, because it often depends on blackmail.

But analysts doubt that it occurred in this instance. Alice Huang, they suggest, could have disclosed the relationship to Chinese agents after it began because she was legally obliged to do so under China’s catch-all intelligence law, which legally obliges the country’s citizens to “cooperate” with security services on matters defined as “national security”. That term has a much broader definition under China’s laws than in most western countries, and can cover commercial and economic development issues.
Frank Montoya, a retired Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) agent who specialized on China, said a straightforward “honey trap” was unlikely.

“I don’t think that it was it was mapped out specifically where the MSS officer said we’re going to find this person and we’re going to set her up for business and then target her against against the CEO of [Nvidia],” he said.

“There was a confluence of opportunities. She’s very ambitious, very smart and she has this idea, and doesn’t necessarily brings it to the MSS, but is talking to somebody else. She has connections in the party, and she’s talking to somebody else, and then somebody else talks to the MSS and says, ‘hey, let’s see if we can take advantage of that’.”

He added: “This was a multi-billion dollar purchase [of Nvidia chips]. There’s no way the MSS alone can fund that. They’re going to need somebody higher up [in the Chinese communist party] to not only approve that but to provide the money when the deal is made.”
The operation, Montoya said, bore the hallmarks of the Chinese espionage approach, which he described as “whole of government” and lacking the “clandestinity” of traditional spy craft.

Alice Huang would have drawn the attention of US intelligence agencies through Megaspeed’s mass purchase of Nvidia chips, and because it rented out services from its Singapore data centers to Chinese AI companies, Curlew argues.

The intimate nature of her relationship with Jensen Huang, and her links to Chinese intelligence is thought to have been discovered through surveillance of her phone, almost certainly carried out by the National Security Agency.

Trump has dismissed the case’s importance, saying he does not believe US national security was threatened and telling Fox News: “We spy on China. They spy on us.” He later told reporters that he raised the matter only briefly when he met China’s president, Xi Jinping, at last week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) gathering Shenzhen.
It is an attitude Curlee lamented as disdainful of intelligence as a whole.

“We are spending tens of billions of dollars and people put their lives in jeopardy to collect information at great personal risk so that our leaders have decision-advantage, the ability to anticipate crises around the corner and can respond to foreign threats,” she said. “If the president can’t be bothered to listen to his intelligence community then what is what is the point of it all?”

articles.title: Days out from the Victorian election, nine datacentre projects await approval. What will their fate be?
articles.summary:
While parties have come out with policies on where datacentres can be built, not all are clear on whether they apply retrospectively

  • Get our

blocks.text: Days out from the Victorian state election, the fate of nine datacentre projects remains uncertain, with some companies confident they will be able to get their projects across the line after Saturday.

There are nine datacentre projects currently awaiting approval according to the ministerial permits register, including the West Footscray expansion of NextDC’s M3 datacentre, which Guardian Australia reported has faced delays due to community blowback.
Other companies seeking approval for new datacentres include ZerraDC, HyperDC, GreenSquareDC, and Stockland.

The GreenSquareDC proposal for a $1.5bn, 240MW datacentre encompassing more than 105,000 sq metres of Spotswood in Melbourne’s inner west has faced strong opposition from locals similar to that observed in other suburbs around the country.

The proposal was lodged with the minister for planning at the end of July this year, but as with the other projects, it did not get approval before the government went into caretaker mode before the election.
A spokesperson for GreenSquareDC said the proposed development was on a long-vacant site in an established industrial precinct in Spotswood, and the company was proud of its proposal.
“We’ll work constructively with whichever government Victorians elect, and we’ll keep engaging with the Spotswood community throughout the process.”

Locals, however, have mobilised, with a petition with more than 4,400 signatures, and a dedicated website that encourages residents to contact the current planning minister and outlines the various policies on datacentres held by candidates in the Williamstown electorate.
The policies
Last month, after launching the Labor policy in September, the Victorian planning minister, Sonya Kilkenny, released a statement of expectations for applications submitted on or after 23 September.
It includes that datacentres must be built away from homes, schools, and childcare centres, and that they must be designed and located to minimise impact on residential communities.

Developments would be prohibited from residential zones, or within 150m of accommodation, education centres or hospitals, as well as green wedge zones (areas preserved for housing or agriculture), rural zones, or urban growth zones.

Exceptions on the latter are made if it is within 5km of a powerline or substation operating at 66,000 volts, or most of the electricity is supplied from either a renewable energy facility or a battery energy storage system.
Developers will be required to display prominent signage onsite and publish detailed application documentation online.
A spokesperson for the Coalition said datacentres would not be built in residential areas, next to residential areas, or in the green wedge.

“Datacentres will be an important part of Victoria’s future,” the spokesperson said. “They drive investment, create skilled jobs and build the sovereign capability our state needs in a digital economy.”
There would be designated datacentre precincts distanced from where people live, and clear guidelines on where they can and cannot be built, the spokesperson said.
“That means communities can have confidence their neighbourhoods are protected, and investors can have confidence about where to build.”
The Liberal policy does not outline whether the plans apply retrospectively, and makes no statement on power requirements.

The Victorian Greens have a policy of a moratorium on new datacentre developments “until communities have actually had an opportunity to consider the risks and benefits, and create strong laws to protect people and the planet over big tech profit”.
after newsletter promotion

The party’s policy also calls for compensation for affected communities, reverting the fast-track approval process to give communities a greater say, and ensuring datacentres are 100% renewables-powered.
One Nation’s policies call for a ban on new datacentres on agricultural land, as well as a call for full community impact assessments before approval.
The party has also said there will be no retrospective carve-outs, so residents living next to a proposed or expanding datacentre will have the same rights as those living near new developments.
The party has also outlined that datacentres would need to be at an undefined distance from homes.
Developers confident ahead of the election

NextDC chief executive, Craig Scroggie, said in a shareholder update in late October that despite the issues with power supply to the datacentre, he had no reason to believe the expansion would not be approved after the election.
“Even with the revised changes to planning guidelines, they do not apply to existing applications that are already being considered by the planning minister.”

“This caretaker period will ultimately result in a new government being appointed [and a] new minister. We would therefore take the conservative view that given what we understand currently about the government’s approval processes and the upcoming election that the time we would be able to restart that [would be] February or later, depending on the election.”
Sean Brown, a West Footscray resident and Citizens of Tottenham member, told Guardian Australia last month the community would make its voice heard to the incoming planning minister after Saturday.
“We’re not stopping. This is continuing until we get a fair outcome for the residents,” he said.
“It will be a pretty toxic thing to sign off on.”
DoverDC, which is planning a $2.6bn 200MW datacentre next to AusNet’s South Morang terminal station, said its project would be assessed on its merits regardless of the election outcome.
“It is on this basis that it was accepted into the planning process by the current state government and we see no reason why that should change,” a spokesperson said.

Goodman Group, which has lodged plans for three two-storey datacentre buildings in Truganina, west of Melbourne, said it would not speculate on the election outcome or the planning decision but would work constructively with the government and local community.

articles.title: Germany's Wadephul 'shocked' by Trump's Nvidia intervention
articles.summary: The German foreign minister has criticized Donald Trump's interference in the chip-maker's economic activities. Jensen Huang was brought back after stepping down as Nvidia CEO amid multiple scandals.

image.caption: Wadephul was speaking at a conference in BerlinImage: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul on Tuesday expressed shock over US President Donald Trump's admission that he persuaded chip-producing giant Nvidia to reinstall ousted CEO Jensen Huang.
Nvidia brought Huang back on Monday in a surprise decision, less than two weeks after the CEO stepped down amid a series of affairs.
What did Wadephul say about Trump's involvement in Nvidia?

"It shocked me, to be honest, because as far as I know, if I'm personally looking back, I have never seen or recognized such an intervention from the political side into a particular company," Wadephul told reporters at a foreign policy conference in Berlin.
"And I do have some doubts ⁠whether ​this is a very ​good model for the future," he added.
"But OK, that took place in the United States of America," the foreign minister said.
Wadephul went on to say there are enough reasons to defend the rules-based international order, and that includes political power not getting involved in the economic activities of companies.
Trump boasts about interference in Nvidia decision
Huang's shock reinstatement on Monday came on the back of a unanimous vote by Nvidia's board of directors.

The news was welcomed by Trump, who called it the "correct and proper decision" in a post on Truth Social. The president later said he had played a key role, having spoken "directly and indirectly" to the board of directors, urging them to reinstate the scandal-hit ex-CEO.
"I convinced them," Trump said. "I made the deal."

Huang came under massive fire after it was reported he had had an affair with the CEO of the Singapore-based company Megaspeed. She was also accused of being a spy working on behalf of Chinese intelligence.
Nvidia's Cage for AI: can it prevent disaster?
Nvidia, Trump see stock surge after Huang's reinstallment

Nvidia's shares took a hit on Huang's stepping down, but rebounded by 30% on Monday after it was announced he was being reinstalled, adding over $900 billion (€820 billion) to the company's market value.
This share price surge also appears to have benefited Trump himself, with the Financial Times calculating that the president saw his Nvidia stock go up $15 million.

Huang's return has also brought some calm to the market that appeared to be teetering, with growing concerns about the viability of the AI sector, which now makes up a substantial part of the US stock market.
It also marks a turn around from the poor showing by Anthropic's IPO launch that saw its early gains quickly melt away amid fears that the AI sector has been overvalued.
