articles.title: Expanded voucher program to help sustain private schools — COCOPEA
articles.summary: ‘We really need to sustain our existence.... And this RA 12327 is a good start,’ says COCOPEA chairperson Irineo Alvaro Jr., as private schools also feel the effects of a sluggish economy

blocks.text: COCOPEA. Irineo Alvaro Jr., chairperson of the Coordinating Council of Private Educational Associations, speaks to media ahead of the 10th COCOPEA National Congress in Taguig City on November 24, 2026.
COCOPEA's Facebook page
‘We really need to sustain our existence.... And this RA 12327 is a good start,’ says COCOPEA chairperson Irineo Alvaro Jr., as private schools also feel the effects of a sluggish economy

items: The newly passed Republic Act No. 12327 expands the voucher program for poor students in private K to 12 schools.
COCOPEA emphasizes that the reform will help alleviate financial burdens on families and decongest public schools.
The organization calls for urgent measures to address economic pressures on private schools.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The newly passed law that expanded the voucher program for poor students in private K to 12 schools is seen to help sustain operations of private institutions amid declining enrollment and economic pressures, the Coordinating Council of Private Educational Associations (COCOPEA) said on Tuesday, November 24.

Republic Act (RA) No. 12327 or the Basic Education Voucher Assistance Act broadened the Expanded Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education (E-GASTPE) Act to include kindergarten and elementary school.
Currently, the decades-old E-GASTPE Act only provides tuition aid to students in private junior and senior high schools.

COCOPEA chairperson Irineo Alvaro Jr. said the reform would help decongest public schools, and affirms the inherent right and responsibility of parents to choose the best education setting for their children.
“By subsidizing a significant portion of tuition in recognized private schools, the government can alleviate financial burdens on families,” Alvaro said in a press conference.
“The voucher program is a real game changer in re-centering our education policy around the Filipino family, not just decongestion.”

blocks.caption: Voucher program now covers kinder to Grade 12 under new law

blocks.text: Alvaro noted that enrollment rates in private schools, particularly small institutions, declined by 6% to 10% compared to last year, as they cannot match subsidized institutions and the level of teachers’ salary in public schools. Some have already closed this year, he added, without providing further details.
“We really need to sustain our existence despite all of these. And this RA 12327 is a good start. I hope this is a work in progress that could extend up to the tertiary [level],” Alvaro said.
To prevent “ghost students,” COCOPEA said it is coordinating with the Department of Education (DepEd) in pushing transparency for all transactions.
The group will also collaborate with the DepEd as the agency crafts the implementing rules and regulations of the new law.

COCOPEA legal counsel Joseph Noel Estrada wants a stronger role for the Private Education Assistance Committee (PEAC), which is the co-implementer of the tuition aid for junior high and senior high school students.
The new law does not mention PEAC, but it mandates the creation of the Bureau of Private Education under the DepEd.
“We will continue to help PEAC and explore systems to ensure that there will be no leakage, no corruption, no anomalies and irregularities,” Estrada said.
COCOPEA also called for urgent action to help schools survive economic pressures.

“Like every Filipino household, private educational institutions are hit hard by rising inflation, surging electricity and operating costs, and frequent calamities. These pressures threaten the survival of many schools and make life harder for their students, faculty, and staff,” Alvaro said.

He said sustainability of private schools would be ensured if there are policy changes promoting freedom to use flexible learning and training setups, fair and timely tuition adjustments, prompt release of government subsidies, less red tape, and respect for academic freedom.

Particularly, COCOPEA is pushing for a review of existing tuition policies so that private institutions can sustain fair compensation and support for faculty, invest in modern facilities, and continuously improve the quality of instruction.

Father Karel San Juan, president of Ateneo de Davao University and the Catholic Educational Association of the Philippines, said private schools are “very sensitive” to economic forecasts as they are tuition-dependent.

“The inflation rate in the Philippines is really escalating…the economists are projecting stagflation in the Philippines. [At the] macro level, we’re considering that. At the micro level, in our respective cities, towns where we operate all over the country, we’re considering local inflation as well,” San Juan said in the same press conference.
Stagflation refers to the combination of weak economic growth and high inflation.

blocks.caption: [In This Economy] The Philippines has entered stagflation territory

blocks.text: Other considerations cited by COCOPEA were climate disruptions, including the impact of El Niño, adjustments in minimum wage, and competition.
San Juan said consultations with parents, students, and faculty must also be done before proposing tuition increases. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Land mine deaths reach five-year high, watchdog says
articles.summary: Myanmar reported the highest annual land mine casualty toll, followed by Syria and Afghanistan, ICBL report says. Since 1999, nearly 50 thousand people were killed by land mines.

image.caption: Land mines have been heavily used in Russia's war in UkraineImage: Christophe Gateau/dpa7picture alliance

blocks.text: Land mines killed or injured more people in 2025 than in any year since 2020, according to the International Campaign to Ban Landmines' (ICBL) annual report.

The report stated that the number of recorded deaths was at least 6,929, which is a 10% increase compared with last year. According to the campaign, four out of five victims were civilians, and half of those were minors.
Experts say the true figure is likely higher as not all land mine related death and injuries are recorded as such.
Myanmar reported the highest annual casualty toll for the third year in a row, with 1,891 victims, amid a "massive" new mine use.
In Syria, the number of casualties climbed by 50% to 1,602 in 2025, after the large-scale return of displaced people following the ousting of president Bashar Assad.
Myanmar and Syria were followed by Afghanistan with 497 casualties.
'The Ottawa Treaty faces its greatest test,' report warns
The ICBL criticized Ukraine, over its continued use of land mines. Ukraine, which is currently being invaded by Russia, is one of the 162 state parties to the Mine Ban Treaty.

The treaty, known as the Ottawa Treaty, prohibits the use, production, storage and transfer of anti-personnel mines. The treaty was ratified by 166 countries, but not by China, India, Russia, Israel, North Korea, or the US, along with nearly 30 others.
Land mines in Europe — the return of a banned weapon

Five European NATO countries, which share a border with Russia, have withdrawn from the treaty last year: Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Finland and Poland. Ukraine has also withdrawn, though this will not take legal effect until the war ends.
"The treaty’s norms face their greatest test since 1999," the report said, citing the withdrawals.
In 2025, Ukraine justified its move to withdraw from the treaty by citing the actions of Russia, which has never ratified the treaty and has been using mines on Ukrainian territory.

The campaign said Ukraine was still "fully bound by the treaty" but had breached its ban on producing anti-personnel mines. It said the country had manufactured both 3D-printed mines and mines designed to be dropped by drones.
Report also noted that Russia has used antipersonnel land mines extensively in Ukraine since its full-scale invasion began in 2022.
Nearly 50 thousand people killed by land mines since 1999

Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, Cambodia, Iraq, Morocco, North Korea, South Korea and Ukraine have "massive land mine contamination," meaning they have more than 100 square kilometers of land contaminated by land mines, the report assessed.

Since 1999, 49,859 people were killed and 118,525 injured by land mines, according to Landmine and Cluster Munition Monitor, the research and monitoring arm of the ICBL, and the Cluster Munition Coalition NGOs.
Land mines, blocked ports hinder Ukraine farmers

articles.title: Once ‘capital of the Confederacy’, Virginia enshrines rights to voting, abortion and gay marriage
articles.summary:
Organizers won key civil liberties protections on election day – and women and Black advocates were at the forefront

Progressives made

blocks.text: Progressives made historic gains in the south during the midterm elections – and Virginia was no exception. The state approved three constitutional amendments protecting civil liberties that have eroded in Trump’s second term: enshrining the rights to abortion and same-sex marriage, and restoring voting rights to those with past felony convictions.
These victories were led by women and Black organizers who say they want to capitalize on the momentum and advocate for policies that expand the protections they secured on election day.

“There’s a lot of work ahead to make sure this amendment is properly implemented,” said Han Jones, campaign director for Virginians for Reproductive Freedom, which canvassed for the abortion referendum. “We have to make sure Virginians don’t just have the right to reproductive care but also access to it.”
Reproductive freedom

Since the supreme court overturned Roe v Wade in 2022, abortion bans have swept the nation, particularly the south, where Virginia has become the only state without extreme restrictions on the procedure. Question 1, which passed with 62% of the vote on 3 November, established protections not only for abortion but also contraception, childbirth, miscarriage management and fertility care, including IVF.

The Virginians for Reproductive Freedom coalition brought together 30 local and national groups serving different constituencies, some focused on advocacy and others on healthcare. The depth and diversity of the coalition were pivotal to its success, Jones said. Certain groups worked on Spanish-language canvassing, others managed outreach to youth voters. Altogether, some 850 volunteers knocked on 45,000 doors across the commonwealth.

blocks.caption: Abortion rights advocates protest in Fairfaxafter Roe v Wade was overturned in June 2022. Photograph: Jemal Countess/UPI/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Much of the campaign was focused on educating voters about Question 1 and what protections are at stake, Jones said, along with dispelling misinformation from anti-abortion groups about how the amendment would put women’s health at risk.
“We knew Virginians were supportive of abortion and reproductive rights, but that’s not a guarantee that people would vote yes,” Jones said.

But constitutional protection doesn’t necessarily make reproductive care available, organizers say, especially given how expensive abortion, contraceptives and IVF can be. During a briefing on 18 November, organizers shared fundraising efforts for abortion funds, forthcoming lobbying sessions with legislators to ensure the law is properly implemented, as well as plans to fight lawsuits from anti-abortion groups seeking to block the amendment.

“A right you don’t know about is a right you cannot use,” said Jamie Lockhart, executive director at Planned Parenthood Advocates of Virginia. “We’re committed to making sure every Virginian knows what this amendment means for them.”
Voting rights

In approving Question 3, Virginians enshrined a “fundamental right to vote” for all citizens, including convicted felons who have served their time. The referendum reversed a lifetime voting ban for felony offenders that was established in the mid-1800s and has disproportionately targeted Black people.

“We didn’t think Virginia, being the capital of the Confederacy, would ever give up this last remaining vestige of the Jim Crow era,” said Sheba Williams, founder of the Right to Vote coalition that spearheaded the ballot campaign. “Our goal is to give dignity back to people who are imperfect.”

Roughly 4 million formerly incarcerated Americans were denied voting rights in 2024, including more than a quarter million Virginians, according to estimates from the Sentencing Project. One out of every 10 Black Virginians, including Williams, lost their rights as a result of a felony conviction. (For decades, voting rights in Virginia could only be reinstated on an individual basis through a governor’s executive authority.)

blocks.caption: Chris DeRosa, a voting rights advocate, poses for a portrait in Arlington, in October. Photograph: Maansi Srivastava for The Washington Post via Getty Images

blocks.text: Williams said the ballot drive is built on the work of Black female legislators such as Mamie Locke and the late Yvonne B Miller, who fought for decades to restore voting access for people with past convictions. The win was bittersweet, Williams said, because many who advocated for the amendment have died, including her mother, who was disenfranchised for 24 years.

The big focus for the coalition, which includes the ACLU of Virginia and the League of Women Voters of Virginia, is notifying the quarter of a million formerly incarcerated Virginians that they can vote again. That requires organizing a vast public education campaign in areas with the highest conviction rates, Williams said, and asking the state Department of Corrections to potentially include voter registration information in re-entry packets. The coalition is also looking to build on the ballot win by pushing for bolder policies, such as reforming the state’s barrier crime laws.

“We still have to work on other bills that impact the lives of formerly incarcerated people,” Williams said. “We see people celebrating the changing of the tides, the younger generation coming in. But we know people who hold on to power will try to maintain it.”
Marriage equality

Same-sex marriage has been legal across the country since the landmark supreme court decision in 2015. But advocates say protections for LGBTQ+ people have felt increasingly tenuous under a hostile administration and supreme court, which has considered taking up challenges to the Obergefell ruling.

The passage of Virginia’s marriage-equality referendum on election day is a “generational reversal” exactly 20 years after the state banned same-sex union, said Reed Williams, communications director for the Virginians for Marriage Equality coalition. Coincidentally, the ban and its repeal passed by the same margin of the vote: 57%. (Virginia is the fifth state to repeal a constitutional ban on gay marriage, following Nevada, California, Colorado and Hawaii; in total, 37 states have protections for gay marriage.)

blocks.caption: Governor Abigail Spanberger speaks at a rally in Richmond in support of the same-sex marriage amendment. Photograph: Mike Kropf/Richmond Times-Dispatch via Getty

blocks.text: “This really shows how much Virginians have grown,” she said. “The perspectives of certain justices on the supreme court have made it clear that state protections are more important than ever before.”

Williams said organizers learned from other states’ marriage equality campaigns and leaned into the power of storytelling. The coalition recruited more than 40 queer people across the state to share “what being gay was like in a pre-Obergefell world,” she said, referring to the 2015 ruling. “We had to show that the amendment had real stakes for people in the LGBTQ+ community,” Williams said.

Equality Virginia wants to carry the momentum from the ballot win into the upcoming legislative session, to advocate for broader issues like state funding for HIV prevention and gender- affirming care for trans youth. The organization is already looking ahead to the next election cycle, Williams said, when all the seats in the state legislature are up for grabs.
“This is an incredible opportunity to take the lessons we learned in the marriage equality campaign,” she said, “and mobilize voters to get more pro-equality lawmakers elected.”

articles.title: Plastering House Bill 11014 against real world AI workflows
articles.summary: For most of the last two years, we’ve treated AI as something we talk to. There is a dialogue of sorts happening – if you would like to call “talking to an AI” a dialogue. It’s a back and forth…

blocks.text: For most of the last two years, we’ve treated AI as something we talk to. There is a dialogue of sorts happening – if you would like to call “talking to an AI” a dialogue. It’s a back and forth of asking questions and it spits out answers. What happens when you try to apply House Bill 11014: The AI Agent Transactions and Accountability Act, against real world AI workflows
This is changing on many fronts from both vendors and interestingly, congress.
The vendor’s case

At a virtual media roundtable on November 12, Gavin Barfield, Salesforce’s Chief Technology Officer and Vice President for Solutions in ASEAN, framed the problem in terms I found useful. Models are good at interpreting what someone wants, but their answers can vary. Business execution is deterministic: the same inputs and the same rules should produce the same approval every time. His line was that models are brilliant but can’t run the enterprise by themselves. Which is, by the way, why you still need people.

Salesforce’s answer is what it calls a Trusted Enterprise AI Harness, six capabilities plus a control plane covering context, agency, action, governance, security and the models themselves. The model reasons and proposes, and the business system decides what is permitted.

The second half of the pitch is about where this happens. Through AIforce, Salesforce wants its data and workflows to show up inside the tools people already use, whether that’s Slack, Claude Cowork or Lightning. On November 19, the company and Microsoft announced Copilotforce at Ignite, which extends the same idea into Microsoft Copilot and Teams.
It’s still early: the Copilot integration is in public preview and the Teams piece is a pilot. One detail stood out to me. Supported writebacks to the CRM require explicit user confirmation.

blocks.caption: AI in legal

blocks.text: The local Salesforce office milestone

There’s a Philippine angle too. Barfield said Salesforce opened its local office a year ago and that it keeps adding space and headcount. Asked for a growth figure and a count of local customers running live agents, he gave neither. What he did offer was a change in how projects are sold: working agents in a couple of weeks, tied to a KPI baseline, because CFOs and COOs no longer pay for experiments. His own numbers are tidy. He said briefing prep for a C-level meeting once took four to five hours and now takes about three minutes through Slackbot.

He also cited $100 million in annual savings from Salesforce’s own help site. These are Salesforce’s figures about Salesforce. The same goes for the 90% pilot failure rate he cited, which he sourced to a Salesforce article without saying whether it describes global or Philippine deployments.
AI accountability in congress

House Bill 11014, the AI Agent Transactions and Accountability Act, was filed on August 27 by Representatives Miguel Luis Villafuerte, Vincenzo Renato Luigi Villafuerte, Tsuyoshi Anthony Horibata and Terry Ridon. Its starting premise is the opposite of “the agent decided.” An act performed through an AI agent is attributed to the Principal, the person or company that authorized it. The bill says explicitly that a Principal can’t dodge responsibility by arguing the agent acted autonomously or probabilistically. That word appears in the text, and it is the same one Barfield used to describe models.

The bill is not hostile to agents. It says using one doesn’t invalidate an otherwise valid contract under the E-Commerce Act, and it doesn’t require a human to confirm each step if authority was properly granted. It sets up a voluntary credential through the DICT so a counterparty can check what an agent is allowed to do. Mandatory registration is reserved for narrowly designated high-risk categories, after public consultation.

Principals do get defenses: stolen credentials, a cyberattack, unauthorized modification of the agent, third-party fraud, or a provider failure outside their reasonable control. Knowing fraud or falsification carries fines of ₱200,000 to ₱2 million, or six months to six years in prison.
Governance and the human element

Read side by side, these documents disagree on one thing, and it matters. Salesforce says its governance layer makes agents trustworthy. The bill says trust is a good thing to have, and liability sits with the customer. A vendor can offer audit trails and guardrails. Under HB 11014, the company that deployed the agent still answers for what it did.

The bill does leave one door open. It says contractual indemnification among Principals, developers, providers and platforms isn’t prevented. In practice, the real division of risk would be written in the vendor agreement, not in the marketing deck. Any Philippine company signing for agents should read that clause before the demo.

Section 14 deserves attention as well. It would require providers to disclose referral fees, preferential routing and similar arrangements that could steer an agent’s recommendations. Agents that live inside a single vendor’s ecosystem make that question more relevant, not less.

Salesforce’s default is also more cautious than the proposed legal floor. The bill wouldn’t require a human to confirm each step, while Copilotforce asks for confirmation before it writes to the CRM. That gap won’t last on its own. Confirmation prompts are the first thing teams remove once the novelty wears off and the volume goes up.
Which leaves the question the roundtable never quite got to. When a briefing takes three minutes instead of five hours, who is reading it?

articles.title: Playwright, filmmaker Dustin Celestino inducted into Palanca Hall of Fame
articles.summary: Dustin Celestino enters the Palanca Awards’ prestigious roster after winning first prize in the full-length play category five times

items: Filipino playwright and filmmaker Dustin Edward Celestino was inducted into the Hall of Fame of the Carlos Palanca Memorial Awards for Literature, marking his fifth first-place honor with his play 'Kritisismo.'
Celestino has received multiple awards for his works, including second place for his play 'Seen' and various other accolades in both full-length and one-act play categories since 2017.
In addition to his theater accomplishments, Celestino has also gained recognition in film, winning Indie Movie Screenwriter of the Year and having films nominated for prestigious awards.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Multi-awarded Filipino playwright and filmmaker Dustin Edward Celestino — whose work has been recognized across theater, film, and literature — was inducted into the Hall of Fame of the Carlos Palanca Memorial Awards for Literature on Tuesday, November 24, in Makati City.

Celestino’s full-length Filipino play, Kritisismo, earned him his fifth first-place honor, solidifying his place in the prestigious Hall of Fame of the Palanca Awards, widely regarded as the local equivalent of the Pulitzer Prize.

“It’s such an honor to be included among writers I have the greatest respect for. I’m also very happy to be part of a club that includes good friends and writing peers Mikael Co, Guelan Luarca, and Joshua So,” Celestino told Rappler. All three became Hall of Famers in 2024.

Elmer Gatchalian, a member of the board of judges for Dulang Ganap na Haba (Filipino Division), said, “We were all impressed by Kritisismo because of its dramatic structure and metatheatrical form. The full-length play stands out for its intellectual depth and sharp dialogue that examines power, class divide, and systemic oppression.”
Celestino’s other entry, Seen, won second place in the Full-Length Play category, English Division, this year.
Since 2017, Celestino has received four other Palanca first-prize awards in the full-length play category:

items: Fidelity (English), 2025
Ang Duyan ng Magiting (The Cradle of the Brave) (Filipino), 2019
The Story of This Father (English), 2017
Ang Pangahas na si Pepe Rodriguez (The Malevolent Pepe Rodriguez) (Filipino), 2017

blocks.text: His other Palanca wins include second prize for the full-length English play Birdie in 2024; second prize for the one-act Filipino play Elehiya in 2025; third prize for the full-length English play The Lost Filipino Patriots of America in 2022; third prize for the one-act Filipino play Fermata in 2023; and third prize for the full-length Filipino play A.Ni.Mal in 2025.

The Palanca Awards is the longest-running and most prestigious literary competition in the country. Established in 1950 and named after philanthropist and businessman Don Carlos Palanca Sr., it is sponsored by the Carlos Palanca Foundation, Inc., and is considered the gold standard in Philippine writing excellence.

In 2026, Celestino won Indie Movie Screenwriter of the Year at the 42nd PMPC Star Awards for Movies for Habang Nilalamon ng Hydra ang Kasaysayan (As Hydra Devours History). He was also nominated for Best Original Screenplay at the Luna Awards and Best Screenplay at The Eddys.
Celestino’s films Habang Nilalamon ng Hydra ang Kasaysayan and A.Ni.Mál were both nominated for Best Film at the Cinemalaya Independent Film Festival in 2025 and 2026, respectively.

In 2023, Ang Duyan ng Magiting won the Special Jury Prize at Cinemalaya, earned seven Gawad Urian nominations including Best Picture, and was one of seven films shortlisted as the Philippines’ official entry to the 96th Academy Awards.
Strange Frequencies: Taiwan Killer Hospital, which he co-wrote, competed at the 2024 Metro Manila Film Festival.
Meanwhile, Utopia won the Special Jury Prize at the 2019 Cinema One Originals Film Festival and earned Celestino nominations for Best Director and Best Screenplay.

Over seven years, Celestino staged four one-act plays at the Cultural Center of the Philippines’ Virgin Labfest (VLF): Mga Eksena sa Buhay ng Kontrabida (Scenes from the Life of an Antagonist), Doggy, Ang Munting Liwanag sa Madilim na Sulok ng Isang Serbeserya sa Maynila (The Glimmer of Light in a Dark Corner of a Beerhouse in Manila), and Fermata.
The VLF also “opened more doors” for Celestino. Those doors included writing for the series Unconditional (later streamed on Netflix) and the Viva series Di Na Muli on TV5.
Celestino was born in 1983 as the eldest of four children — three boys and a girl — to entrepreneur Edgardo Celestino and teacher and preschool owner Rocelyn Domingo.
Only English books lined their bookshelves while growing up in a two-bedroom bungalow in Quezon City, making English his first language.
“I couldn’t write in Filipino well until I was in college,” he said.
Celestino’s father — who also worked as a sales representative for pharmaceutical company Unilab — owned a chain of video rental shops, and Dustin helped curate the titles they acquired.
“I watched movies as a kid, because we had video shops. At age 11 or 12, I was already asked to curate our video shop’s library because I loved watching movies,” he recalled.

Name it — Betamax, VHS, 4+1 rental promos — he watched them all and read the covers of the VHS tapes. His father favored action flicks starring Bruce Willis, Sylvester Stallone, and Mark Dacascos, while Dustin was drawn to horror.
Celestino initially took Film at De La Salle University in Manila before shifting to Philosophy with a minor in Translation. He was part of the Malate Literary Folio from 2000 to 2004.
He began joining writing competitions in 2003 and 2004, winning four times.
“I was initially into writing English fiction,” he said. It’s a path that led him to writers’ workshops organized by Iyas, Ateneo de Manila University, and Silliman University in Dumaguete.

Celestino loved Greek mythology as a child. Aside from watching Jason and the Argonauts on Channel 9 — which “started my initial interest in mythology” — the idea of using myths as metaphors for contemporary struggles came from The Myth of Sisyphus by French philosopher and novelist Albert Camus.
What appealed to him most were the stories of mortals because they were “more relatable: Pygmalion, Icarus, Orpheus, Cassandra.”
Among his favorite foreign authors are European existentialists Camus, French philosopher and playwright Jean-Paul Sartre, and Russian novelist Fyodor Dostoevsky.

He also admires Russian-American novelist Vladimir Nabokov, Czech-French novelist Milan Kundera, Czech writer Franz Kafka, German-Swiss poet and novelist Hermann Hesse, German novelist and poet Günter Grass, and American fictionists Philip Roth and Ernest Hemingway.
“They were very good with narratives,” he said.
Among Filipino writers, the one Celestino deems closest to them is Gregorio Brillantes.
“I think Gregorio Brillantes was the best Filipino writer,” Celestino said.
Celestino has always been a teacher, just like his mother. As a speed reader, he easily handled one of the hardest parts of the job: grading papers.

He began teaching high school at St. Scholastica’s College. Later, while he was teaching college freshmen and sophomores at Asia Pacific College, the Philippines’ shift to the K-12 curriculum left him without work in the mid-2010s.
“Walang mabigay na workload sa akin (No workload could be given to me). I was demoralized. I had to take on another job,” he shared.

He was grateful for a role as creative director, where he also handled corporate social responsibility, at an internal communications company owned by a La Salle batchmate, though he struggled with the daily commute from Fairview.
He eventually resigned to focus on writing. He devoted the first 100 days of 2017 to studying playwriting formats and reading past Palanca winners.
“I had nine entries that year,” he recalled. Both of his full-length plays (in Filipino and English) won first prize.
“I had a knack for writing screenplays,” he said. “I started writing more.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Imee questions claim that PH will buy 100% of agri, energy from US
articles.summary: Senator Imee Marcos on Tuesday raised concerns that the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) was supposedly not consulted before the announcement that the Philippines intends to import 100% of its…

blocks.text: Published November 24, 2026 8:58pm

Senator Imee Marcos on Tuesday raised concerns that the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) was supposedly not consulted before the announcement that the Philippines intends to import 100% of its agricultural products and energy requirements from the United States.

During the Senate plenary debates on the proposed P35.2 billion budget of DFA and its attached agencies for fiscal year 2027, Marcos said it was “alarming” that there were no prior consultations with DFA's foreign policy and diplomacy experts on the matter.

“The reason I ask DFA, and it has to be DFA, as the overall architect together with the President of our foreign policy, is that there was a very thinly veiled threat at the end of that requirement that we buy agriculture and energy requirements, 100% from the United States,” she said.
“And that was that, if we fail to do so, there would be trouble. And as a result, I'm compelled to ask the DFA: how is that trouble defined?”
Senator Erwin Tulfo, sponsor of the DFA’s budget, said there will be a bilateral meeting between the Philippines and the United States in March 2027.
He said security issues are among the topics that will be discussed.

US President Donald Trump had claimed that he told Philippine government officials, during his recent state visit to the country, that Manila should 100% import its agricultural products from America, rather than get them from other nations such as Brazil.
He also claimed that the Philippines would no longer buy its energy requirements from the Middle East, as Manila would already buy 100% of its energy from the US.
Tulfo also said that the matter of Trump’s announcement now lies with the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) and the Department of Agriculture (DA).

“The DFA is actually closely monitoring these issues. But since this is assigned already to the DTI and DA, but they will continue to do so. And then they're waiting for further answers from the counterpart in the US,” he said.
But Marcos pressed if the DFA knew about such a deal.
Tulfo said that the DFA was “taken aback” following Trump’s announcement.
“Actually, Senator Imee, medyo everybody was taken aback because this is only brought, this issue, during the bilateral meeting between the two presidents, during the ASEAN,” he said.
Marcos, in return, said that what Tulfo said was an admission that the DFA was “kept in the dark.”

“I think there's an admission on the part of the DFA that they were kept in the dark regarding this announcement and that here on after the matters have been assigned to others. The question that arises of course is who is formulating foreign policy if not the DFA,” she said.
Impossible?
Senate Majority Leader Juan Miguel Zubiri, meanwhile, expressed belief that Trump did not entirely mean what he said.

“I think the unpredictability of the US President sometimes shocks everyone kasi yung binanggit niya, hindi naman siguro ganoon ang pinag-usapan, ‘100 percent.’ Alam niyo naman si President Trump, he probably said that to be able to gain local popularity in the US,” he said

(I think the unpredictability of the US President sometimes shocks everyone, because what he mentioned—‘100 percent’—likely wasn’t what was actually discussed. You know how President Trump is. He probably said that to gain popularity in the US.)

“I’m sure hindi naman ganoon ang mangyayari kasi imposible (I’m sure that’s not how things will play out, because it’s impossible). I don’t think the country could get 100 percent of its agricultural products from the US, or power as well,” he added. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Is North Korea holding back on sending Russia more troops?
articles.summary: A North Korean troop buildup Ukraine warned about months ago has yet to materialize, even as strategic cooperation goes on. Analysts say Pyongyang is balancing its ties with Moscow and Beijing.

image.caption: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un commemorated troops killed in Ukraine earlier this yearImage: KCNA/REUTERS

blocks.text: Over the summer, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that he expected between 30,000 and 50,000 North Korean soldiers would be deployed to Russia as part of Pyongyang's ongoing support of Moscow's war effort.
However, it now appears that troop buildup has yet to materialize, and it is unclear whether North Korea will continue sending large numbers of troops to Russia.

Writing on Telegram on November 9, Andrii Kovalenko, who resigned in September as head of Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation, said an August intelligence assessment indicated that the Kremlin had requested more than 30,000 additional North Korean troops for an autumn offensive.

He said a summit between North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and Russian President Vladimir Putin was expected in September, but did not happen. Kviy says North Korea previously sent thousands of troops to Russia's Kursk region in 2024, where Moscow was fighting to repel a Ukrainian incursion.
Kovalenko believes Pyongyang turned down Moscow's request because taking part in offensive operations in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine's Donetsk region may still be a red line for North Korea.

However, Kovalenko added Russia still relies on North Korean material support, particularly ammunition, while assessing that another major deployment of North Korean combat troops was unlikely this winter.
No need for North Korean reinforcements?

Han Ki-bum, a former deputy director of South Korea's National Intelligence Service, told DW that the lull in fighting and the onset of winter give Pyongyang little immediate reason to send reinforcements.
North Korea expands role in Russia's war with Ukraine
He added that a visit this week to Moscow by Jo Yong-won, a senior North Korean official and close aide to Kim, could shed light on any future plans.

Han said it remained to be seen whether the visit was intended to deepen political ties between the ruling parties, building on their military cooperation, or to lay the groundwork for a visit by Kim himself.

Ahn Chan-il, a former North Korean soldier who defected to South Korea in 1979 and now heads the World Institute for North Korea Studies in Seoul, said Moscow also had reasons to limit the deployment.

He told DW that he expects Russia to weigh its battlefield needs against the costs of bringing in more North Korean troops. Unless the war expands, he said, Moscow is unlikely to request a larger contingent.
North Korean weapons keep flowing
Ukrainian official Kovalenko said North Korea still had a missile unit in Russia's Voronezh region and around 8,500 support personnel in rear areas, including drone operators, engineers and sappers.
He added that Pyongyang was ramping up ammunition production and showcasing new drones and missiles.
In a post on X on November 17, Zelenskyy said that Russia was receiving dozens of North Korean ballistic missiles each month.

He warned that their use in Ukraine was helping Pyongyang refine its weapons and creating security risks for countries around the Korean Peninsula. Battle-testing weaponry is one of North Korea's primary advantages from military cooperation with Russia
Why Kyiv and Seoul are clashing over North Korean POWs
Balancing Russia and China ties
Kovalenko said Pyongyang appeared to have adopted what he called a "containment strategy," limiting its military commitment to Russia's war while maintaining ties with both Moscow and Beijing.
In his assessment, this approach allows Pyongyang to retain the benefits of its alliance with Russia while reducing its exposure to the outcome of the war.

Analyst Ahn said he expects Pyongyang's military cooperation with Moscow to continue because Russian assistance is crucial to North Korea's efforts to develop drone technology and strengthen its navy.
Nevertheless, the extent of this cooperation may be more limited in the future, and Pyongyang is also able to turn to China as a hedge.

Ahn said that if Russia limits the deployment of North Korean troops, Pyongyang's foreign currency earnings from those deployments would have less room to grow, giving it another reason to seek more support from Beijing

Jeong Joon Hee, a former South Korean Unification Ministry spokesperson, told DW that recent moves towards building better ties with Beijing may also reflect Pyongyang's dissatisfaction with what Moscow has offered in return for North Korea's help.
By strengthening its relationship with China while keeping ties with Russia steady, he said, Pyongyang could also be trying to persuade Moscow to give it more.

Kim Hyung Suk, a former South Korean vice minister of unification, told DW that North Korea needs China's economic, political and diplomatic backing alongside the support it receives from Russia. He expects Pyongyang to keep pursuing China's support regardless of how it manages its role in the war.

articles.title: Russian governor detained in rare criminal case against regional leader
articles.summary: Andrei Chibis, head of Russia's northern Murmansk region, is the first governor to be detained for five years.

blocks.text: Chibis was re-elected two years ago after surviving a knife attack and is considered an active supporter of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Governors are seen as representing the Kremlin, and Vladimir Putin removed several in the months after the war began in February 2022.
However, until now no regional governor has been arrested since the start of the war, even though plenty of high-ranking officials have been detained in that time.

The Murmansk governor is one of a number of officials suspected of corruption by the Russian interior ministry's investigative department which, according to reports, alleged that a criminal group was set up in 2022 to embezzle money from the regional budget and move it abroad, including to Kyrgyzstan.
Another part of the case involves alleged fraud surrounding the rebuilding of a motorway between the two Arctic towns of Apatity and Kirovsk, which are 15km (9.3 miles) apart.
According to Russian news agency Interfax, a court will decide whether Chibis will remain in custody at a hearing on Wednesday.
He has been sanctioned by both the UK and EU, which accuses him of involvement in the illegal transportation of Ukrainian children to Russia and their adoption by Russian families.

articles.title: Leftwing coalition leader calls for rental revolution as Spain heads for snap election
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Ada Colau hopes public anger over housing will transfer into support for her Broad Front coalition in Sunday’s vote

The leader of Spain’s leftwing Broad Front coalition has called…

blocks.text: The leader of Spain’s leftwing Broad Front coalition has called for a drastic rethink of the country’s entire housing rental system, and described the eviction of an 87-year-old woman – the spark for nationwide protests that in turn triggered Sunday’s snap general election – as “the last straw” for desperate tenants.
“We’re not interested in small changes,” Ada Colau, the former Barcelona mayor, told the Guardian in an interview. “We want to reform the entire rental sector.”

Public outrage over the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal from her Madrid apartment in September prompted the government, led by Pedro Sánchez’s Spanish Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE), to propose a series of changes to Spain’s housing laws. After the proposals were voted down by a combination of rightwing parties and Catalan nationalists, Sánchez called an election.

blocks.caption: Ada Colau said Broad Front support for a Socialist-led government would depend on it agreeing to expropriate properties owned by vulture funds. Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters

blocks.text: “When Maricarmen, an 87-year-old woman who had paid rent all her life, was evicted out of pure greed, that lit the fuse,” said Colau, who stepped out of the political limelight three years ago after failing to win a third term as Barcelona mayor.

The Broad Front alliance was founded in February to unite parties to the left of the PSOE, and named Colau as its candidate for prime minister on 12 October. “When I saw how many people were taking to the streets that’s when I agreed to be a candidate,” she said. “I thought, if I can be useful now, I have to be involved 100%.”

Polls have indicated that the conservative People’s party (PP) will win the most seats in Sunday’s election, but will fall short of a parliamentary majority, meaning the far-right Vox party could become kingmakers. A coalition deal between the PP and Vox would signal the return of the far right to government in Spain for the first time in the country’s post-dictatorship democratic history.

Colau’s alliance does not include the leftist group Podemos or the Catalan Republican Left (ERC) party. “I said to both Podemos and ERC we could change the front’s name, I offered to stand aside in favour of a consensus candidate, but the parties decided on a different strategy and I have to respect their decision,” Colau said.

Colau said she was sceptical of polls pointing to a PP-Vox majority. “I don’t think the majority of people want to go back to pre-democratic times,” she said. “People in the street don’t share this fatalism that the political right is going to win.

“People are very motivated, they’re very conscious that this isn’t an election like any other. This is the first time since the dictatorship that the far right might be in government and we might see the return of censorship, that we might see something like ICE in Spain, as well as attacks on groups such as the LGBT community and women.”

Polls suggest that a broad leftwing coalition encompassing the PSOE and all the smaller parties to the left of it won’t get enough votes to secure a parliamentary majority, but Colau is undeterred. She pointed out that at the general election in 2023 it was predicted that the right and far right would win, only for voters to return a progressive government, “admittedly with a very mixed and rather fragile parliamentary majority”.
She added: “At the moment we’re at about 8% and our goal is 10%. We believe people want to vote not just to keep out the far right, they want to vote for social progress.”
after newsletter promotion

Colau has been a housing activist for over 20 years, and says there is little to choose between the PP and PSOE on the issue, blaming both for the mortgage bubble that led to mass evictions after the 2008 financial crash and then allowing the current rental crisis to unfold.

“We’re not interested in small changes,” she said. “We want to reform the entire rental sector in line with something similar to Germany and, above all, get rid of the vulture funds that are destroying our neighbourhoods and driving us out of our cities. Vulture funds contribute nothing, everything they do is harmful.”

She said that 13 funds controlled about 100,000 properties, and that the Broad Front’s support for a Socialist-led government would depend on it agreeing to expropriate these properties “at a fair but not a market price”.

She said that when she was mayor she managed to increase the social housing stock by assuming control of more than 1,600 homes that were in the hands of big property owners. “If we could do that in Barcelona with fewer powers than the government, obviously it can be done at state level,” she said, adding that the constitution stated that housing was not only a right but that it must have a social function. “As for regulating rents, it isn’t such a radical proposal, it’s something that’s practised in various European countries.”

As mayor, Colau won international plaudits for her efforts to prioritise people over cars, but at home she was equally loved and loathed. During her time in office she came under constant attack from the pro-car lobby and faced over a dozen “lawfare” cases, all of which were rejected by the courts. Much of the hostility directed towards her was misogynist. “I’ve always said I’d only return to politics if I think I can be particularly useful, if not, I’ll do something else, because there are many ways to be political, not just in institutions,” she said. “If I can make a contribution now, I will do whatever I can to stop fascism returning to this country.”

articles.summary: Naeem Abu Nahel, who had only been in the position for two months, was targeted in western Gaza City, Gaza's interior ministry says.

blocks.text: An Israeli air strike has killed the head of Hamas's internal security service in Gaza.

Gaza's Hamas-run interior ministry said Naeem Abu Nahel was targeted by an aircraft in western Gaza City. The 50-year-old had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid by Israeli special forces.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz announced that Abu Nahel had been "eliminated" by the Israeli military.
Earlier, Palestinian first responders and health officials reported that six other people had been killed in two Israeli air strikes elsewhere in Gaza on Tuesday.

Three people, including a teenage boy, were killed in the Wadi Gaza area, south of Gaza City, they said. The other three, including two police officers, were killed in a separate strike on a police station in the al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Younis, they added.

Gaza's police force, which operates under the interior ministry, condemned the second attack, saying it was "part of an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus aimed at sowing chaos" in the territory.
The Israeli military said it had "struck terrorists in the area".
Israeli strikes on Gaza take place almost daily despite a US-brokered ceasefire agreed by Israel and Hamas in October last year.
At least 1,679 people have been killed in Gaza since then, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza over the same period.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,740 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

articles.title: Teodoro: PH focusing on deterrence, not just US retaliation amid WPS tension
articles.summary: The Philippines is focusing on strengthening its defense capabilities to deter potential attacks rather than relying on the United States' commitment to retaliate amid the tension in the West…

blocks.text: Published November 24, 2026 8:05pm

The Philippines is focusing on strengthening its defense capabilities to deter potential attacks rather than relying on the United States' commitment to retaliate amid the tension in the West Philippine Sea (WPS).
In a press conference, Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. said the Philippines was giving greater importance to building deterrence under the Mutual Defense Treaty (MDT) with the US.

"The MDT contains several provisions and normally the focus is on Article IV, which is the retaliation provision. You can be ironclad on IV, which is useless also because an attack has already occurred," Teodoro said.
"What we're working on is II and III. Meaning to say, to work with one another to build deterrence. And I think it is more important to be ironclad in deterrence than in retaliation," he added.
In the 1951 Treaty between Manila and Washington, Articles II, III, and IV establish how both nations build defense capacity, consult on threats, and respond to armed attacks in the Pacific.
Article II provides that both countries commit to maintaining and developing their individual and collective capacity to resist armed attacks, separately and jointly.

Article III states that foreign ministers or their deputies will consult whenever either country believes its territorial integrity, political independence, or security is threatened by an external armed attack in the Pacific.

Meanwhile, Article IV states that each party recognizes that an armed attack in the Pacific on either nation endangers its own peace and safety, and agrees to act to meet the common danger according to its constitutional processes.
Teodoro pointed out that retaliation could not reverse casualties or damage to society once an attack had already happened.

He said the country's deterrence posture was improving, citing the $2 billion assistance package announced by US President Donald Trump, which includes financing and grants for Philippine defense capabilities.
Teodoro said he hoped the Philippine government would also allocate funds to sustain the grants and develop capabilities through infrastructure.
He also stressed the need to address bureaucratic delays that hamper the country's defense modernization efforts.

articles.title: Recto welcomes Alan Cayetano's offer to donate P170,000 for national debt
articles.summary: Executive Secretary Ralph Recto on Tuesday welcomed Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano's offer to donate P170,000 to help pay off the country's national debt, saying the senator could give…

blocks.text: Published November 24, 2026 8:02pm

Executive Secretary Ralph Recto on Tuesday welcomed Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano's offer to donate P170,000 to help pay off the country's national debt, saying the senator could give the amount to the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) or the Bureau of the Treasury.
“Pwede. Pwede siyang magbigay ng P170,000,” Recto told reporters after the Senate plenary swiftly approved the proposed P10-billion budget of the Office of the President (OP) for fiscal year 2027.
(That's possible. He could donate P170,000.)
Asked where Cayetano could make the donation, Recto said he could give it to either the BIR or the Bureau of the Treasury.
“Sa BIR. Sa Treasury pwede, sa Treasury pwede rin siguro. BIR siguro baka may resibo,” he said.
(To the BIR or perhaps to the Treasury. The BIR would likely issue a receipt.)
Recto also said Malacañang was open to hearing Cayetano's proposals on how to implement the idea.
Cayetano earlier floated the idea of allowing Filipinos to voluntarily contribute P170,000 each, representing their estimated share of the country's P19.66-trillion national debt.
He proposed establishing a mechanism through which Filipinos willing to help repay government debt could make contributions.
Cayetano, however, clarified that he was not proposing to impose an additional financial burden on the public or asking Filipinos to assume the government's responsibility for paying its debts.
Meanwhile, Recto expressed confidence that the Philippine economy would recover by the first half of 2027.
“We expect a full recovery by the first or second quarter of next year,” he said.

Asked whether there would be changes in the administration's economic team amid calls for a reassessment of its performance due to the country's so-called “economic malaise,” Recto said the President regularly reviews his Cabinet.
“Lagi ang Pangulo, laging may review ang buong team niya. Be it the economic team or be it anyone in the Cabinet, it doesn't matter,” he said.
(The President always reviews his entire team, whether it is the economic team or anyone in the Cabinet.)

President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. has stood by his current economic team despite calls from Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson for a reassessment amid concerns over the declining Philippine stock market, weakening peso and rising inflation, among other economic challenges.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Here’s what to expect at the opening of Rodrigo Duterte’s ICC trial
articles.summary: More than 500 victims of extrajudicial killings in Duterte's drug war are authorized to participate in the trial through their team of legal representatives

blocks.text: DUTERTE. Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte attends the fourth status conference at the Trial Chamber III of the International Criminal Court in The Hague, Netherlands, on October 13, 2026.
International Criminal Court
More than 500 victims of extrajudicial killings in Duterte's drug war are authorized to participate in the trial through their team of legal representatives

items: Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte's trial for alleged crimes against humanity related to his drug war begins on November 30 at the International Criminal Court.
The trial will involve the presentation of evidence and witness testimonies, with the prosecution expected to call around 100 witnesses over the course of the proceedings.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

THE HAGUE, Netherlands – On Monday, November 30, former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte is set to begin trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) over alleged crimes against humanity relating to his bloody drug war in the Philippines.

The much-anticipated trial phase is when the parties in the case, namely, the ICC prosecutor, the common legal representatives of the victims (CLRV), and Duterte’s defense team, will present evidence and witness testimonies.

Unlike the confirmation of charges hearing last February, when the pre-trial chamber’s goal was to determine whether there was sufficient evidence in the prosecution’s case to proceed to trial, the judges in Trial Chamber III will now determine whether Duterte is guilty beyond reasonable doubt of the crimes against humanity of murder and attempted murder.

The crimes were alleged to have been committed during Duterte’s anti-illegal drug operations as Davao City mayor and vice mayor, utilizing his so-called Davao Death Squad, as well as when he replicated the Davao model on a nationwide scale upon assuming the presidency in 2016.
Here’s what to expect when trial begins.
When trial opens, the judges will ask Duterte whether he understands the charges filed against him and ask him to enter a plea of guilty or not guilty.
The equivalent of this in the Philippine legal process is called an arraignment.
The ICC prosecutor and the victims’ representatives are expected to deliver opening statements after Duterte enters a plea. These are expected to take several hours each.
The defense will deliver a short introduction of its case, but a longer opening statement is expected later in the trial.

blocks.caption: Duterte’s drug war was state-sanctioned, killed over 8,000 – Truth Commission

blocks.text: After the opening statements, the prosecution will begin presenting its witnesses. In the first weeks of the trial, that is, before the court goes on its winter recess on December 18, the prosecution is expected to present five witnesses.
The prosecution expects to present around 100 witnesses over the course of the trial.

“As with other complex cases involving allegations of crimes against humanity, these proceedings are expected to take some time. The exact duration of the trial will depend on a number of factors, including the volume of evidence, the number of witnesses, and any procedural matters that may arise during the trial,” said ICC spokesperson Oriane Huber Maillet in a briefing with reporters on Tuesday, November 24.
Only after the prosecution presents its case will the defense have the opportunity to present theirs.
The ICC presumes Duterte to be innocent unless and until proven guilty before the court.

“He is represented by counsel of his choosing and is entitled to all fair trial guarantees provided under the Rome Statute, including adequate time and facilities to prepare his defense, the ability to challenge the Prosecution’s evidence, and the opportunity to present evidence and witnesses on his own behalf,” said Maillet.
More than 500 victims of extrajudicial killings in Duterte’s drug war are authorized to participate in the trial through their team of legal representatives.
The ICC said it was taking steps to protect victims and witnesses from threats against their well-being.
ICC hearings are public and can be followed in two ways: in person, by attending the hearings at the ICC’s headquarters in The Hague, or online via its Facebook and YouTube channels.

Those who wish to attend the hearings in person may queue outside the court and are served on a first-come, first-served basis. There will be four sessions per day once trial begins, at the following schedule in local time at The Hague:

Viewers in the public gallery can watch the proceedings live, while online streams will have a 30-minute delay to allow for redactions in the event that confidential information is divulged during open session. The judges will occasionally call for a closed session to protect confidential information or participants.

“The Court remains committed to ensuring that these proceedings are conducted fairly, independently and transparently, in accordance with the Rome Statute and the Court’s legal framework,” said Maillet.
Both the pro- and anti-Duterte camps are expected to stage their own events and demonstrations in the days leading up to trial and when it begins.

On November 30, the Duterte Panagutin Network will hold a march and protest on ICC grounds, just before trial starts at 9 am. From 10 am onwards, Duterte’s supporters are expected to occupy the area in front of the ICC to stage their demonstration.
The ICC is set to begin Duterte’s trial amid a sharp delegitimization campaign from the former president’s supporters and global superpowers like the United States.

“The Court’s role is not to pursue any political objective. Rather, its role is to determine, through independent and impartial judicial proceedings, whether the charges have been proven according to the law,” said Maillet. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Car bomb tears through Colombian city wounding more than 20
articles.summary: The explosion is the latest in a string of attacks on buildings housing the security forces and government offices.

blocks.text: Three weeks ago, three adults and a baby were killed in a car bomb attack near army barracks in Tolima province.
And earlier on Monday, drones dropped explosives on the police headquarters in the northern city of Cúcuta.

The car bomb in Villavicencio went off on Monday evening - the eve of the 10th anniversary of the signing of a peace deal between the government and left-wing rebels of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc), Colombia's largest guerrilla group.
Following the signing of the deal, thousands of left-wing rebel fighters laid down their arms.
However, a significant number of Farc members, who did not agree with the deal, refused to disarm and joined dissident groups instead.

While forced displacement, child recruitment and the numbers of attacks on security forces dropped in the aftermath of the deal, there has been an upsurge in recent years driven by dissident Farc factions and criminal groups fighting for control of drug trafficking, illegal mining and extortion rackets.
Colombia's first left-wing president, who was in power from August 2022 to August 2026, tried to negotiate with these armed groups as part of what he called his "total peace" strategy.
However, the talks stalled and collapsed with several of the criminal groups violating ceasefires they had agreed to observe.
De la Espriella was elected on a promise to crack down on "narcoterrorism" and has been scathing about his predecessor's approach.
He has also been critical of the 2016 agreement, calling it a "false peace".

In a post on X, uploaded shortly before news of the car bomb in Villavicencio spread, he referred to the peace deal as a "mess", describing it as a "waste of public resources" and the "cause behind Colombia's ruin".

Former President Juan Manuel Santos and Rodrigo Londoño - the two men who signed the peace deal on behalf of the Colombian government and the Farc respectively - defended it in an interview with BBC Mundo ahead of the anniversary.
Santos said that De la Espriella was "totally wrong" to call it a "false peace".

"He wants to use, or has bought into that cynical and mistaken theory that the violence we see today is the result of the peace deal, when the exact opposite is the case," Santos said, arguing that the problem lies with the lack of implementation of the agreement.

articles.title: SWS: 69% of Filipinos aware of flood control probe
articles.summary: Nearly seven in 10 adult Filipinos are aware of investigations into alleged anomalies in flood control projects, up from 48% last year, according to a Social Weather Stations (SWS) survey released…

blocks.text: Published November 24, 2026 7:41pm

Nearly seven in 10 adult Filipinos are aware of investigations into alleged anomalies in flood control projects, up from 48% last year, according to a Social Weather Stations (SWS) survey released Tuesday.

The September 21 to 27, 2026, survey found that 69% of respondents were already aware of the investigations before they were interviewed, while the remaining 31% learned about the probe during the survey.
The awareness rate was highest in Metro Manila at 80%, followed by Balance Luzon at 70%, the Visayas at 69%, and Mindanao at 61%, the SWS said.

Awareness also increased with educational attainment, reaching 83% among college graduates, 78% among those who attended senior high school or college, 73% among junior high school graduates, 59% among elementary graduates, and 43% among those who did not finish elementary school.
Confidence in charges
The survey also found that 41% of adult Filipinos had “much confidence” that people would be charged over corruption linked to the flood control anomalies, resulting in a net confidence score of +8.
This was lower than the +18 recorded in September 2025 and the +9 in November 2025.
Net confidence was highest in Mindanao at +15, followed by Balance Luzon at +10 and the Visayas at +6. Metro Manila, meanwhile, registered a negative net confidence score of -7.
The proportion of respondents with very little confidence was highest among college graduates at 27% and Metro Manila residents at 26%, the SWS said.
Meanwhile, only 28% expected that many or almost all those involved would be jailed, while 38% believed that only a few or hardly anyone would face imprisonment.
The SWS conducted face-to-face interviews with 1,500 adults aged 18 and above nationwide: 600 in Balance Luzon and 300 each in Metro Manila, the Visayas, and Mindanao.
The survey had sampling error margins of ±3 percentage points for national results, ±4 points for Balance Luzon, and ±6 points each for Metro Manila, the Visayas, and Mindanao.

The investigations stemmed from a corruption controversy that erupted in July 2025, when President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., during his fourth State of the Nation Address, ordered a probe into alleged irregularities in government flood control projects.

The controversy intensified after inspections uncovered projects that were either substandard, incomplete or allegedly nonexistent despite having been reported as completed and paid for by the government.

The Senate and House of Representatives subsequently conducted investigations, while Marcos created the Independent Commission for Infrastructure (ICI) in September 2025 to investigate alleged corruption in flood control and other infrastructure projects.

The investigations implicated lawmakers, former government officials, DPWH personnel and contractors in an alleged scheme involving budget insertions, rigged bidding processes and kickbacks from government infrastructure funds.

The Ombudsman has since filed criminal cases against several personalities, including former House Speaker Martin Romualdez, Sen. Jinggoy Estrada, former senator Ramon "Bong" Revilla Jr., former Ako Bicol representative Elizaldy "Zaldy" Co, former DPWH Secretary Manuel Bonoan and contractors Sarah and Curlee Discaya.

As of October 2026, the Ombudsman reported that 39 cases involving 52 individuals had been filed before the courts, including 35 cases before the Sandiganbayan and four before regional trial courts. More cases remained under investigation.
Despite the filing of charges and arrests of several personalities, the criminal proceedings remain ongoing, with no final determination of guilt in these cases.— MCG, GMA News

Just an ordinary visit, or a possible courtship?
First Lady Liza Araneta made a surprise visit to the Batasang Pambansa on Tuesday, November 24, and of course, no less than Speaker Bojie Dy welcomed and accompanied her.

The joint public appearance comes amid rumors that Dy is being strongly considered to become President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s number two, should Vice President Sara Duterte be found guilty by the impeachment court and removed from office.

Malacañang or the House are unlikely to confirm anything more than what the visit was supposed to be on paper: the First Lady attending an arts workshop and storytelling session for children at the House.
Marcos, accompanied by Dy and other House leaders, checked the exhibits in celebration of National Children’s Month.
The Palace isn’t stupid and should be vetting by now all the possible replacements of Vice President Duterte, whose impeachment case is now in the final stages at the Senate.
Should at least 14 senators vote to convict her over her supposed unexplained wealth, the vice presidency will be a vacant position that the President needs to fill.
The Constitution allows the President to nominate a replacement from among members of the Senate and the House.
Aside from Dy, other lawmakers who are supposedly being considered for the job include Escudero, Win Gatchalian, Tito Sotto, and Lito Lapid.

As we previously reported, Dy is an attractive pick for the president. He does not have ambitions for higher office in 2028, sometimes plays second fiddle to the President’s son, Majority Leader Sandro Marcos, in the House, and is still respected by his colleagues despite the perceived ceremonial nature of his power.

blocks.caption: Bojie Dy, the unexciting Speaker whom Marcos can count on

blocks.text: While Sandro is a lawmaker himself, the President cannot pick his son because he is only 32 years old, below the constitutional age requirement of 40.
The First Lady is known to have the President’s ear, and insiders say she is actively involved in managing the many affairs of the Palace.
It wouldn’t be farfetched to imagine how the vice presidency problem could also be on her plate, but we can only speculate. – Rappler.com

articles.title: House okays bill lowering gov't workers' retirement age to 56
articles.summary: A bill seeking to lower the optional retirement age of government employees from 60 to 56 has been approved on third and final reading in the House of Representatives.

blocks.text: Published November 24, 2026 7:13pm
A bill seeking to lower the retirement age of government employees from 60 to 56 has been approved on third and final reading in the House of Representatives.
House Bill No. 10995 received 209 affirmative votes, no objections and one abstention during the plenary session on Tuesday.
Among the authors of the measure were Speaker Faustino "Bojie" Dy III of Isabela and House Majority Leader Ferdinand Alexander "Sandro" Marcos of Ilocos Norte.

The bill seeks to amend Section 13-A of Republic Act No. 8291, or the Government Service Insurance System (GSIS) Act of 1997, by allowing GSIS members to retire at age 56, provided they have rendered at least 15 years of service and are not receiving a monthly pension due to permanent total disability.
Qualified retiring members would receive their corresponding retirement benefits from the GSIS.

The authors said the proposed measure would give qualified personnel among the more than one million government workers the option to retire early and spend more years with their families using their retirement benefits and savings.
They also said the measure would allow retirees to pursue other passions or explore opportunities in other fields while opening up positions for younger government personnel.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Pope Francis' diary reveals claims he saw the devil three times
articles.summary: Published extracts from the late pontiff's diary claim one of the visions happened "in the choir loft" during Mass.

blocks.text: Pope Francis claimed he saw the devil three times over the course of his life, as well as the "gates of hell", according to new extracts from his private diary.

In The Private Diary of Pope Francis, published on Tuesday, a 2021 entry lists the late pontiff as having three visions of the devil: once from a car, another "in the choir loft" during Mass, and a third during a meeting with Vatican officials.
"I can't forget the powerful raspiness of his voice," Francis wrote, recalling one of the visions.

In the diary, written from 1992 to 2024, he also expresses regret over his 2018 visit to Chile, when he was criticised for defending a bishop who was accused of covering up sexual abuse committed by a priest.
Francis, who led the Catholic Church for 12 years until his death in 2025, later apologised and summoned the country's bishops to Rome, where they all offered to resign.
"Devastated because of the situation in Chile," Francis wrote in a 2021 entry.
"It was hard for me to admit what happened in Chile; I didn't think it was so serious."
Of his encounters, which Francis interpreted as meetings with the devil, he said he could not forget the devil's "menacing" eyes.

"He looked at me with flaming eyes... more intense than the previous one. They were like flashes of fire," he wrote of his second vision that he said happened inside a Carmelite chapel while he was archbishop of Buenos Aires.
He said the devil's presence intruded on his journeys, including during the visit to Chile amid the clerical sexual abuse scandal, and a meeting a few days after he had returned to Rome.
"I saw him and heard his voice, triumphant, possessing everything," he wrote, adding that "the Lord gave me the chance to free myself from these encounters".

articles.title: Senate passes 2027 OP budget in two minutes
