blocks.text: PALACE. Malacañang Palace riverside facade in 2013.
Presidential Museum and Library
The new recommended appropriation for the Office of the President is P10.83 billion
MANILA. Philippines – The Senate on Tuesday, November 24, swiftly approved the P10 billion proposed budget of the Office of the President (OP) for 2027 in just two minutes.
Senator JV Ejercito, sponsor of the budget, noted during the plenary deliberations the new recommended appropriation for the OP is now P10.83 billion.

“Out of courtesy, and historically, we give due courtesy to the budgets of the Office of the President and Office of the Vice President,” Senate Majority Floor Leader Juan Miguel “Migz” Zubiri said in moving for the passage of the proposed budget.
Senate President Pro-Tempore Vicente “Tito” Sotto III approved the motion sans objections.
The OP initially sought P10.158 billion, roughly one-third of its current 2026 budget and over two-thirds of its 2025 budget, in the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP).

Executive Secretary Ralph Recto previously said that the staggering budget cut was because the Philippines’ 2026 chairmanship of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) was lodged under the OP and is broken down based on the various agencies involved in the preparations related to hosting different meetings and the summits under the regional grouping.

“We’re asking for less while remaining fully prepared to do more. We believe this amount is sufficient for the Presidency to meet the exacting demands of leading the nation at a time of overlapping domestic and external challenges,” Recto said during the OP’s budget briefing before the House committee on appropriations on September 1. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Five women killed every hour by family members or partners — UN report
articles.summary: On average, 129 women or girls were killed every day in 2025 by someone in their close social circle, UN data showed.

image.caption: The UN report noted that women often face barriers to accessing the justice systemImage: Ihsaan Haffejee/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

blocks.text: Around 47,000 women and girls — or five every hour — were killed by intimate partners or family members in 2025, according to a United Nations report released on Tuesday.

This figure equates to around 60% of women and girls who were victims of intentional homicides last year, the report said ahead of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on November 25.
The total fatalities were calculated based on statistics from 122 countries and territories. They translate to an average of 129 women and girls killed by their close social circle each day.
Africa recorded the highest number of femicides, at 22,100. Asia followed, with 15,100 victims, ahead of the Americas with 7,400, Europe with 2,100 and Oceania with 300.
Femicide is a hate crime broadly defined as "the intentional killing of women or girls because they are female."
Why so many women fear for their lives in South Africa
One in three women experienced physical or sexual violence
The report also found that although global homicide rates have declined, femicide rates have fallen at a slower pace, particularly in the Americas and Europe.
According to the UN, this shows the barriers women often face in accessing the justice system and that "these crimes are deeply rooted in social norms and gender stereotypes."
Nearly one in three women worldwide have experienced physical or sexual violence, yet only 7% reported it to the police, a separate UN Women report found.

According to estimates by UN Women and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC, the number of women and girls killed by a family member or an intimate partner has wavered between 45,000 and 51,000 over the past several years.
Gang warfare in Ecuador fuels wave of femicides

"Frightening attitudes, social norms, and the failure of institutional safeguards create an environment in which killing a wife, daughter, mother, or sister becomes 'tolerable,'" UNODC director Monica Juma said. "Changing this reality calls for sustained action across all levels of society."

Sima Bahous, executive director of UN Women, said that the world needed to "act urgently to ensure no warning sign is ignored, no survivor is left without protection, and no perpetrator escapes accountability."

articles.title: Researcher who helped improve melanoma survival rates among winners of top Australian science prize
articles.summary:
Georgina Long and subatomic physicist Anthony Thomas recognised in Prime Minister’s Prizes for Science

  • Get our
articles.byline: Donna Lu Assistant editor, climate, environment and science

blocks.text: When Prof Georgina Long was starting out in melanoma treatment and research, “my waiting room would change so rapidly”.

Referring to her patients with stage 4 melanoma, the oncologist and medical director at the Melanoma Institute Australia said she wouldn’t “see the same face for more than nine months, 12 months maximum”.
“We’ve flipped that … now over 50% of people are cured with melanoma that once was almost universally terminal,” Long said.
Her research, which has led to effective drug therapies for the cancer, has improved five-year survival rates 10-fold for people with stage 4 melanoma.
In recognition of her pioneering immunotherapy work, Long was one of two researchers awarded the top gong at the Prime Minister’s Prizes for Science on Tuesday night.

The prize was also awarded to Prof Anthony Thomas, a subatomic physicist at the University of Adelaide whose work has “redefined humanity’s understanding of the proton, dark matter and neutron stars, helping unlock the mysteries of the cosmos”.

The predictions of his “cloudy bag model” have led to experiments around the world, he said in a statement, including “to understand the results of supercomputer calculations of quantum chromodynamics”.
‘Huge honour’
Long said receiving the $250,000 prize was “a huge honour”.
“Although it’s awarded to me, it really does belong to a lot of people,” she said, crediting her colleagues, international research collaborators and patients.

“What we do in melanoma has impacted other cancers,” said Long, who was named Australian of the Year in 2024 alongside the late Prof Richard Scolyer. “Immunotherapy started in melanoma – that’s the cancer that set the bar.”

Last month, Long announced the results of a clinical trial which found that intismeran, a personalised mRNA-based melanoma vaccine, significantly reduced the risk of cancer recurrence or death within two years.
The research – which did not form part of her prime minister’s prize nomination – was the first time an individualised cancer vaccine showed positive results in a phase 3 clinical trial.
“It’s taken decades to try to outsmart cancer,” she said. “It’s still difficult – we’re not curing the other 50% [of melanoma]. We’ve got a lot of work to do.”
after newsletter promotion

Prof Mark Smythe of the University of Queensland was awarded the prize for innovation. The co-founder of six biotechnology companies, Smythe has turned Australian research into approved medicines for psoriasis and polycythaemia vera, a slow-growing blood cancer.

Among the other award recipients was associate professor Fengwang Li of the University of Sydney, who won the Malcolm McIntosh prize for physical scientist of the year. Li was recognised for his expertise in converting carbon emissions into clean energy and sustainable manufacturing materials.
Li “solved a longstanding international roadblock in carbon capture known as the ‘carbonate paradox’, where captured carbon dioxide dissolves into carbonate salts that escape into the atmosphere”.

blocks.caption: Prof Anthony Thomas. Photograph: Prime Minister's Prizes for Science

blocks.text: The prizes, now in their 27th year, are Australia’s most prestigious awards for achievements in scientific research, innovation and teaching, and the practice and preservation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander knowledge systems.
The science minister, Tim Ayres, said the prizes recognise “Australians from different backgrounds, disciplines and perspectives whose work is strengthening Australia’s scientific capability”.
“This year’s recipients demonstrate the extraordinary breadth and depth of Australian science, and I congratulate each of them,” Ayres said in a statement.

articles.title: Bombed factories, billion-dollar opportunity: Why German companies keep investing in Ukraine
articles.summary: German companies remain committed to Ukraine despite million-dollar losses, an unreliable energy supply and a shortage of skilled workers. They are betting on new markets and long-term growth.

image.caption: Foreign companies operating in Ukraine see big opportunities, but also face substantial risksImage: Sergey Bobok/AFP

blocks.text: Power plants, train stations, shopping centers, warehouses, and residential buildings: the massive Russian attacks on civilian targets across Ukraine continue unabated. Industrial facilities have also come under attack, affecting German companies.

"Over the past few months, goods and facilities worth several hundred million euros have gone up in smoke," reported Oliver Gierlichs, who heads Bayer's operations in Ukraine and serves as president of the German-Ukrainian Chamber of Industry and Commerce (AHK Ukraine). The damage is estimated at €500 million ($544 million).

At the 9th German-Ukrainian Business Forum, held in Berlin on November 20, Gierlichs described the situation on the ground. Together with two other German business associations, the AHK had invited around 500 participants from politics and industry, including German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi.

According to the AHK, just over 2,000 German companies are active in Ukraine. German direct investment in the country totals around €1 billion ($1.1 billion). The situation remains critical due to the ongoing attacks, Gierlichs said. "We are preparing for a difficult winter."
Made in Germany — Rebuilding Ukraine
Ukrainian economy under pressure
After posting comparatively strong growth rates in recent years, Ukraine's economy has slowed sharply since the summer.

"The intensified Russian attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure and production capacity in recent months have significantly worsened the economic outlook," according to the latest analysis by the Kyiv School of Economics (KSE), which warns of "substantial risks."

Energy supplies are under strain, and electricity remains in short supply. Companies are also grappling with a worker shortage, as many people have been mobilized for military service or have fled abroad to escape the attacks. German business leaders also cite burdensome approval processes and unclear regulations in Ukraine.

"Not a single German company has left Ukraine since the start of this war," Merz emphasized at the business forum. He also pointed out that "in 2025, trade between Germany and Ukraine exceeded €12 billion, an increase of 4.4% compared with the previous year."
EU releases €3.2 billion from Ukraine recovery fund
Benefits extend beyond Ukraine

Military cooperation currently tops the agenda in German-Ukrainian relations. Germany continues to supply large quantities of defense equipment, but new capabilities are increasingly being developed through joint ventures. At the business forum, held at the House of German Business Associations in Berlin, the long-range combat drone "Anubis," produced by the German-Ukrainian joint venture Auterion Airlogix, was displayed in the foyer. The drone was developed in Ukraine, and the software in Germany.

A total of 5,000 drones are to be produced near Munich. This marks the first time Germany has established industrial-scale production of heavy attack drones on its own soil. "Through this cooperation, Germany's technological capacity for innovation is expanding in ways that would have been unimaginable just a few years ago," Merz said.

The chancellor is convinced that cooperation between the two countries will also benefit Germany's civilian industries. "What we invest in Ukraine today will be repaid many times over through stability, export opportunities, joint projects, and economic growth," Merz said.
$524 billion for reconstruction

For foreign companies operating in Ukraine, it is a continuous balancing act: on the one hand, substantial risks persist; on the other, Ukraine represents a land of opportunity, with a market size virtually unmatched anywhere else in Europe. In February 2025, the European Commission and the Ukrainian government estimated that Ukraine would need $524 billion in funding for reconstruction and recovery over the following ten years. This figure has likely grown even larger since then.

In this context, Ukraine is increasingly seen not merely as a recipient of aid but also as a potential future business destination. The country aims to modernize its economy, bring it into alignment with EU standards, and achieve deeper integration into the European single market over the long term.
Can Ukraine still count on Germany?
Mechanical engineering, energy, and infrastructure opportunities

"We see significant opportunities in the defense industry, the energy sector, infrastructure, information technology, and many other industries," Ukrainian Prime Minister Koretskyi said in Berlin. "German expertise and Ukrainian drive, combined with unity and determination, make for a powerful partnership," Oliver Gierlichs noted.

However, achieving this will require greater support, the AHK president emphasized. "Companies need reliable financing and investment guarantees, as well as effective instruments to protect themselves against war-related risks." Reliable logistics, predictable business conditions, and faster administrative procedures will also be essential, he said.
Investment guarantees and reforms as prerequisites for new projects

At the business forum, Chancellor Merz pledged support in these areas while also calling on Ukraine to pursue further reforms, particularly to strengthen the rule of law and combat corruption. "These reforms are a prerequisite for additional financial assistance and investment."

Another challenge stems from the differing interests of the partners. German companies are seeking to expand into new markets, while their Ukrainian counterparts seek technology transfers and local production to keep as much value creation as possible in the country. "Export fees or legal restrictions on the transfer of intellectual property rights stand in the way of joint innovation efforts," the chancellor cautioned.
High-tech revolution in defense
Who is financing Ukraine's reconstruction?

Representatives of Ukrainian business associations estimate that the private sector could cover up to 40% of Ukraine's reconstruction costs in the long term. For now, however, many projects rely on support from international development banks, government guarantees, or public funding programs. Without such support, many investments would be difficult to undertake.

In principle, business investment follows a straightforward model: companies commit their own capital and bear the losses if a venture fails commercially. When bank loans are involved, the risk is initially shared by the company and the lending institution. Government-backed projects are different: when investment guarantees are in place, companies are compensated for any losses incurred.

This does not apply when companies incur losses as a result of their own business decisions. Compensation may, however, be available in cases involving political actions, such as expropriation, or when war destroys assets and disrupts operations. Under a government guarantee, the taxpayer ultimately bears the risk in such circumstances. By the end of 2025, the German government had provided investment guarantees covering a total investment volume of €558 million ($611 million) in Ukraine.

German companies hoping to benefit from Ukraine's reconstruction need to establish partnerships and build a long-term presence in the country now. After all, the competition is already heating up. At the German-Ukrainian Business Forum, participants noted that German business leaders have often been more risk-averse than their counterparts from Turkey, India, and China. International interest in Ukraine's reconstruction is considerable, and German companies are far from the only ones vying for contracts.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: EU to impose cap on Chinese hybrid EV imports next month
articles.summary: Temporary quotas on vehicles entering the bloc tariff-free will also apply to cars from the UK, Japan and Turkey

blocks.text: The EU will next month impose its threatened caps on the number of Chinese hybrid cars that can be imported into the bloc without facing a tariff, the European Commission has announced.

The quotas will also apply to hybrids from Japan, Turkey, South Korea and the UK, but the principal purpose is to limit imports from China after an agreement with Beijing in October that has led to a rise in exports to the bloc.

The quota, under World Trade Organization rules, is temporary and will apply for 200 days from 1 December during an investigation into imports of plug-in and battery-powered hybrid vehicles. The EU is attempting to cut its huge trade deficit with China.

“In view of the sensitivity of the hybrids sector, its strategic importance to the union economy in terms of innovation, electrification and employment, and the existence of sufficient evidence showing that imports of hybrids threaten to cause serious injury to the union industry,” the official journal said on Tuesday.
It will limit tariff-free imports of Chinese vehicles to 350,000 in the first year or about 191,000 over 200 days.
First-year quotas would be set at 310,000 for Japan, 230,000 for Turkey, 105,000 for South Korea and 190,000 for the UK, which last year exported 166,000 hybrids to the EU.
The quota amounts to about half of the number of Chinese hybrids expected to be imported to the EU in the next 12 months.
Figures in the journal showed that imports of Chinese EVs rocketed from 21,000 units in 2020 to 438,000 in 2024 when tariffs were imposed.
After the tariffs were imposed, imports of EVs began to “flatten out”, with a “clear shift” from EVs to hybrids from China, it said.
Worldwide exports of hybrids from China rocketed from 191,000 vehicles in 2023 to 1.124m in 2025, the EU said.
To head off “the likelihood of substantially increased imports into the union”, the EU now is imposing a quota.

The volume limits are “safeguard” measures that have to apply to all big exporters of ‌hybrid cars to the EU. Other countries to which the import caps apply are South Korea, Mexico, Morocco, Serbia and the US, but they are most restrictive for China.
after newsletter promotion
According to industry reports, non-EU countries including the UK have questioned the allocations.
At a WTO goods council meeting last week, South Korea questioned whether the investigation was fair and transparent. Japan, the UK, Switzerland and Turkey stressed transparency and due process.

China’s commerce ministry said it hoped the EU would abide by the consensus the two sides had reached, and that it reserved all rights to firmly safeguard the legitimate interests of Chinese industries.
The European Commission said imports from China came not just at the expense of EU production, but were also eating into the market shares of other exporters such as Japan and South Korea.
The UK is still fighting against a 10% tariff on all exports of EVs to China, due to come into force on 1 January under the 2020 Brexit trade and cooperation deal.

It has now been intrinsically linked to Andy Burnham’s attempts to get the UK classified as a European manufacturer in the EU’s still-to-be-finalised “Made in Europe” scheme, which protects against cheap Chinese imports.

articles.title: How cautious investors are struggling to avoid the AI bubble
articles.summary: From Nvidia to Coreweave, AI and tech stocks have swung sharply in recent months. Some investors still see plenty of room to run, while others are trying to diversify — and finding it harder than…

image.caption: One day green, the next day red — global stock markets have swung wildly in recent monthsImage: Yuki Iwamura/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index roared back to life this week after a worrying sell-off recently that saw huge falls in technology and artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks.
After suffering its worst week since the pandemic crash of March 2020, the Nasdaq opened Monday nearly 1,700 points, or 7%, higher.

The AI trade received a further boost after Nvidia reinstated CEO Jensen Huang on Monday, just 11 days after he was forced to resign amid a scandal involving extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
The chipmaker's stock rose more than 30% on the news, opening at nearly $170 (€155.5) per share and recovering most of the losses since last month, when the affair was first reported.

The surge helped propel US stock indices to their best day since last year. But in premarket trading on Tuesday, Nvidia fell about 5%, underscoring the volatility of the market and the risks facing the AI sector and the broader tech industry.
Will Anthropic put profits over security?
How passive investing is fueling the AI trade
The recent volatility around AI, memory chips and other technology stocks has unnerved even the most experienced and bullish investors.

Yet, those seeking a haven away from the United States stock market, which has enjoyed the majority of the AI hype — along with Taiwan and South Korea — are increasingly finding few places to shelter.

Economists warn that this is partly due to the way index funds, including exchange-traded funds (ETFs), work. These funds hold the pensions and other savings of hundreds of millions of passive investors.
These indices have become increasingly exposed to the AI boom.

blocks.caption: The rise of neo-stock brokers, like Trade Republic in Europe, has spurred public interest in investingImage: Claudia Nass/CHROMORANGE/picture alliance

blocks.text: Riding the winners works — until it doesn't
Most flagship index funds are keen to ride winners, so they automatically buy stocks according to a company's market value. The bigger a company grows, the more of it they hold.
The values of Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet and other US technology giants have benefited from this effect, with many soaring after ChatGPT was first released in late 2022.

The US also has an outsized position in funds that track the global economy. Nine of the top 10 holdings of the MSCI All Country World Index (ACWI), an index of more than 2,400 firms across 47 developed and emerging markets, are US Big Tech names.
The other is TSMC, a Taiwanese chipmaker that produces 90% of the high-end AI semiconductors.
Together, these 10 holdings make up nearly a quarter of the index.
Although it's a global index, nearly two-thirds of MSCI ACWI's value is in US-listed companies, even though they make up only around a fifth of its firms.
Don't put all your chips in AI stocks
"A well-diversified portfolio should ... reasonably represent the entire global economy," Gerd Kommer, founder of the Munich-based asset manager Gerd Kommer Invest, told DW.
"That's not the case if 70% of the portfolio is concentrated in just one country — the US. The global economy is more resilient than any national economy."
Kommer, who is known as Germany's "ETF pope," said investors need exposure to all economic sectors and that no single sector should make up more than a quarter of a portfolio.
Yet, even if investors want to avoid US-dominated World funds altogether, the AI trade still overshadows several other top index funds.

In MSCI's Emerging Market index, for example, the top 10 make up 37.5% of its value and TSMC alone accounts for almost 16%. Tech, chip and internet firms make up eight of the largest holdings, alongside two banks — one Chinese, one Indian.

blocks.caption: President Donald Trump has pressured TSMC to move some chip production from Taiwan to the USImage: Cheng-Chia Huang/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: How funds fuel investor hubris
That matters, according to Dimitri Vayanos, a finance professor at the London School of Economics who studies how passive investing pushes up the prices of the biggest firms.
"My model suggests that the effects of flows into index funds are larger when the large stocks happen to be in the same industry," Vayanos told DW.
When some investors get over-optimistic about a company and push the stock price up, index funds add to that price pressure.

Professional investors then often bet against overpriced stocks, a practice known as "shorting," which helps pull prices back down. But that's far riskier with, say, a tech giant than with a small firm.
"Being short 1% of SpaceX involves much more risk than being short 1% of a small company," said Vayanos.

The problem gets worse when the biggest firms are all in the same sector, as they are now. As short-sellers hold back, the biggest stocks climb further, creating what he calls an "amplification-overpricing spiral."
Lower AI risk outside of US, Asia
To cut exposure to AI-related stocks, investors may have to turn to developed market funds outside the US and Southeast Asia. These funds have offered lower returns over the past decade.
In the MSCI Europe, Australasia and Far East (EAFE) index fund, the top 10 holdings make up about 14.5% of the index, about 40% lower than the all-country world index.
EAFE's major holdings include healthcare giant Roche, oil major Shell, HSBC bank and Nestle — the world's largest food and beverage company.

However, its biggest holding, ASML, is still very much part of the AI trade. The Dutch tech firm sells the equipment that firms such as TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK Hynix and Micron need to make their chips.
Are AI companies becoming more powerful than governments?
AI crash will have ripple effects

If Monday's rebound in the AI trade is sustained, stock prices may move sharply higher over the next few months. Yet if history is a guide, the bubble will eventually burst, leaving both institutional and passive investors nursing heavy losses.
Kommer warned that if the AI bubble bursts, "in all likelihood it will drag down the global stock market," though the damage would be most severe in tech and AI stocks.

Those hit hardest would be retail investors "with heavy portfolio weights in tech and AI stocks," he said, including "a lot of people who have bought individual AI-related stocks on top of their equity ETFs."
LSE's Vayanos thinks it is still "certainly safer to hold an ETF than to hold individual stocks."

But as index providers add mega-IPOs such as SpaceX and Claude-maker Anthropic to benchmarks within weeks of their debut, and money continues to pour into passive funds, he warned that "the conditions are present for the effects of our theory to be even stronger."

articles.title: ICC prosecution to present 100 witnesses; protective measures may be implemented
articles.summary: The International Criminal Court (ICC) spokesperson on Tuesday said the prosecution team is expected to present over 100 witnesses during the trial of former president Rodrigo Duterte, with the…

blocks.text: Published November 24, 2026 6:53pm

The International Criminal Court (ICC) spokesperson on Tuesday said the prosecution team is expected to present over 100 witnesses during the trial of former president Rodrigo Duterte, with the tribunal possibly implementing protective measures for them.
Duterte’s trial is set to begin on November 30. In a statement to the media, ICC Spokesperson Oriane Maillet said this would be the first trial pertaining to a situation in the Philippines.

“The prosecution currently anticipates calling about 100 witnesses over the course of the trial, and after that, after the prosecution's case, the defense will have the opportunity to present its own evidence and its own witnesses,” Maillet said.
However, while 100 are expected to participate, Maillet said the court has authorized more than 500 victims to partake in the trial through legal representatives.

“The court also has a legal obligation to protect victims and witnesses, and depending on the circumstances of each individual, the judges may order protective measures to safeguard the security and the well-being of these witnesses,” Maillet said.
According to the ICC spokesperson, the exact duration of the trial will still depend on different factors, such as the number of witnesses and volume of evidence.
Maillet said the court has extensively prepared for Duterte’s trial, noting that it has generated national and international public interest.
The ICC briefings can be followed in person or online. However, the judges may move to a private or closed session to protect confidential information.

“Let's be clear, the court's role is not to pursue any political objective. Rather, it's to determine through independent and impartial judicial proceedings whether the charges have been proven according to the law. A fair trial is a fundamental principle of the Rome Statute,” Maillet said.
“Mr. Duterte is presumed innocent, unless and until proven guilty before the court,” she added.
What to expect
With Duterte’s trial set to open on November 30, Joanna Korner is set to return as the Presiding Judge, alongside Judge Keebong Paek and Judge Nicolas Guillou.
The judges will first check if Duterte understands the charges being lodged against him and then he will enter a plea.
Maillet said that after this, the prosecution and legal representatives of victims will deliver opening statements. The defense’s opening statement will be heard later on in the trial.

“Following these opening statements, the testimony of the prosecution's first witness is expected to begin. Following that, the first five prosecution witnesses are expected to testify before the winter judicial recess, starting on the 18th of December,” Maillet said. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Private diaries of Pope Francis reveal spiritual crisis and visions of the devil
articles.summary: The late Pope Francis suffered a two-year spiritual crisis starting in 2021 when he felt tempted by the devil and struggled with how to wield power over the Catholic Church, a new collection of his…

image.caption: The Private Diary of Pope Francis collects entries that Pope Francis made in a small planning notebook from 1992. (Andrew Medichini/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World

The late Pope Francis suffered a two-year spiritual crisis starting in 2021 when he felt tempted by the devil and struggled with how to wield power over the Catholic Church, a new collection of his private diaries published on Tuesday revealed.
Diaries provide insight into the faith and struggles of late pope

Francis, who led the Church for 12 years until his death in April 2025, experienced visions of the devil and hell and battled against not wanting to be someone "who uses others like puppets," according to the diaries and accompanying commentary.
The volume does not specify whom the late pope might have treated like a puppet.
"It was all mixed with governance issues, pressure regarding decisions to make, and aridity and desolation," said a December 2022 entry from Francis describing his crisis.

items: Pope vows to end coverups, fight sex abuse with 'wrath of God'
Pope Francis, committed to service, humility and healing, dead at 88

blocks.text: Considered a reformer who tried to open the staid Church to the world, Francis encountered unusually strong resistance to his papacy from conservative cardinals, who worried he would water down the Church's firm teachings.

Cardinal Victor Fernández, a close Francis collaborator, collected the diaries — the first by a pope to be released to the public since the 1960s — and arranged them into a volume with his own accompanying commentary.

The late pope "ultimately recognized that it was the worst trial that had tormented him ... and that he felt that he was in a continual battle not to fall into this demonic seduction," wrote Fernández.
Believed he had seen the devil
The Private Diary of Pope Francis collects diary entries that Francis, an Argentine and the first pope from the Americas, made in a small planning notebook from 1992.

The diaries provide a rare and striking insight into the faith and mental struggles of the late pope. Most recent popes have directed that their papers be burned after their deaths, although some papers of John Paul II, pope from 1978 to 2005, were later made public. The last pope to have diaries published posthumously was John XXIII, who died in 1963.
Fernández, a fellow Argentine whom Francis appointed in 2023 to lead the Vatican's powerful doctrinal office, does not present the full diary but gives excerpts, arranged by theme.
Pope Francis receives a traditional drum as a gift during a public event in Iqaluit, Nunavut, during his 2022 papal visit across Canada. (Nathan Denette/The Canadian Press)

Totalling 160 pages, the diaries offer few direct comments on the events of Francis's papacy or about Vatican officials. They focus instead on the late pope's spiritual life, including his belief that he had seen the devil and the entrance to hell and that God spoke to him in dreams.

An entry from January 2021, at the beginning of the late pope's self-described spiritual crisis, lists three times throughout Francis's life when he thought he had seen the devil, including once as pope in a meeting with Vatican officials.
"I can't forget the powerful raspiness of his voice," Francis wrote in the entry about the later vision. "The Lord granted me an opportunity to leave that meeting, and he thus freed me."

The diary entries begin in December 1992, when the future Francis, then known as Jorge Mario Bergoglio, was an auxiliary bishop of Buenos Aires. They run until August 2024, about eight months before his death aged 88.
Did Pope Francis make the Catholic Church more inclusive?

Addressing Francis's spiritual crisis, Fernández recounts being in a meeting with the pope in 2023, when another bishop asked Francis why he did not chastise an unnamed Vatican official who had been speaking badly about Francis in public.
Vision of hell

"[Francis] responded by explaining that he felt a strong sensation in his heart that God did not want him to become a puppeteer who uses and manipulates people according to his own convenience," Fernández states.
Francis recounted seeing a vision of hell in a June 2018 entry. "Last night I saw the entrance to Hell," he wrote. "I peeked in to look a little, and it terrified me."
"I grabbed the Rosary as a weapon," Francis wrote, referring to Catholic prayer beads. "I thank the Lord for this help."

The diary does refer directly to a few events of Francis's papacy, including his contested 2018 visit to Chile, when the late pope was sharply criticized for dismissing allegations of sexual abuse and cover-up against a bishop there.
During Pope Francis's 2018 trip to Chile, he was criticized for dismissing allegations of sexual abuse and cover-up against a bishop there. (Alessandro Bianchi/Reuters)
Francis later apologized and summoned the country's bishops to Rome, where they all offered to resign in an unprecedented move.
"Devastated because of the situation in Chile," Francis wrote in a 2021 entry. "It was hard for me to admit what happened in Chile; I didn't think it was so serious."

items: Pope Francis set the Vatican on a path toward tolerance in a changing world
The legacy of Pope Francis

blocks.text: Fernández also recounts Francis commenting on some senior officials, including U.S. Cardinal Robert Prevost, who in May 2025 was elected Francis's successor and became Pope Leo. Francis called Prevost "a great pastor, a generous missionary, and an irreproachable man," Fernández states.

Francis also offered kind thoughts about Guinean Cardinal Robert Sarah and German Cardinal Gerhard Müller, two of his most vocal critics. He said Sarah had "a refined spiritual sensitivity" and that Müller "seems aggressive, but he's a good man," according to Fernández.
As for his own election as pope, Francis made one simple entry in July 2013, more than four months after he became pontiff. "They elected me pope on March 13," he wrote.

articles.title: Who was left in the dark on Trump’s ‘magnificent’ PH-US deal?
articles.summary: Senator Erwin Tulfo, sponsor of the DFA budget, says the agency was 'taken aback' by Trump's pronouncements

blocks.text: SURPRISE APPEARANCE. UFC CEO Dana White listens as US President Donald Trump speaks in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House in Washington, DC, US, November 9, 2026.
Aaron Schwartz/REUTERS
Senator Erwin Tulfo, sponsor of the DFA budget, says the agency was 'taken aback' by Trump's pronouncements

items: Senator Imee Marcos questioned the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) about US President Trump's claims regarding a trade deal that would have the Philippines sourcing all its energy and agricultural imports from the US.

The DFA, represented by Senator Erwin Tulfo, indicated they were unaware of Trump's assertions and that the economic aspects were managed by the Department of Trade and Industry and the Department of Agriculture.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Was the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) left out of the loop on what US President Donald Trump claimed to be the “biggest trade deal” between the Philippines and the United States?

During the plenary debates on the DFA’s proposed P35.2-billion budget on Tuesday, November 24, Senator Imee Marcos sought clarification on Trump’s claim that the Philippines had agreed to source 100% of its energy and agricultural imports from the US, a supposed highlight of his recent state visit to Manila.
Imee also flagged Trump’s “very thinly veiled threat” that there would be “trouble” if the Philippines failed to uphold its end of the bargain.

Senator Erwin Tulfo, sponsor of the DFA budget, referred the questions to the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) and the Department of Agriculture (DA). Malacañang had tasked these agencies to handle the economic aspects of the agreement, he said, while the DFA continued to monitor developments.
Tulfo also said the Philippines and the US would hold a bilateral meeting in March 2027, where security issues would be in the agenda.

Imee pressed the DFA on the implications of Trump’s warning. “I’m compelled to ask the DFA that trouble is defined how? Certainly, neither the DTI nor the DA is capable of understanding what that threat actually meant,” she said.

Following his Asia trip, Trump claimed the Philippines had accepted his offer to source all its imported agricultural requirements from the US instead of other countries, including Brazil. He also claimed that Manila had agreed to stop relying on the Middle East for its energy supplies.
Responding to Marcos’ questions, Tulfo said the DFA was “taken aback” by Trump’s claims.

“I think there’s an admission on the part of the DFA that they were kept in the dark regarding this announcement and that hereafter the matters have been assigned to others,” Imee said. “It’s really alarming that, in fact, there are no prior consultations with the foreign policy and diplomacy experts in the DFA.”
Senate Majority Leader Juan Miguel “Migz” Zubiri, for his part, cast doubt on Trump’s announcement, describing the supposed commitments as “impossible.”

“We know US President Trump, he probably said that to be able to gain local popularity in the US. I’m sure that’s not what they agreed on because that is impossible. I don’t think the country could get 100% agricultural products from the US, or power as well,” Zubiri said.
Executive Secretary Ralph Recto, in a separate interview, also expressed skepticism over Trump’s claims.
“I doubt very much that, that would happen. What’s important is we are diversifying sources of energy and food,” Recto said.

For now, the administration appears to be tempering Trump’s sweeping claims. But Marcos’ questions raise another concern: If it were true, why was the country’s foreign policy experts not consulted on the supposed commitments, and what did the Philippines exactly agree to? – Rappler.com

articles.title: EU imposes import quotas for hybrid vehicles from China
articles.summary: The EU is trying to protect its own car manufacturers from what it called "overcapacity" in China. Carmakers in the bloc, especially in Germany, have been lagging behind their Chinese rivals.

image.caption: China has been able to mass produce electric and hybrid vehicles at low costs that risk putting European competitors out of businessImage: DW

blocks.text: The European Union announced on Tuesday that it was capping the number of hybrid vehicles that can be imported into the bloc from China.
The quota is to stand at around 15% on top of the volume imported in the previous year.
The announcement follows an agreement made between the EU's trade commissioner Maros Sefcovic and Chinese Trade Minister Wang Wentao in October.
China, on Tuesday, called on the EU to stick to the "compliant, and balanced" agreement the two sides had reached.
The cap is set to come into effect on December 1.
What did the EU say about the import quota for Chinese hybrid vehicles?

"These restrictions are needed to protect EU industry against a sharp recent increase in imports of such vehicles … [following] an investigation that showed imports of hybrid vehicles into the EU have increased significantly since 2023," the European Commission said in a statement.

"The surge in imports of hybrid passenger vehicles into the EU has been driven by growing global production overcapacity. It is also prompted by increased use of trade-restrictive measures in other major markets," it added, in reference to the range of tariffs introduced in the US under the Trump administration.
Is Europe still a global power? The brutal free trade debate

According to the statement, the import quota covers two types of hybrid vehicle: "full hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs), including mild hybrid electric vehicles (MHEVs)."

Although specifically designed to deal with the influx of Chinese cars into the European market, the country-specific import quota will be valid for all countries whose imports made up more than 2% of EU imports in 2025. Other importers will face a residual cap.
Why is an EU import quota important for Germany?
The goal behind import quotas is to protect a country's, or in this case the European Union's, own producers.
China has become a major player in the car manufacturing market in recent years, especially when it comes to electric and hybrid vehicles, a sector where European manufacturers have fallen behind.

Germany, as the EU's largest economy and a major exporter of vehicles, is a primary beneficiary of the import quota. Several of Germany's car manufacturers have announced widespread layoffs as they see their market shares shrink.

In October, German car manufacturers saw their sales fall by 5.7% in the EU despite a growing market. This meant their market share in the bloc fell from 41.5% to 38.2%, according to consulting firm EY.
How China is upping pressure on German businesses
Europe's booming hybrid and electric market

A report by the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) published on Tuesday found that electric vehicles and hybrids have seen a large uptick in new registrations in Europe in October over the same time last year.
It found that new electric car registrations were up 61.4% across the bloc while plug-in hybrids were up in particular in Italy (+73.1%), Spain (+32.3%), and Germany (+11%).
Hybrid electric vehicles were around a third of all new registrations, with plug-in hybrids making up around 10%.

"The main beneficiaries of this trend are in China," EY said in comments to AFP. "Chinese manufacturers, which are heavily focused on electric cars and plug-in hybrids, increased their EU sales by 73.4% and achieved a new record market share of 13.1%."

"The market share losses suffered by German manufacturers are not an outlier and are not a problem limited to individual countries — it is a clear trend that is now evident in all major European markets," said Constantin Gall of EY. "This is alarming, because Europe is the home market of the German auto industry."

articles.title: Office of the President's proposed P10-B budget breezes through Senate plenary
articles.summary: The Senate plenary on Tuesday afternoon quickly approved the proposed P10 billion budget of the Office of the President (OP) for fiscal year 2027 in two minutes.

blocks.text: Published November 24, 2026 6:25pm
The Senate plenary on Tuesday afternoon quickly approved the proposed P10 billion budget of the Office of the President (OP) for fiscal year 2027 in two minutes.
Budget sponsor Senator JV Ejercito noted that the recommended new appropriations for the OP now amounts to P10,083,518,000.
Senate Majority Leader Juan Miguel Zubiri then moved to terminate the deliberations on OP’s budget “out of courtesy.”
Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente “Tito” Sotto III approved the motion with no objections.
Executive Secretary Ralph Recto was present in the session hall for the plenary debates.
Under the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP), the OP originally sought a total of P10,155,758,000 budget, about 64% lower than the 2026 budget.

Recto previously said the substantial reduction reflected the "lower operational requirements of [the OP's] delivery units and the completion of activities related to the Philippines' hosting of the ASEAN Summit for which no additional funding will be required next year."
"In short, we're asking for less while remaining fully prepared to do more," Recto said the House Committee deliberations into OP’s proposed 2027 budget.
"We believe this amount is sufficient for the Presidency to meet the exacting demands of leading the nation at a time of overlapping domestic and external challenges," he added. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: Palace urges Lacson to file charges on flood control double funds

Malacañang on Tuesday urged Senator Panfilo Lacson to file charges on the alleged duplicate appropriations for some flood control projects and multipurpose buildings in the proposed 2027 national budget.

"Kung may nakita na po si Senator Lacson na naging ghost project sa sinasabi niyo ng mga multipurpose buildings, umpisahan na po nating sampahan ng kaso," Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said in a press briefing.
(If Senator Lacson has already found any ghost projects among the multipurpose buildings he is referring to, start filing cases against them.)
"May mga verified documents po siyang pinanghahawakan para masimulan ang pagsampahan ng kaso," she added.
(Lacson has verified documents to start filing the charges.)
GMA News Online has reached out to Lacson for comment on the matter.
Castro said a thorough investigation is needed since not all repeated appropriations are double appropriations since some projects are funded by phase.
"Since ito ay suspected ghost projects, mas mabuting ipagbigay alam ni rin ni Sen Lascon sa DPWH ang mga maaring anomalya," she said.
(Since these are suspected ghost projects, it is better for Lacson to inform the Department of Public Works and Highways of the possibly anomalies.)
Castro said President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. would veto the proposed 2027 budget should any anomaly be found.
Lacson earlier criticized P241 billion worth of fragmented assistance programs in the Senate version of the proposed 2027 national budget.

Lacson said the Senate should reconsider the allocations, arguing that the P241 billion in "fragmented" aid programs and funding for thousands of multipurpose buildings would not address the country's economic concerns.
The senator also flagged duplicate appropriations for some flood control projects.
“We found more irregularities. Double appropriations. Not only are these flood control projects, but they have also been allocated funding twice,” he said. — BM, GMA News

House Lead Impeachment Prosecutor Rep Gerville Luistro on Tuesday said Vice President Sara Duterte is the best witness that the defense panel can present in the impeachment trial.

"Basing it on the witnesses I have seen so far from the defense, it appears to us na talagang isa lang ang may kakayanang magpaliwanag ng lahat ng ito (there is only one person who can explain all these). And that is the respondent vice president," Luistro said in an interview today.

"So I hope that she avails of this opportunity para maipaliwanag ang kanyang sagot or depensa dito sa mga (to explain her answers or defense regarding these) specific allegations of the prosecution. After all, she has repeatedly said that she will be answering in the proper forum. This is the proper and the best forum," Luistro added.
The legislator from the second district of Batangas is hoping that the next batch of defense witnesses will give testimony that will be relevant.

She said that it is the defense panel's exclusive prerogative to choose which witnesses and documents to present but "we can't help but expect explosive evidence. But that explosive evidence, we haven't seen."
Luistro said the Vice President "should be able to give a reasonable explanation to the Filipino people on why there are specific allegations by the prosecution."
She said Duterte should explain the P817 million in assets that were not declared.
Luistro believes it is possible to conclude the impeachment trial before Congress goes on recess on Dec 19.

"Well, what I can say is I look forward to the conclusion of this process... We have spent so much time on this and I think this is high time for us to put a closure on all of this and for the Filipino people to move on," Luistro said. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: Manitoba wildfire response in 2025 hampered by equipment shortages and fatigue among staff, report concludes
articles.summary: Manitoba was unprepared for the disastrous 2025 wildfire season and needs to devote more money, staff and equipment to ensure it can respond to all manner of emergencies, a new report says.

image.caption: Wildfires at Wanless in spring 2025, a disastrous wildfire season in Manitoba. (AP)

blocks.text: Manitoba
Manitoba was unprepared for the disastrous 2025 wildfire season and needs to devote more money, staff and equipment to ensure it can respond to all manner of emergencies, a new report says.
Province must spend more on people and equipment in order to prepare for future emergencies: document

The 97-page report into the emergency management response for the 2025 wildfires, made public by the province Monday, concluded Manitoba suffered from equipment shortages, staff shortages and poor communication, both among staff members and with the public.

The province also had trouble keeping track of wildfire evacuees, providing accommodations and health services to them, managing fatigue among trained staff and providing psychological support for untrained volunteers, the report said.
Between May and October 2025, 445 wildfires scorched 22,000 square kilometres of the province, which is equivalent to about four per cent of Manitoba's land mass.
Two people died, and almost 33,000 people were displaced from about 12,600 households, with most of the evacuations occurring at First Nations in northern Manitoba.
The report into Manitoba's wildfire response was prepared by Brandon University, with help from the Alberta Emergency Management Agency and the Manitoba Emergency Management Organization.
It concluded trained staff and volunteers in municipalities and First Nations did their best to manage the prolonged burden but ultimately were not prepared for a wildfire season of this magnitude.

items: Northern Manitoba fire chiefs look for new equipment, more volunteers following wildfires

blocks.text: "The duration and scale of the response ... placed sustained pressure on personnel, facilities, accommodation capacity, and co-ordinating organizations," the report stated.

"The experiences gathered through the review reinforce the need for arrangements that can be maintained across extended and concurrent evacuations, including adequate staffing, relief capacity, continuity procedures, suitable facilities and clearly assigned operational responsibilities."
Some of the most acute problems involved "shortages in several categories of critical operational equipment," including wildland pumps, hoses, radios, vehicles and fuel, the report stated.
The lack of resources affected front-line operations, impaired deployment and hampered communications, the report continued.

items: What have Manitoba leaders learned from a summer of wildfire evacuations?

blocks.text: "These challenges were identified by multiple departments and agencies, indicating a systemic preparedness and logistics issue," the report stated.

The report made multiple recommendations, which included spending more money and hiring more staff members to ensure emergency management organizations can better plan for emergencies and respond to them.
Infrastructure Minister Lisa Naylor said the provincial government has accepted all the recommendations.

"It was a really challenging summer, with fires lasting from May until September, and with some communities being evacuated, going home and then being evacuated again," she said in an interview Monday.
"We're looking at expanding our services within Emergency Management Organization and then continuing our work on training."
Naylor would not say whether her government regrets ignoring advice in 2023 from the outgoing Progressive Conservative government to conduct an external review of wildfire preparedness.
The province chose to conduct an internal review instead, based on verbal reports and no written recommendations.

items: Manitoba declined to follow through on urgent plans to review wildfire preparedness after NDP took power
Manitoba wildfire review consisted of ‘meeting notes and verbal discussion’ but no written reports: documents

blocks.text: Naylor said she did not recall the province's decision to forego an external review of wildfire preparedness and does not recall any media coverage about this.
"A lot was happening last summer," she said, referring to 2025.
Interim PC Leader Konrad Narth said Monday he is pleased to see the province express a desire to improve wildfire preparedness but wants to know when those improvements will be made.

Eric Reder, a campaigner for the Wilderness Committee, an environmental organization, said he is pleased to see the report attribute the severity of wildfires to climate change but is disappointed the report does not advocate any form of climate action.
"This report doesn't say that we have to act on climate in order to eliminate the fire risk, and that is a critical takeaway from other folks who have looked at the situation," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Bartley Kives joined CBC Manitoba in 2016. Prior to that, he spent three years at the Winnipeg Sun and then 18 at the Winnipeg Free Press, writing about politics, music, food and outdoor recreation. He's the author of three books — two of them Canadian bestsellers — and the winner of a Canadian Screen Award for reporting.

articles.title: Malacañang dares Alan Cayetano to donate P170,000 for national debt
articles.summary: Malacañang on Tuesday challenged Senator Alan Peter Cayetano to donate P170,000 to help pay off the country's national debt, saying he could set an example for other Filipinos.

blocks.text: Published November 24, 2026 5:56pm
Malacañang on Tuesday challenged Senator Alan Peter Cayetano to donate P170,000 to help pay off the country's national debt, saying he could set an example for other Filipinos.
Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said Cayetano's donation would encourage other Filipinos to voluntarily contribute to the government, on top of paying their taxes.
"Kung may mga mababait na puso at siya naman nagpasimula nito, mas maganda siguro makita mismo natin [kay Cayetano]," Castro said in a press briefing.
(If there are indeed kind-hearted people, and since he was the one who started this, perhaps it would be better for us to see him do it himself.)
Cayetano had floated the idea of Filipinos voluntarily contributing their P170,000 share of the country's P19.66-trillion national debt.
"We don't even have the mechanism for donating," Cayetano said. "What if we start the rich businessmen?"
However, the senator said the government must ensure that public funds and foreign loans are spent wisely to encourage Filipinos to contribute.

In a statement, Cayetano clarified that he was not proposing to impose an additional financial burden on the public but was exploring a voluntary mechanism for those willing and able to help reduce the national debt.

"There's no mechanism [for voluntary contributions] because no one thinks that anyone will donate because we think our government, not just this government, but government after government, it's just kung sino mas corrupt (who's more corrupt)," Cayetano said.

"The proposal to allow ourselves to pay part of our loan or get other people, one, is purely voluntary. Two, dapat gastusin nang tama ng gobyerno ang pera na nakokolekta. Three, i-monitor nang husto y’ung loans," he added.
(Second, the government should spend the money it collects properly. Third, loans should be closely monitored.)— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: German directors' doc on stolen film wins International Emmy Award
articles.summary: Two German film students confronted the American who won festival prizes with their animated movie. "The Talented Mr. F," their documentary on their fight against plagiarism, is now in the spotlight.

image.caption: The movie 'Butty' was suddenly called 'T-130'Image: MDR/Neue Flimmer GmbH

blocks.text: It sounds like the plot of a screenplay, but it happened to two Berlin film students in real life. The documentary they made out of their unusual story, "The Talented Mr. F," has now won an International Emmy Award.
Moritz Henneberg and Julius Drost had created an animated short film for their final project at university.
"Butty" tells the tale of a household robot that gets kicked out when it can't do its job properly.

When the two filmmakers posted the work on YouTube, this touching tale quickly went viral. After generating a huge amount of hits, the duo decided to submit their work to festivals — but they were in for a shock: Organizers told them the film had already been submitted under a different name.
How could that have happened?

US student Samuel Felinton downloaded the film, made minimal edits, gave it a new title, "T-130," and removed the original credits. As the alleged author, he went on to win numerous prizes and made a name for himself in the United States.
A story turned into a documentary, 'The Talented Mr. F'

Shocked by the blatant theft of their work, Henneberg and Drost sought legal advice. They were told that if they opted to sue, the process would be arduous and costly. So, the filmmakers took matters into their own hands and went to the US to confront Felinton — filming their journey along the way.

blocks.caption: Moritz (l) and Julius on a research trip to New York  Image: MDR/Benedikt Hugendubel

blocks.text: "We'd already made documentary films," Henneberg told DW. "And the idea just popped into our heads: This is a brilliant story — let's make a documentary about it."
The two directors had developed a kind of fascination for the man who'd stolen their film.
"We looked at his vlogs and sort of took a deep dive into his world," said Drost. "We almost saw him as a kind of celebrity. We discovered a lot about him and really wanted to meet him in person."
Fascination instead of anger

While family and friends reacted with anger, the two young filmmakers remained surprisingly calm. They were more perplexed than anything: "Our families and friends hated Samuel. But we just wanted to understand what had happened," they said.

The pair put together a film crew and traveled to Morgantown, West Virginia — the university town where Felinton lives. With the help of a New York filmmaker pretending to make a documentary about young animators, they won Felinton's trust — and then Henneberg, Drost and Felinton were finally in a room together.

blocks.caption: Julius and Moritz gather information about Samuel FelintonImage: MDR/Benedikt Hugendubel

blocks.text: The two German filmmakers had prepared for all manner of scenarios ahead of the meeting: "We expected an emotional reaction — that he'd run away, cry, be ashamed or get aggressive. But he remained completely calm. That was the only thing we hadn't bargained for. We thought his world would implode. But he showed barely any emotion at all," they recalled.

Felinton explained how he'd shortened and "improved" the film and that this was how it became such a success. He agreed to transfer any prize money. His manner was cool and matter-of-fact, which Drost and Henneberg found both unsettling and fascinating. After their chat, the three barbecued together and played a round of basketball.
Sue or stay creative?
Later, many viewers accused the two German filmmakers of being too soft on the plagiarist. Others praised their approach.
"The reactions were very divided," said Drost. "Some said we should've sued him or punched him in the face. Others said we'd shown new ways to resolve conflicts."

"And in the end, it wasn't personal," added Henneberg. "He wanted to make something of himself — he could've taken another film. But if a big studio like Pixar had stolen our film, that'd be quite a different story."

blocks.caption: Samuel Felinton says he doesn't want to be 'forgotten'Image: MDR/Neue Flimmer GmbH

blocks.text: And so, Henneberg and Drost made the conscious decision to keep things respectful.
They didn't want to "publicly embarrass him or punish him any more than necessary," they said, adding that their documentary was sufficient "revenge."

The title of the documentary, "Der talentierte Mister F." ("The Talented Mister F."), is no coincidence. It's a play on the movie title "The Talented Mr. Ripley," the story of a young man who assumes the identity of a wealthy heir and ends up mired in a web of lies, fraud and, finally, murder. And just like Mr. Ripley, Felinton had also assumed a false identity.
Award-winning works
Felinton did actually end up sending them the trophies he had won, as well as a sum of money.

For their part, however, the festivals preferred to keep their distance from the saga. As one organizer said: The prize has been awarded, and there's nothing we can do about it — it's up to these guys to work things out between themselves.

For the original filmmakers themselves, the scandal has also had a positive impact: Since the documentary was released in Germany in October 2025, their animation film has garnered even more attention on YouTube. Henneberg and Drost uploaded it again, and in the credits, special thanks also go out to Samuel Felinton.
And now, the documentary is winning its own awards: Before being honored with the International Emmy Award, it also won a Grimme Prize, one of Germany's most prestigious television awards.

blocks.caption: The team celebrating their International Emmy Award for the documentaryImage: Anne Pollmann/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: 'Don't be afraid to show yourselves'
Felinton was able to steal the film in the first place in part because when it first appeared online in 2023, it could just be downloaded from YouTube.
Drost and Henneberg say uploading "Butty" back then wasn't a mistake, saying that was the risk of putting something online.
The alternative would have been not to show the film at all, they said; then no one would have seen it.
They have a clear message for young creatives.

"Don't be discouraged. Be aware that something like this can happen — but stay creative in how you deal with it. Suing is expensive and often doesn't do much good. Instead, show the world that you're the authors."
What started out as film plagiarism ended up becoming material for another project. And that's perhaps the most unusual twist in this very quirky story.
This article was originally published in German in February 2026 and was updated on November 24, 2026, following the International Emmy Awards.

articles.title: Istanbul 'lion hunt' ends with no big cat found after all
articles.summary: After a major search operation for a lion on the loose in Istanbul woodlands, Turkish authorities said "the animal was neither a lion nor any other big cat."

image.caption: Turkish authorities say the animal was not a lion after all [FILE: January 14, 2026]Image: Tokyo Zoological Park Society/REUTERS

blocks.text: A large-scale search operation for a suspected lion sighted in woodland north of Istanbul has ended, with the animal in question found to be neither a lion nor any other type of big cat, according to the Istanbul governor's office.

The governor's office first issued a statement on Sunday evening saying that security cameras had captured footage of a lion on the loose in Sariyer, north of Istanbul's European side. It said "the lion has been located and the efforts to capture it were underway."
The parks authority also said in an online statement that police officers in the area had spotted "an animal resembling a lion" on surveillance cameras.
Turkish media published grainy images purportedly showing a lioness walking through a grassy area. Some media reports suggested it had escaped from a nearby home.

blocks.caption: Turkish media published thermal images of a 'lioness roaming free'Image: Anka

blocks.text: The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office also issued a statement saying it had launched an investigation focused on identifying the lion's owner.
After a day of searching, however, the Istanbul governor's office said "no ​concrete evidence indicating ‌the presence of a lion was found."
It said ⁠based on new footage, "it has been determined ⁠that the ​animal in the footage is neither a lion nor any other species of big cat."
The governor's office did not provide further information about what the animal seen in the footage was.
Outcry among activists
The earlier reports about a lion on the loose had sparked an outrage among activists.
Northern Forests Defense, an independent ecology advocacy movement, called for "the individuals who illegally held this lion captive to be identified and brought to justice."
"Removing wild animals from their natural habitats and keeping them in captivity in villas is a crime," the organization said on X.
Wildlife conservationist Gokce Coskun said on X that "there are thousands of people keeping lions illegally in Turkey" and "licensed 'lion parks' have sprung up everywhere."
Last year, a lion that escaped from a "theme park" near the southern city of Antalya was shot dead after attacking a man.

Doganay Tolunay, an ecology professor at Istanbul University, said questions must be asked about how a globally threatened species was brought into Turkey, how it passed through customs and why those keeping it have not been identified.
Although keeping wild animals as pets is forbidden in Turkey, the country has become a hub for the illegal wild animal trade as traffickers exploit its air links to Africa and Asia.
In December 2024, a young gorilla was rescued after being discovered in a crate at Istanbul Airport.

articles.summary: Newly-released bodycam footage shows the moment troops detained 'El Chapo Isidro', who had managed to evade capture for years.

blocks.text: Newly-released bodycam footage shows the moment troops entered a house and detained a Mexican drug lord who had managed to evade capture for years.
The video shows armed personnel entering via a garage and finding Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, also known as 'El Chapo Isidro', who was on the FBI's most wanted list.
Seven suspects were killed in last Friday's operation, as were four members of the Mexican army who were travelling to reinforce security in Guasave, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
The arrest of Meza Flores in the northern Sinaloa state sparked a wave of unrest, which led to eight alleged drug cartel members being detained for their involvement in the retaliatory violence.

articles.title: Pakistani astronaut to join Chinese space mission
articles.summary: A Pakistani astronaut is set to become to the first foreigner to board China's Tiangong space station. Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a payload specialist, will join the Shenzhou-24 mission when it launches…

image.caption: Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali (left) is set to become the first foreigner to join a Chinese space missionImage: Tingshu Wang/REUTERS

blocks.text: China on Tuesday unveiled the crew for this week's Shenzhou-24 space mission, with a Pakistani payload specialist set to become the first foreign astronaut to board its Tiangong space station.

The China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) said that Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a 40-year-old former Pakistani air force pilot, would join two Chinese colleagues when the mission launches from the Jiuquan launch center in China's northwestern Gobi Desert at 8:18 a.m. local time (0018 GMT) on Wednesday.
"I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis," Ali told a news conference on Tuesday, switching between Urdu, Mandarin and English.
"To every child who is watching while I'm in orbit, just look up at the sky and remember that I am up there with your dreams," he said.
Pakistan's first astronaut to fly with China
Pakistan: 'Source of joy and pride'
Pakistani officials welcomed Ali's selection as a significant milestone in relations between Islamabad and Beijing who are this year marking 75 years of cooperation in space.

Information Minister Attaullah Tarar described the mission as a "source of joy and pride for the entire nation" and Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said the mission underscored the "iron brotherhood" between the two countries.

"This mission is not a finish line; I hope the next chapter of China-Pakistan space cooperation will grow from one astronaut and one flight to multiple joint flights, to the Moon, to Mars, and beyond," said Ali.
"Together with my Chinese crew mates, I will show that this friendship is real, not only on paper, but also in orbit."

blocks.caption: Muhammad Zeeshan Ali (left) will accompany two Chinese colleagues on the missionImage: Xinhua/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What will Pakistani astronaut Ali do in space?

Ali will not be the first Pakistani in space, with Monaco-based polar explorer Namira Salim having flown on Virgin Galactic's Galactic 04 mission in October 2023. But he will be the first foreign astronaut to join a Chinese mission.

During a short orbital flight expected to last around five days, Ali will carry out a series of experiments in the fields of biotechnology and photosynthetic microorganisms before returning to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft, which docked at the Tiangong in May.
China has poured billions of dollars into its space program. Its prized Tiangong space station is stewarded by teams of three astronauts that are typically rotated every six months.
Beijing is aiming to land Chinese astronauts on the moon for the first time by 2030 and is seen as the main space rival to the United States, which is hoping to return to the lunar surface in 2028.
