articles.title: N.B. teen's life marred by sexual abuse after RCMP, other institutions failed to protect her
articles.summary: Kim Budd spent much of her childhood on the run. When she thought she'd finally found a safe place to stay, it turned out to be anything but, and the adults and institutions that were supposed to…

image.caption: (CBC News Graphics)

blocks.text: On a bone-chilling night in January 1983, Kim Budd, just 15, sits in handcuffs at the Riverview RCMP detachment in a suburb of Moncton, N.B.
She’s run away from home — again.
"I spent the whole night with them," recalled Budd, now 59 and living in western Quebec. "They locked me to a chair."

There's no mug shot and no charges because the teen has committed no crime. But the officer who picked her up off the frigid street isn't sure what to do with this runaway, and worries she'll bolt if she isn't restrained.
Tired and uncomfortable, the girl sits there until the morning shift arrives. One of the Mounties who has just come in pays her special attention.
"The first time I ever laid eyes on him I had a cold pit in the centre of my stomach," Budd recalled decades later. "He was sitting on the desk and he kept looking at me and watching me."
Budd, with her dark eyes and hair cut in an '80s shag, glares back with a scowl perfected by teenagers.
Then the Mountie approaches with an unexpected offer. He tells her he and his wife run an emergency foster home for kids like her. Would she like to stay with them?
The teen, who has already bounced from abusive home to group residence to reform school and then back to the same abusive home, agrees.
"He just wanted to help me. That's what I thought," she said.

In fact, the Mountie would demand much more from the troubled runaway, and the shelter and security he offered her would soon turn into a new form of confinement. She would learn that none of the adults who were supposed to protect her — not the police, not the doctors, not the child welfare officials — could be trusted when she needed them most, and the more she cried out for help, the less anyone would listen to the terrible truth she struggled to tell.
Kim Budd, now 59, at an Ottawa-area horse farm where she says she finds a sense of peace and security after everything she's been through. (Turgot Yeter/CBC)
Kim Budd was a runner. She ran away from adults, and often into trouble.

Born in a small town along New Brunswick’s Miramichi River, Budd was the youngest of six children and the only girl. Her father took off for good a few weeks later, leaving the family struggling financially.
Budd describes a difficult childhood, including being molested by a neighbour when she was four.
"I had some issues with that growing up," she said.
Her mother later remarried a man Budd remembers as volatile, strict and abusive.
"The physical abuse was as long back as I can remember," she said. "I was about nine or so, he would start putting his hands on my breasts or between my legs and he almost made it into a game."
Budd’s step-father denies the abuse, and it’s unclear what her mother, a woman Budd describes as passive and unaffectionate, actually knew over the years. She did not want to talk to CBC.
Budd first ran away from home at 13. 'The physical abuse was as long back as I can remember,' she told CBC. (Submitted)
By 13, Budd was starting to act out. She shoplifted, drank alcohol, experimented with drugs and hitchhiked, earning the label "juvenile delinquent."
Budd says in reality, she was shy, vulnerable and often frightened.
"I had some anger issues, but I wasn't tough," she said. "I didn't care whether I lived or died. I knew it was risky."
By the time she turned 14, her mother and step-father had had enough. They called New Brunswick’s social services and the girl was placed in a group home, then reform school.
After 11 months at the Nova Scotia School for Girls in Truro, Budd was sent back to live with her mother and step-father. But that didn't last long.
"I needed to make some changes," Budd recalled. "My parents needed to make some changes…. They never recognized what they were doing that contributed to my running away."
So she ran again, and that's when the RCMP picked her up.

Gilles Plouffe had been with the RCMP for about five years when he first encountered Kim Budd. Due to his standing in the community, he and his wife were quickly approved to be foster parents. (Submitted by Gilles Plouffe)
In 1983, Const. Gilles Plouffe had been with the RCMP for four years and was already on his third posting.
Plouffe was fluently bilingual and stood over six feet tall with broad shoulders and a wispy mustache. As a kid he’d been an altar boy, a boy scout, an air cadet and a school crossing guard.
He married his high school sweetheart when they were still in their teens, and by 25 they were helping raise other people's children in addition to two young kids of their own.
In a system desperate for foster parents, the young couple was welcomed with open arms. He was an officer of the law, after all.
"I think they saw us as a blessing," he recalled in a recent interview with CBC. "They cut corners like you wouldn't believe. We didn't have any formal background check."
Soon, the Plouffe foster home became a handy option whenever the RCMP picked up a young person like Budd. They'd simply notify social services, and that was that.

Michel Cormier, a retired social worker in Moncton, N.B., stands near the Petitcodiac River in the early fall of 2026. Despite dealing with hundreds of cases over his career, he says he still remembers Kim Budd from the 1980s. (Michael Heenan/CBC)
Michel Cormier, a New Brunswick social worker tasked with overseeing the care of teens in the early 1980s, got that call the day Budd arrived at the Plouffe foster home.
Budd had been under Cormier's supervision during her months in group homes and reform school, and he can still remember her all these years later.
"She was a nice kid," Cormier told CBC. "I tried to respect her, not treat her like a juvenile delinquent — basically as a child that was in a difficult situation."
Placing Budd with the Plouffes seemed like an ideal solution.
"These were the perfect foster parents," Cormier recalled everyone thinking at the time. "This Disney kind of family, that everything was beautiful."
A recent photo of the house in Riverview, N.B., where Gilles Plouffe and his wife fostered children in the 1980s. (Michael Heenan/CBC)
Budd, a kid who had long dreamed of belonging to a "normal" family, settled in with the Plouffes and started Grade 9 at Riverview Junior High.
While her basement bedroom was being prepared, the teen slept on a pull-out couch.
One night when her foster mother was away, Gilles Plouffe came in wearing only a bathrobe and slipped under the covers with her.
"I kept falling asleep off and on, and he kept getting closer. And he had intercourse with me that night," Budd recalled. She remembers being afraid.
Plouffe apologized to the teen shortly after, telling her what happened had been an "accident." But the abuse continued, becoming more frequent and opportunistic.
"There was never a choice for me," Budd said. "He was my foster father and what he did to me that night, and the many times afterwards, was illegal."
While Plouffe disputes certain details, he now acknowledges he had sex on multiple occasions with the teenager in his care.
"It wasn't set out to be a predator looking for a prey," he told CBC. "I didn't mean to do anything bad, I just wanted to have a girlfriend."
Gilles Plouffe talked openly with CBC's Julie Ireton about his history with Kim Budd. He wore his RCMP-issue leather boots to the interview. (Francis Ferland/CBC)
Now 69, Plouffe needed no convincing to talk openly with CBC about his history with Kim Budd. Plouffe's then wife, Budd’s former foster mother, died in 2007.
During a lengthy interview, Plouffe showed no anger, hostility or concern. Rather, he appeared to welcome the opportunity to provide his own version of what happened in the foster home.

"It was a love connection," he insists. "And it's hard to say, 'Hey, you're a Mountie and you're supposed to enforce law and you're supposed to know better,’ and all this kind of stuff. I know all that."
Plouffe acknowledged he was aware of the sexual abuse Budd had endured as a child and as a runaway.

"It's not like she hadn't done it before. OK, I said it. It's not nice to say that, but she did do it before," said Plouffe. "I was showing her that people could be gentle, that it wasn't like the truckers she had met while running, that she could be passed on as a slave from one truck to the next."
The way he tells it, he provided the teen with food, shelter, clothing and "good values."
And yet he was keenly aware that what he was doing to his foster daughter was illegal.

Every male person who has illicit sexual intercourse with his step-daughter, foster daughter or female ward ... is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years.Section 153, Criminal Code of Canada c. 1983

Back then, Section 153 of the Criminal Code clearly stated that a man who has "illicit sexual intercourse with his foster daughter … is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years." (Today the crime falls under sexual exploitation.)
"I had the Criminal Code in the house, and I showed her," said Plouffe. "I told her, as a Mountie, I had no intention of going into jail. That's the last place any police officer wants to end up."
"He showed me in the book that he could go to prison," Budd recalled. "He just thought he was above the law."
The abuse continued. But almost two years into her stay with the Plouffes, it's Budd who would find herself in handcuffs once again, being taken away in a police car.
Two days after Christmas 1984, Budd, by then 17, got into a heated argument with her foster mother.
"She started going on and on about responsibility," Budd recalled. "She had been irresponsible in my view. She wasn’t being a responsible wife and I had to have sex with her husband."
The argument escalated and the woman threw a slice of pizza in Budd's face, then ran to her bedroom.
Budd followed. She had had enough of the lying and sneaking around, and of her foster father's late night visits. She was going to reveal the secret.
"I was running to tell her that Gilles had been sleeping with me," Budd said.
But Gilles Plouffe was right behind her.
"He grabbed me and put the chokehold on me and he made me unconscious," Budd said.
When she came to she was handcuffed, put in the back of Plouffe's RCMP cruiser and driven to the Moncton Hospital.
Moncton Hospital documents from December 1984 and early 1985 detailed Budd's admission, diagnosis and discharge. CBC has redacted some private information. (Submitted)
Hospital documents from December 1984 confirm that Budd arrived in restraints and that Plouffe told hospital staff the teen had "threatened to kill his family."
"Foster father is an RCMP officer. He used force to subdue her," the emergency admission form notes. "He feels the death threats are real."
Budd insists the only threat she'd made was to tell her foster mother that her husband had been having sex with her.

The 17-year-old was admitted to the adult psychiatric ward where she was medicated, underwent tests and attended group therapy. The hospital psychologist noted that Budd was insecure, impulsive, angry and suicidal, and that she felt "unloved" and had a "strong need for affection."

A couple weeks into her hospital stay, Budd disclosed to the staff psychologist what was really happening in the foster home. Documents from the time refer to Budd’s "alleged accusations" but provide no details.
"I just needed to get it out. I needed the sex to stop," Budd recalled telling the psychologist.
Then she told Plouffe what she had done. That forced him to admit the truth to his wife.

Budd spent three weeks in the psychiatric ward of the Moncton Hospital when she was still 17. She told a hospital psychologist here that her foster father had been abusing her. (Marc Grandmaison/The Canadian Press)
The psychologist summoned the Plouffes to the hospital for a meeting. Eventually, Budd was brought into the room.
"They told me never to talk to anyone about the abuse that had happened in their home," she said. "They made me promise."
Looking back, Budd says staff at the hospital never regarded her as a child, but as a mistress.
"I had a nurse reprimand me: ‘How dare you sleep with a married man?’ So she blamed me for the abuse, and that’s pretty much how I got blamed for what happened, instead of Gilles."
The teenager had endured two years of abuse in her foster home. She’d finally worked up the courage to tell someone in a position of authority. And then the adults colluded against her.
Plouffe said he informed child welfare authorities that he and his wife would no longer be fostering children, but no one reported the abuse to the RCMP.
"I didn't ask anybody to cover anything," Plouffe insists. "I don’t know. They see me as a Mountie. What are you going to do?"
Budd models a borrowed outfit for an upcoming job interview. (Submitted)

In fact, in yet another incredible twist, Budd — not Plouffe — would find herself in trouble with the law once again, this time as part of a spurious murder claim made by her abuser in January 1984, shortly after she was hospitalized.
"She had told [us] that she had killed somebody," Plouffe told CBC.

While the details remain vague, Plouffe said Budd had admitted to him that she’d killed a trucker in the U.S. after he had "taken advantage of her." He told his superiors at the RCMP and an investigator was assigned to the case.
Today, Budd calls it all a fiction concocted by Plouffe to distract his superiors from what was really happening to her in the foster home.
"I’ve never killed anybody — never," Budd said. "Gilles made me go through and told me to tell them."
But at the time, Budd, still just 17, went along with the ruse.
"I was just trying to protect Gilles," she said. "It’s hard to explain it now, but I was a shell."
RCMP files confirm an investigation in 1984, but no charges were laid and the case was quickly closed when no evidence was found to corroborate Budd's confession.
Still, the teen was now firmly under Plouffe's control, as though handcuffed once again.
Budd and Plouffe married in 1988 and moved from New Brunswick back to Plouffe's hometown of Gatineau, Que. (Submitted)
Budd was released from hospital in the winter of 1984 and went back to live with her mother and step-father. She dropped out of school and worked nights cleaning offices.
Before long, Plouffe, now separated from his wife, reappeared. He would turn up suddenly in his police vehicle, letting Budd know he was never far away.
"He was supposed to stay away from me, but he never did," she said. "I couldn't go to the RCMP because he was the RCMP."
Budd knew she couldn't run again.
"I believed he could have found me anywhere," she recalled. "I was afraid he was going to make me disappear…. He had weapons at the house, in his police car."
Eventually, she relented to his frequent calls. The sex continued.
"I can’t explain the hold Gilles had over me," Budd said. "He didn’t court me. We didn’t go to movies or restaurants, he didn’t buy me gifts. I was his toy."
Shortly after turning 18, Budd moved in with Plouffe and his two young children. When her former foster mother found out she became furious, and this time went to the police.
Gilles Plouffe tells his side of the story

The RCMP began an investigation in 1986, according to documents obtained by CBC. Plouffe’s police colleagues set out to determine if the sexual relationship had started while Budd was still in foster care.
They never talked to the alleged perpetrator, however.
"They did not interview me. They interviewed Kim," Plouffe confirmed. "But they never asked me if I did anything wrong."

It’s unclear whether the RCMP questioned anyone at New Brunswick’s child protection services, which oversees foster care in the province. And yet both Plouffe and former social worker Michel Cormier confirmed that employees within the department knew about what had gone on in the Plouffe home.

"The people that knew, I imagine probably had the idea that it was not any of their business. So they didn’t go forward with a complaint to the police like it should have been done," Cormier said. (He left the agency shortly after Budd's placement with the Plouffes, but later returned to work there part-time.)

New Brunswick's Social Development office is responsible for child protective services including foster care. Budd was a ward of the province when she was in foster care in the early 1980s. (Michael Heenan/CBC)
According to Budd, Plouffe coached her to tell anyone who asked that the sex had started after she turned 18.
"He kept telling me that if I told his lie often enough, it would become my truth," she said.
Once again, the teen lied for Plouffe and the RCMP wrapped up the investigation.

"The allegation that Cst. Plouffe had sexual intercourse with Kimberly Ann Budd while she was a ward of Cst. Plouffe is unsubstantiated. There is no evidence to support this fact and no way we will ever be able to prove this fact," states an RCMP memo from August 1986.
But Plouffe’s association with this teen runaway and one-time murder suspect created a new problem for him: He was deemed a security risk – not because of anything he'd done, but because of her.

"His security clearance has been downgraded," states the memo. "We do not feel there is any further action to be taken at this point with the exception of verifying periodically if Budd becomes involved in her former activities."
Budd became pregnant with her first child at 19. She and Plouffe would have three sons together. (Francis Ferland/CBC)
Budd was 19 when she became pregnant with her first child, giving birth to a baby boy in May 1987. She would go on to have two more sons with her former foster father.
"I was very trapped," she said.
With no proposal or engagement ring, Budd and Plouffe married in a civil ceremony in January 1988 at the Moncton courthouse. No friends or family attended, and Plouffe did not wear his red serge.
"They harassed him about it until he quit the RCMP," Budd said, suggesting that despite dropping their investigation, Plouffe's superiors may have had their suspicions.
Later that same year the newlyweds left New Brunswick and moved to Plouffe's hometown of Gatineau, Que., initially moving in with his mother.
There, years later during a therapy session for one of their children, Budd told the therapist about the origins of her relationship with Plouffe.
"She kept giving me cards to go see a women's shelter," said Budd. "I started looking at my marriage … how dysfunctional it was."

At 27 — 12 years after first meeting him — Budd finally left Plouffe for good. She took computer courses and eventually secured a job with the federal government where she remained for more than 20 years.

RCMP officer Sandra Lavallee interviews Budd at the national police force's Ottawa office in 2017. During the interview, Budd reported the sexual abuse she suffered as a teen in the Plouffe foster home. CBC obtained a video of the interview through an access to information request. (RCMP)
In April 2017, Budd sat in an RCMP interview room in Ottawa to detail her complaint against Gilles Plouffe for historical sexual abuse.
In a video of that interview, Budd’s pain is raw. Through tears, she recounts what she went through between the ages of 15 and 17 in the Plouffe foster home.
"He told me that I couldn’t tell anyone. Nobody would understand ... it was our secret," Budd told the interviewer.
Shortly after, RCMP Const. Simon Boucher of New Brunswick’s Codiac detachment launched an investigation.
Kim Budd speaks with reporter Julie Ireton outside the RCMP offices in Ottawa where in 2017 Budd reported the abuse she suffered in the 1980s. (Turgut Yeter/CBC)

CBC obtained through access to information the interview video and close to 400 pages of documents related to the 2017 investigation. While much has been redacted, the police files note that Boucher searched "different databases" for witnesses including Budd’s former social worker, Michel "Mike" Cormier.

"The attempt to contact Mike Cormier … were negative," the records state. "Cst. Boucher followed up with social services in Moncton, no one from their office are aware of a Mike Cormier that worked there between 1980 and 1990."
Yet CBC easily found Cormier through social media. He still lives in the Moncton area, and during several conversations shared what he knows about Budd’s childhood.
Cormier said he would have given the RCMP the same information — including the open secret about what went on at the Plouffe home — had an investigator ever called to ask.
Despite the RCMP's claim that it couldn't find him in 2017, Michel Cormier was still living in New Brunswick and employed as a social worker at a Moncton hospital. (Michael Heenan/CBC)
The RCMP closed the investigation into Budd’s complaint in August 2018.
"There is not enough likelihood of conviction," Boucher concluded. "The main issue in the matter is the reliability and credibility of KB because there is no eye witness to the alleged sexual acts."
But there was another eye witness: Gilles Plouffe. Yet the RCMP never contacted him, reducing what Boucher called a case of "he said, she said" to a simple matter of "she said."

Plouffe spent hours talking openly with CBC about his past, demonstrating that he’s not shy to discuss what happened in his foster home in the early 1980s. But he said he was never aware of the RCMP investigation until told about it by CBC.
Once again, Budd had tried to tell the truth, only to be dismissed.
"There was evidence there that he had abused me. They just ignored it," said Budd.

Daphne Gilbert, a law professor at the University of Ottawa, reviewed Kim Budd's legal files. 'We don't believe women when they come forward and talk about sexual assault. We start from the position that they are lying,' she told CBC. (Mathieu Deroy/CBC)

"There's no other victim where we assume that they are lying about what happened to them. That is unique to sexual assault, still today," said Daphne Gilbert, a law professor at the University of Ottawa who reviewed the legal documents in Budd’s case.
"We don't believe women when they come forward and talk about sexual assault. We start from the position that they are lying."
Gilbert thinks Michel Cormier’s evidence could have made a difference.

"I am embarrassed for the RCMP that they couldn't find him," she said. "Even without him testifying, the RCMP speaking to him and hearing that she had disclosed her sexual abuse, I would have thought would have been a persuasive reason to lay a charge."
RCMP Const. Simon Boucher was "not able to do an interview" with CBC, according to the force’s media relations officer in New Brunswick.

According to Sunny Marriner, national lead for the Improving Institutional Accountability Project, investigators displayed "textbook behaviour" when they claimed Budd was an unreliable witness because as a teen she'd lied, done drugs and run away.

"Children who are experiencing sexual abuse may withdraw. They begin to have difficulty attending school or engaging in activities. They frequently run away," she said. "It doesn't undermine credibility, it supports that something was happening to the child at that time."
'It wasn't abuse, it was love,' Plouffe said of his relationship with Budd when she was still in her teens and he was her foster father. (Francis Ferland/CBC)
Decades later, Gilles Plouffe still frames what happened in his foster home not as abuse, but as a love story.
"It's wrong, but that doesn't mean we have to go and and really shove it down my throat and say that was really wrong, beat me on the head," Plouffe said. "It wasn't abuse, it was love.”
That’s a story Marriner says she’s heard before in her work with survivors.

"It is not love, it is exploitation," she said. "Many people will be familiar with the term grooming.… It means very slowly creating a bond with the person that you intend to exploit that makes them believe that the two of you are on the same team together against the entire world."
Looking back, Budd realizes the odds were stacked against her.
"He got away with it because he was in the RCMP, so it got covered up for him and he got protected and he'll never be charged," she said.
Budd, right, shows Ireton the statement of claim in her case against her former foster father. (Francis Ferland/CBC)
In the spring of 2019, Budd filed a lawsuit against the province of New Brunswick, the Moncton Hospital, the regional health authority and Gilles Plouffe.
"Plouffe was given the power and duty to discipline and punish the plaintiff, which he used to perpetrate the physical, emotional and sexual abuse," noted the statement of claim.
The lawsuit alleged the institutions were negligent and the hospital psychologist breached his fiduciary duty by failing to report the sexual abuse to the RCMP.

Those institutions denied all allegations, and in formal statements of defence noted that any injury, loss or damages suffered by the plaintiff were no fault of theirs. They also declined to talk to CBC about the case.
In July 2026 a judge at the Moncton Court of King's Bench heard a trial for damages against Gilles Plouffe. A decision is pending. (Michael Heenan/CBC)
There was no trial, and in 2024 the suit was resolved out of court. Details are not public.

Plouffe didn’t defend himself against the claim and in November 2019 was found in default — the civil court’s way of saying he didn't bring forward any evidence to deny the allegation that he repeatedly sexually abused, assaulted and molested Budd for two years, starting when she was 15.
This July, the Court of King’s Bench in Moncton heard a trial for damages in the case of Kimberly Anne Budd vs. Joseph Yves Gilles Plouffe.

"I want his acknowledgement. I want some accountability for it," said Budd, who has been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety disorder and a persistent depressive disorder — conditions that will require treatment for the rest of her life.
Budd and her lawyer are still waiting for the judge’s decision in the case.
Kim Budd says she hopes her family will now understand her past
Plouffe has never acknowledged that what he did changed the course of a teen girl’s life, and no one has ever asked him to. Marrying Budd and having children with her didn’t change anything.
For two years, between the ages of 15 and 17, she was a child and her foster parents were in charge. Institutions failed her, and worse, sought to discredit her when she tried to tell them the truth.

Gilles Plouffe’s position with the police gave him privilege and standing in the community. The reaction of the systems intended to protect children exemplifies the entitlement he enjoyed as an officer.
It's why Budd feels she has to keep telling her side of the story, over and over again.
"Some people might call it revenge, but it's not — it’s justice," said Budd. "I want the record set straight."
Budd’s story is tragic, and repeating it is embarrassing and painful, but she realized long ago that she needed to stop running from it.
"I want my kids to hear it. They're old enough now they can process it … and they can make their decisions."
Kim Budd was a troubled teenager, a vulnerable kid whose imperfections placed her in a perfect position to be victimized over and over again.
Today, she’s a survivor.
How her search for safety turned into a twisted nightmare of control
If you need help: Sexual Assault Centres, Crisis Lines, and Support Service in Canada

articles.title: Instead of getting recycled, many EV batteries are being repurposed
articles.summary: As EV sales grew, many worried about what would happen to all those toxic batteries. Now, amid the demise of two big Canadian EV battery recyclers, another Canadian firm is building megafactories to…

image.caption: Sandra Aragon Aviles, battery systems engineer at Mapleview Energy, looks at a wall of mining vehicle batteries being repurposed as part of a pilot project at a farm in Elora, Ont., funded through the Ontario government's Ontario Vehicle Innovation Network. (Nick Nesbitt/Mapleview Energy)

blocks.text: As EV sales grew, many worried about what would happen to all those toxic batteries.
Recycling was once touted as a solution, but in the past two years, two major Canadian EV battery recyclers have gone bankrupt.
Meanwhile another Canadian firm, Moment Energy, is building megafactories to repurpose EV batteries for a surging industry — energy storage.
Here's a closer look at what's happening to EV batteries at the end of their lives as vehicle batteries.
Options for getting rid of an old EV battery
EV batteries are considered no longer suitable for driving after about a dozen years of use, when they reach about 80 per cent of their original capacity.
Automakers betting on EV rebate revival to turbo-charge sales
Federal and provincial regulations, which treat EV batteries as dangerous goods and hazardous waste or hazardous recyclable materials, effectively ban them from landfills.
That leaves two options: reuse and recycling.
Lithium battery recycling in Canada typically recovers metals such as nickel and copper, but burns off graphite and lithium, which make up half the battery.

Startups such as Quebec-based Lithion Technologies and Ontario-based Li-Cycle aimed to recover lithium and graphite (alongside the metals) through a new, high-tech process called hydrometallurgy. But both Li-Cycle and Lithion went bankrupt within the last two years.
Turning old electric vehicle batteries from trash to treasure

Maria Kelleher, a Toronto-based environmental consultant who has advised governments on what to do with old EV batteries, said the companies suffered from a lack of EV batteries to recycle. That was partly because EV batteries were lasting longer in vehicles than expected — 12 to 15 years instead of eight — and partly because an industry developed to reuse them.
"Recycling is what you would do when you can't do anything else with something," she said. "But reuse is much better."
How old EV batteries found a new life

According to the International Energy Agency, battery storage is the fastest-growing power technology in the world, with a 40 per cent jump in new capacity in 2025, to 108 gigawatts. In Canada, capacity doubled in 2025 to nearly a gigawatt and is expected to hit 15 to 23 GW by 2050, playing an "increasingly important role in providing system flexibility and reliability," according to the Canada Energy Regulator.
Amid slow electric vehicle market, NextStar prioritizes a different kind of battery

Surrey, B.C.-based Moment Energy tests and repackages old EV batteries for energy storage, marketing them at facilities such as factories, data centres and airports as a way to save on energy costs and help supply extra energy or backup power when needed.

Gurmesh Sidhu and three former classmates from Simon Fraser University's engineering program co-founded the company in 2019 after working in California, where EVs and solar panels were extremely popular.

They observed that recycling EV batteries was expensive. Meanwhile, there was a lot of solar power during the day, but that didn't match up with the need for EV charging and other power consumption at night.

The four co-founders of Moment Energy, Gabriel Soares (back-left), Gurmesh Sidhu (back-right), Sumreen Rattan (front-left) and Edward Chiang (front-right) showing models of their energy storage units inside the new Surrey, B.C., factory. (Moment Energy)
Sidhu said he believes "the only way to solve that sustainably is batteries."

Seven years later, this past June, the company officially opened what it believes to be the world's largest battery repurposing facility in Surrey, B.C. It's building an even bigger facility in Taylor, Texas, set to open next year, after raising more than $100 million US from investors. Last week, the company unveiled its newest, next-generation Nova battery made from repurposed EV batteries.
On Nov. 17, 2026, Moment Energy unveiled its newest, next-generation Nova battery made from repurposed EV batteries. (Moment Energy)
Meanwhile, other battery repurposing companies have been popping up in both Canada and the U.S.
Last week, one of the companies showcasing its technology at the MaRS Climate Impact Conference in Toronto was Ontario-based Mapleview Energy.

It's testing repurposed batteries from mining vehicles in a solar and battery storage system at a farm in Elora, Ont. Since the pilot launched this summer, it has cut the farm's power costs by 37 per cent, founder Nick Nesbitt said during a panel session.
The cost of a second life
Repurposing batteries also comes with costs and challenges.
Quebec based EVB360 developed a storage battery using refurbished Tesla Model 3 and Tesla Model Y batteries.

Martin Ménard, the company's director of project development, told CBC News in an email that the company recently decided to suspend its EV battery repurposing operations due to challenging market conditions.

items: Canada had big EV battery recycling plans, but without regulations it's the 'Wild West,' expert warns
Does clean energy generate too much waste? Hannah Ritchie checks the data on climate action

blocks.text: In order to be repurposed, batteries from different brands with different chemistries and remaining capacities must be tested and evaluated. Special technology is needed for them to connect and work together safely. Then the system must undergo safety testing and certification.
It's something Moment Energy has successfully done, but it can be challenging for smaller companies. Ménard says it requires "significant investments."
Then there's the used battery supply problem.
An electric vehicle battery is displayed open during a demonstration at the EV & Charging Expo in Toronto in April. (Oksana Shtohryn/CBC)
Ménard recalled approaching automaker Stellantis about that. "I was told, 'Martin, come back and see us in 15 years' … There simply aren't enough end-of-life EV batteries available today."
Nesbitt acknowledges it's a challenge but believes it's solvable by tapping a wider range of EVs, from farming to mining to other industrial and delivery vehicles.

He added that repurposing companies can out-compete recyclers for batteries because their end product — stationary batteries — has a higher value than "black mass," the powdered mixture of metals and minerals produced by recyclers.

Ziyu Wang, a doctoral student at Concordia University in Montreal, did a study comparing recycling and repurposing EV batteries on Vancouver Island. In his study, he found that even regular recycling cost about $750 per EV battery, and hydrometallurgical recycling that recovers the lithium would cost about double that. Both are far from breaking even when the recovered materials are sold.
But even the cost of battery repurposing was higher than Wang thought it would be.

In all cases, Wang found transporting the heavy battery, which is regulated as hazardous waste, was a big component of the cost, as was evaluating the battery to see if it was suitable for repurposing or recycling.

He said these costs could be reduced by having more repurposing and recycling facilities. Regulations could also help, such as requiring "battery passports" that provide information about a battery's chemistry, history and state of health so less testing is needed. Such passports are being made mandatory in the European Union.
Meanwhile, given the increase in EV battery repurposing, economically feasible large-scale, advanced EV battery recycling may still be 10 to 30 years away, Kelleher estimates.
"We haven't gotten to the end of that life cycle."

articles.title: Quebec grocery store believed to be oldest in North America revived with an Italian twist
articles.summary: Quebec City's J.A. Moisan is believed to be the oldest grocery store in North America. It has survived great depressions and uncertain times, but it’s ready for a new beginning once more. New tenants…

image.caption: After announcing its closure in 2025, J.A. Moisan — believed to be North America's oldest grocery store — reopened its doors on Nov. 20. (Sarah-Kate Dallaire/CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal

Quebec City's J.A. Moisan is believed to be the oldest grocery store in North America. It has survived great depressions and uncertain times, but it’s ready for a new beginning once more. New tenants promise to honour the founding family's legacy, but with an Italian twist.
Quebec City's J.A. Moisan is celebrating its 155th anniversary with a new beginning

A 155-year-old institution in Quebec City — believed to be the oldest grocery store in North America — is back in business, reviving a neighbourhood staple that has fed generations of locals and tourists.
"It's probably the oldest grocery store still in operation in North America," said historian Denis Angers.
J.A. Moisan, opened in 1871 by Jean-Alfred Moisan in the city’s Saint-Jean-Baptiste neighbourhood, has weathered two World Wars, the Great Depression and bankruptcy.
“They were able to survive all that period of time," Angers said.
But, after changing hands multiple times over the decades, the store closed in January 2025 under building owner Donna Willett.
"I fell in love with the old building [but] I had no experience [in groceries]," she said.

Not wanting all the effort — and money — she put into the building to go to waste, she decided to “hang on to it for a while” as its new tenants take root and work toward keeping the shop's legacy alive.
A new beginning
J.A. Moisan officially reopened on Friday, entering a new era under tenants Isabelle Di Pilato and her partner Joseph Di Piliato, who moved from France to Quebec City in April.
The seasoned entrepreneur couple did not know about Moisan's history when they found the space to rent, but they now promise to honour the building's legacy.
"People are thanking us, it means a great deal — it’s a tremendous source of moral support," said Isabelle.
Joseph Di Piliato, Isabelle Di Piliato and their daughter Victoria Di Piliato are excited to welcome customers into J.A. Moisan 2.0. (Sarah-Kate Dallaire/CBC)
The couple says they have plenty of ideas for the store, offering a mix of Quebec, French and Italian cultures and flavours.
"You can look forward to surprises, new offerings and things you might otherwise only get to taste in Italy," said Isabelle.
She adds the building will remain “a friendly, very informal, intimate space," a bit like being at home, "but with an Italian twist.”

items: J.A. Moisan, long a Quebec City treasure, takes fresh approach under new ownership

blocks.text: Joseph adds it isn’t just a business, it’s a family affair, too.

“After all, we are immigrants, and the process of immigration itself is a heavy burden … constant uncertainty and a tremendous amount of resilience," he said. "We've invested all we had in this project.

The new business operators say the support has been immensely surprising since they took over the shop, with several locals knocking at the door and peeking through the windows — even on days the store is closed. (Sarah-Kate Dallaire/CBC)
While anxious to take on a business with such a rich history, the couple says they’re incredibly proud and honoured.
“We know how much this means to the people of Quebec … we absolutely don’t want to let you down," said an emotional Isabelle.
"It’s part of your heritage," adds Joseph, teary-eyed.
‘You can go back in time’
In the early days, grocery stores used to sell exclusively dry food, according to historian Angers.
"If you wanted to buy your fish, your meat, you had to go to the markets throughout the city," he said.
He says J.A. Moisan was one of the first supermarkets in Quebec City "where you can find everything under a single roof.”
What really makes the space special, according to Angers, is its "old-time smell" of wood, spices and freshly brewed coffee.
"This is a place where you can stroll, you can discover things, you can go back in time," he said.
The J.A. Moisan grocery store in 1885, the year Jean-Alfred Moisan became the owner of the building. (Courtesy of Clément St-Laurent)
Isabelle says while the grocery section will remain, the couple added chairs and tables for public use.
"It felt like a shame for people to only spend five minutes in such a beautiful space,” Isabelle said.
“It’s much nicer to be able to sit down for a while, have a coffee, or enjoy a bite to eat.”
LISTEN | Food columnist Allison Van Rassel speaks on store's reopening:
Quebec AM11:00Historic grocery store reopens in Quebec City
Asked if she would take down the store's original sign, Isabelle said not only will she keep it, she also added a photo of J.A. Moisan himself “so that he could keep an eye on us."

The couple says they don't want to erase the past, but rather write a future with the store’s history in mind. To that end, they’re planning to bring back bowler hats and vintage aprons "for an old-school feel."
Founder's family feels honoured
Jacques Faguy, the great-grandson of founder Jean-Alfred Moisan, says he is glad the new owners decided to keep his family's name.
Faguy's 97-year-old mother Thérèse Légaré-Faguy, who spent much of her childhood at the store, still lives in the neighbourhood and plans to visit the new shop soon.
He only hopes the family's store and legacy will remain for decades to come.

"We're struggling now to have shops on main streets, [all] cities are struggling to keep and have local merchants," he said, adding he's grateful a staple of the Saint-Jean Baptiste neighbourhood is still standing.
"The store changed, but the name remains.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Sarah-Kate Dallaire is a regional journalist with CBC News in Quebec City. She can be reached at sarah-kate.dallaire@radio-canada.ca

articles.title: Health Canada seizes peptides from Toronto shop, warns of health risks of unregulated market
articles.summary: Health Canada confirmed it confiscated and is now testing a number of what it called "unauthorized injectable peptides" from the shop, Not Peptides.

blocks.text: Toronto·New
Health Canada confirmed it confiscated and is now testing a number of what it called "unauthorized injectable peptides" from the shop, Not Peptides.
Experts warn products being sold are unregulated and untested
Why Health Canada seized 'unauthorized injectable peptides' from Toronto shop
Health Canada has seized a number of injectable peptides from a store in Toronto's Queen West neighbourhood, CBC News has learned.

Health Canada confirmed it confiscated and is now testing a number of what it called "unauthorized injectable peptides" from the shop, Not Peptides, on Nov. 9. It also seized bacteriostatic water products, which are often used to reconstitute freeze-dried peptides.

The federal health agency has warned the Canadian public against using unauthorized peptides, which many have purchased online or acquired through compounding pharmacies. The agency said it wasn't able to provide any further detail about its ongoing investigation at Not Peptides, which runs both a bricks-and-mortar and online shop.
"Selling unauthorized health products is illegal," Geneviève Lapierre, a spokesperson for the department, said in an emailed statement.
"Health Canada will continue to seize unauthorized peptide products and disrupt distribution channels to remove these products from the Canadian market."
Not Peptides, which remained open after the seizure, did not respond to CBC Toronto's request for comment.

Peptides are short chains of linked amino acids that serve as the building blocks of proteins, and occur naturally in the body. But the injectable peptides being sold by Not Peptides are largely unproven products that, in many cases, have become popular as fitness influencers claim they can fuel muscle recovery and reverse the signs of aging.

One vial for sale at Not Peptides, a mix of three different peptides including BPC-157, is described on the store's website as being "engineered for synergistic skin renewal, connective-tissue integrity, and accelerated wound closure."
Experts have highlighted there are no large-scale human efficacy trials for BPC-157.

items: Doctors are using a regulatory gap to prescribe an unauthorized peptide

blocks.text: What's behind the peptide boom?
Some peptide-based medications have legitimate medical applications and have been approved for use in Canada.

Experts like David Sabatino, a professor in the Department of Chemistry at Carleton University, have pointed out they can be used properly, highlighting the popularity of peptide-based medications like GLP-1 — often better known under brand names like Ozempic.
But that's fueled interest in other untested peptides, which come with more risk.
“We should take extra caution and be very careful with the risks that are associated with using peptides that have not gone through that approval process,” Sabatino said.

One of his biggest concerns is the potential for contamination in products that have not undergone proper quality control. Sabatino pointed to reports of contaminants, toxins and bacteria in unregulated products, which can lead to infections and other serious complications.

items: Are you a Torontonian who uses unregulated peptides? Email us at TOnews@cbc.ca because we'd like to hear from you for future stories on this topic.

blocks.text: Health Canada warns on its website that taking untested peptides increases the risk of hormonal imbalance, mood swings, blood sugar imbalance, liver or kidney damage, blood clots and even the growth of cancerous tumours.

Public Health Ontario told CBC News it does not systematically collect specific emergency department visit data related to peptide use, making it difficult to determine how many people may be experiencing complications.
City not taking enforcement action against shop
The situation has echoes of Toronto’s early cannabis dispensary crackdown, when stores continued reopening despite repeated police raids. Several of those shops are still operating in Toronto.
The City of Toronto said Not Peptides doesn't have a business licence because of the type of service it provides.
"As a result, no city business licence is required and no licensing enforcement action has been taken," spokesperson Mahreen Dasoo said in an email.
How Canadians are getting unauthorized peptides
Toronto police said in an email its officers weren't involved in Health Canada's seizure.

Health Canada has made similar seizures before, including a wellness shop in Ottawa. Three days before Not Peptides was investigated, Health Canada also issued a public warning after lab testing found bacteria in some peptide products sold by two online retailers.
"Do not buy or use these products," the warning states.
'My first concern if public safety,' physician says
The popularity of peptides, particularly among people seeking cosmetic and performance-related benefits, is growing according to Dr. Jennifer Pearlman.
The Toronto physician who administers peptide therapies says social media influencers have also played a role in promoting these products.
Peptides have already been used in cosmetic products for decades, she says.
When administered safely, and under the supervision of a physician, Pearlman says there are benefits and peptides in the world of medicine hold great promise.
Dr. Jennifer Pearlman is the medical director and CEO of Pearl Rejuvenation in Toronto's Yonge-St. Clair neighbourhood. (Submitted by Jennifer Pearlman)
"They hold enormous therapeutic potential but they are biologically active compounds," she said, adding she was alarmed by what she saw on the shop's website.
"My first concern is public safety. Like all medicines, peptides should be prescribed by a physician to a patient, carefully considering both risk and benefit."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Talia Ricci is a TV, radio and web reporter at CBC Toronto. She enjoys covering offbeat human interest stories and exposing social justice issues. Talia has also reported in London, Ont. and Winnipeg, Man. You can email story ideas to talia.ricci@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Wildfire victim trying to buy new Flin Flon, Man., home loses $170K in lawyer impersonation scam
articles.summary: Five Manitobans in the last two months have fallen victim to a fraud scheme where scammers infiltrate lawyers' emails and redirect money. One woman in Flin Flon, trying to buy a new home after losing…

image.caption: Lisa Holmes sits in her parents' home in Flin Flon, Man., where she's lived since her home in nearby Denare Beach, Sask., was destroyed in a 2025 fire. She tried to buy a home of her own in Flin Flon earlier this year, but fell victim to an online scam and lost over $170,000. (Eric Westhaver/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba·New

Five Manitobans in the last two months have fallen victim to a fraud scheme where scammers infiltrate lawyers' emails and redirect money. One woman in Flin Flon, trying to buy a new home after losing hers in a wildfire, is out more than $170,000.
Nearly $1M lost in 5 cases in recent months targeting lawyers and clients: Law Society of Manitoba

A Flin Flon woman whose home was destroyed in a wildfire has lost tens of thousands of dollars after falling prey to an online impersonation scam — one that has cost Manitobans nearly $1 million in just two months.

She was one of several people targeted recently by what the Manitoba Law Society calls a "payment misdirection fraud," where a scammer pretends to be a person's lawyer, orchestrates a large payment, then takes the money, often leaving the victim with little recourse to recover it.

Lisa Holmes was living in the northeastern Saskatchewan community of Denare Beach, about 20 kilometres southwest of Flin Flon, when a forest fire hit the area in June 2025. Her home and possessions were destroyed.
Holmes had limited insurance coverage and couldn't fully rebuild, so she moved in with her parents while trying to buy a new house.
The remains of Lisa Holmes's house in Denare Beach, Sask., which was destroyed by a wildfire on June 2, 2025. (Submitted by Lisa Holmes)

She found one for sale in Flin Flon and began working with a lawyer, Dayna Zaharia in The Pas, Man., to buy it. They communicated through email and used the online Docusign service for contract signatures, Holmes said.

She was instructed to send a wire transfer for more than $170,000 to a bank account, where it would be held until the sale was finalized, and sent that transfer through Flin Flon's RBC branch on Oct. 5, she said.
But she wasn't messaging Zaharia about that transfer — it was a scammer impersonating the lawyer.

"I didn't find out until a few days into it that the email was hacked," said Holmes. "Someone was impersonating myself and my lawyer and they were sending emails to one another, but we didn't know … until after we talked."
By then, the money was gone. Holmes didn't get the house. She's still living with her parents and worried she'll never get her money back.
"I was so excited that I was going to get my home. I never thought I was going to be blindsided like that."
Bank says client responsible
Holmes said she and Zaharia contacted the Law Society of Manitoba, which says they were targeted in a growing wave of payment misdirection fraud.
Zaharia declined an interview request, citing attorney-client privilege. Law society representatives also declined, saying they do not publicly comment on individual cases.
The regulatory body issued a statement Nov. 18, saying it's aware of five cases of "payment misdirection" fraud in Manitoba in the past two months alone, with almost $1 million lost.

The law society said scammers use the "infiltrated" accounts of lawyers or employees to send an email to another lawyer's client, a financial institution or a third party, telling them to send funds to a bank account that's actually controlled by the fraudster.

In most of the recent cases, it appears there was no insurance, the statement said. The scams went beyond real estate transactions, and two cases involved law firms that don't even have trust accounts.
RBC says as scams become more sophisticated, people should independently verify banking information before sending money. (David Donnelly/CBC)
Holmes notified RBC Nov. 4, filing a complaint stating it failed to protect her from financial abuse.
In an email response Holmes shared with CBC, the bank maintained she is "held responsible due to participation in fraud or scam," and said it considers the matter closed.
In a statement to CBC, an RBC spokesperson said as scams become more sophisticated, people should independently verify banking information before sending money.

items: Winnipeg woman slams bank's decision not to refund her after 'dumbfounding' scam

blocks.text: The bank said it provides information about fraud prevention on its website, as does the Canadian Anti-Scam Coalition, which RBC is part of.
"You wonder, how does this happen? How does someone just steal over $170,000 and there's no accountability?" said Holmes.
"It would be so simple for the bank to just do a second check, right?"
Preventative steps
Holmes contacted the RCMP, who said they are investigating hers and similar cases.
Cpl. Ricky Perkins, who works with the Manitoba RCMP's cyber and financial crime unit, says they often see scams begin with clicking a link in a phishing email.
Scammers will "infiltrate the system" and set up rules in email programs like Outlook or Gmail, he said.
"Then they'll monitor the activity to see kind of who's who in the zoo … [and] take over the account."
Cpl. Ricky Perkins works with Manitoba RCMP's cyber and financial crime unit. He says scams like these are becoming more frequent and more sophisticated. (Eric Westhaver/CBC)
He said there are email precautions people can take to avoid being hacked, including checking sent and trash folders for any sent emails that don't look familiar.
"That would be a really good indicator that the account's been breached," he said.

The law society also advises lawyers to check their email folders for suspicious activity. It also says they should tell clients they won't accept or change payment instructions by email, and should confirm any payment information by phone.

items: Same scam. 2 countries. Why Canadians don’t get their money back

blocks.text: If people are targeted in a scam, they can try to cancel or reverse the payment through their bank or contact the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre, said Cpl. Perkins.
"Every case is different. In some cases we have recovered funds. In other cases, unfortunately, we can't," he said.

"There have been instances where people have been charged, and then obviously there's cases where the funds do end up in kind of the multiverse, so to speak. It's a difficult path for us to continue to follow."

Holmes holds one of the few things left after her Denare Beach home burned down in 2025 — a school art project she made as a child, with her handprint pressed onto plaster. She hopes RCMP will catch the person who scammed her. (Eric Westhaver/CBC)
RCMP said no arrests have been made in Holmes's case.
She said she hopes she'll recover her money and buy a new home, but if the bank and insurance can't help, she hopes the Mounties get their culprit — and that person will pay.
"[The courts] can tell them to pay it back if they have the money, but they also tell me that could take years," she said.
"I have a little bit of hope, but I don't have a lot of hope."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Eric Westhaver is a journalist with CBC Manitoba, working out of Flin Flon. Born and raised in the north, Eric worked with the Flin Flon Reminder for nine years before joining CBC in 2025. His email is eric.westhaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI lets you buy flowers for your girlfriend. Some streamers say it's too woke
articles.summary: The new Grand Theft Auto VI brings old classics back to the franchise, but this iteration also has some changes. Instead of hiring sex workers, the early part of the game has you doing chores for…

image.caption: Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, pictured here, are the main characters of the new Grand Theft Auto VI. But some streamers aren't happy with some of the early missions that give you the option to do some chores to improve the characters' relationship. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

The new Grand Theft Auto VI brings old classics back to the franchise, but this iteration also has some changes. Instead of hiring sex workers, the early part of the game has you doing chores for your in-game girlfriend, like buying her flowers and fixing the leak in the roof.
Despite pushback, the game has still made billions in sales since its release
The new Grand Theft Auto VI brings old classics back to the franchise: stealing cars, flying planes, evading cops. But this iteration also has some changes.

Instead of hiring sex workers, the early part of the game has you doing chores for your in-game girlfriend, like buying her flowers and fixing the leak in the roof. And as a result, a fringe group of players and streamers say the latest version of Grand Theft Auto is too woke.

"The game is presenting this option of treating women respectfully," said Joshua Foust, an assistant professor in public relations at Syracuse University, who studies the intersection of gaming and gender.

"And the response, at least from these accounts that seem to be mad about it, is that even the request to treat a woman respectfully in a game, they find offensive and somehow diminishing of their own sense of manhood."
That's apparently not what Braden Eric Peters, better known as the looksmaxxing influencer Clavicular, signed up for.
"GTA 6 is insanely cucked, half of the missions are jestermaxing and simping for girls," Peters, who is currently on trial for rape, posted on X.
Despite pushback, the game recorded $3.79 billion US in retail sales in the first 24 hours of ‌its launch. (Ryan Murphy/Getty Images)

Despite this pushback, the open-world action adventure game isn't struggling to sell. The game ‌recorded $3.79 billion US in retail sales in the first 24 ⁠hours ⁠of ‌its launch, according to game developer Rockstar Games, making it the world's biggest video game release ever.

"If you look at something like Grand Theft Auto, that is a prime example of how the online feedback from certain groups of people in no way mirrors what's actually going on here," said Alyssa Mercante, a culture critic and gaming journalist.
Buying flowers and putting up drywall
The game lets you play as both Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, though you spend a majority of the early missions controlling Jason.

During that time — amid smuggling drugs and stealing cars — players have the option to perform what is essentially a "honey-do" list, including putting up drywall, painting the bedroom and fixing the stairs leading up to your house.
You can even go buy Lucia flowers (she is just getting out of a prison, after all), though all of these tasks are optional.
Early in the game, players are given the option to do some work on Jason's house, pictured here, to improve the relationship between Jason and Lucia. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)
In another part of the early game, you have to unclog a woman's sink for her, which did not impress streamer Zack Hoyt, known online as Asmongold.
"Are you kidding me?" he said while streaming. "Why can't she do this? Why do I have to do this for her?"

Foust says that underneath what he calls this "toxic criticism" is a belief by some that these games should only be made for them and shouldn't serve anyone else. He says this is especially true among streamers who play these games professionally and expect everything in these games to be specifically tailored to them.
"That's not me diagnosing anything, just like, usually, if you're unable to accept that some things are not for you, that's emotionally immature," said Foust.
Monetized rage bait?
Mercante, who is currently working on a book about rage baiting, says all of that pushback may not be totally genuine.

These streamers — such as Hoyt, who has millions of subscribers on his video channels — make their money off people watching their tirades. And clips posted on platforms such as X are often boosted by the algorithm, she says.
"Money is a hell of a drug," said Mercante.
She says many of these streamers who make money of this behaviour either end up believing the things they spout on their streams or adopting it as their online persona.
What makes the release of Grand Theft Auto VI so special?
She says many of the people who follow streamers like Hoyt may watch the clips, and may even share them, but often are still buying the game.
And she says Grand Theft Auto VI isn't an albatross — most major video game releases over the past few years have come under fire by this same group for things it considers woke.

When Assassin's Creed Shadows came out in 2025, some people complained about it featuring a Black lead character. Also last year, the Ghost of Tsushima sequel — Ghost of Yōtei — received some backlash for featuring a female character as its protagonist.

"Of course this was going to happen with GTA. Someone is going to try and find something to trot out as an example of, you know, the 'wokeification' of video games or about how games are being taken away from straight white men," said Mercante.
The game puts a lot of focus on Jason and Lucia, pictured here, and their relationships. And some streamers aren't happy about it. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

Overall, Mercante says studios aren't too concerned with this type of reaction. While an online movement may impact small independent studios, she says large publishers like Take-Two Interactive, which publishes Grand Theft Auto VI, aren't going to see this pushback affect their bottom line.

So, what do you do if you see a particularly outrageous review? Mercante says to take a look at who is posting it, and who stands to gain from it. If someone has a verification checkmark on X, they are paying to be able to monetize their posts.
"Recognize that, in many cases, this type of content is meant to manipulate and is meant to misinform and ultimately is meant to put money in the pocket of the person posting it," she said.
"We live in a place where people don't trust the media anymore, but I promise you a content creator who is monetizing their — for lack of a better term — shit posts, is not more trustworthy."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Philip Drost is a network senior writer for CBC News based in Fredericton. You can reach him at philip.drost@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Social media companies could be fined 5% of global revenue after Labor and Greens join forces on online safety laws
articles.summary: Individual Australians will be able to sue big tech firms for harm suffered online under compromise deal

blocks.text: Big tech companies may face “multibillion-dollar” fines and individuals could sue social media companies in court under Australia’s new digital duty of care laws, with the Greens to support the bill’s passage after extracting major amendments from Labor.
From late 2027, Australians will also be able opt out of addictive online algorithms under the new legislation, while the “endless scroll” of social media feeds may also cease.

The communications minister, Anika Wells, confirmed that, in extreme breaches, social media and tech companies could face fines of up to 5% of their global revenue if they flout the new laws. She said she had already met with the US ambassador, David Brat, to discuss the laws, and had stared down potential legal challenges from some of the world’s most powerful firms.
“I was at the high court a couple of weeks ago as the second respondent in the case against the social media minimum age. If people want to have another go, bring it on,” Wells said on Tuesday.

The government’s legislation will pass parliament this week, potentially as soon as Tuesday afternoon, after the Greens agreed to support the bill after intense negotiations. The Coalition had opposed the laws from the outset, citing free speech and censorship concerns, leaving the Greens to negotiate with Labor.

The planned framework would apply new online safety standards to social media, games, apps and chatbots. Labor said it would place “an overarching obligation” on tech platforms “to provide a safe online environment for all Australians” and replace a range of existing online codes and standards with a broader duty-of-care requirement to protect users from certain “harmful” content. Wells had suggested content promoting misogyny, terrorism, suicide, self-harm and eating disorders would be captured by the laws.

Following discussions with the Greens, Wells on Tuesday confirmed amendments to the bill would see Australians given a “private right of action” – a local equivalent to successful laws in the US allowing citizens to sue large companies.
The government will consider setting up an independent ombudsman or watchdog for big tech, and the maximum fines for breaches of rules could reach $109m, or up to 5% of global revenue.

The Coalition will not support the bill, which is expected to be voted on in the Senate on Tuesday night. The shadow minister for industry, Andrew Hastie, claimed the duty of care would lead to “a massive imposition on free speech and political communication”.
“Whilst the government is dressing this in the language of protecting children, they’re actually moving towards censorship here, which is our main issue here,” he told the ABC.

“It vests huge amounts of power in the minister of communications and the eSafety commissioner, who basically will regulate very vaguely defined definitions of online harm. We think that’s contrary to free speech. We’d rather have debate – and this puts our country and our culture of debate at risk.”
Labor’s legislation could also draw the ire of US-based tech giants and the Trump administration.

Wells has previously said Donald Trump’s Truth Social platform would be subject to the laws but that the government had committed to “constructive dialogue” with the US, including during her Tuesday meeting with Brat.
“I think we would say there are points of differences, and we’re ironing them out,” she said.
after newsletter promotion

Meta, Google and TikTok were contacted for comment. The Tech Council of Australia, an industry body which counts Google, Microsoft, LinkedIn, OpenAI and Pinterest among its members, said it supported the legislation, but voiced concern about the amendments.

“A private right of action is a complex undertaking with significant consequences. How this is implemented is critical, and we need proper consultation to ensure that businesses are not hindered from investing in Australia. If we get this wrong, it will be counterproductive to encouraging innovation in Australia,” a spokesperson said.

Other major changes to the bill include adding “addictive” features to the list of risks that tech platforms must address, and clarifying the definitions of “hostile attitudes to women and gender equality”. Wells said this was “not about disagreeing with feminism or expressing an opinion”, but would force tech platforms to avoid exposing children to content promoting hatred of women, including violence, death threats, coercion or harassment.
She has previously stated “manosphere podcasts” would not be affected.
Amendments to the bill will also expand eSafety Commissioner powers to remove “nudify” apps and content, and stronger privacy protections.
“The Greens have long campaigned for big tech to be held accountable for the harm they profit off online,” the Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young said on Tuesday.

The party had long pressed for stronger fines, an ombudsman scheme and stronger action on addictive design features. Hanson-Young said that provision would have the effect of “dumping the doomscroll with rules that force tech companies to prevent harm from their addictive design feature”.
This would go alongside original requirements for social media platforms to offer an “opt-out” feature for its algorithm and suggested content.

Wells said those elements would come into force 12 months after the laws passed. She nominated design features such as “the toxic popularity meters, the endless scroll” as those which could be banned under the addictive features stipulation, but said final decisions would be made by eSafety.
The Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman, which has volunteered to act as a big tech watchdog, welcomed the move to set up an independent complaints mechanism.
“Online services are a core part of our lives. It’s great that Australians will soon have access to a free, fair and independent dispute resolution scheme when big tech gets things wrong.”

articles.title: Asia-Pacific markets rally as Huang’s return to Nvidia reignites AI trade, despite US political backlash – business live
articles.summary: Republicans and Democrats object over Trump’s role in Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO, following an affair with an alleged Chinese spy

blocks.text: Introduction: Asia-Pacific markets rally on Huang's return, despite backlash
Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.
Jensen Huang’s surprising, and controversial, return to run Nvidia has sparked a strong rally in Asia-Pacific stock markets today,
Stocks have surged in Taiwan, South Korea, Japan and Australia, as the AI trade lurches back into life.
The Taiwanese TW50 index has surged by 9.5%, away from the seven-month high touched yesterday. In Seoul, the Kospi index has jumped by 6.5%, led by chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics.
Tokyo’s Nikkei gained almost 4%, and Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 has risen by 1.8%.
That followed a surge on Wall Street last night, where Nvidia’s shares rocketed by 31.5% – adding around $950bn to the company’s value as Huang returned to the company’s HQ.

blocks.caption: Jensen Huang gestures as employees applaud his return to office after NVIDIA reinstated him as the company’s CEO, in Santa Clara, California, US November 23, 2026, in this picture obtained from social media. Photograph: NVIDIA/X/Reuters

blocks.text: Huang’s return “removes an important source of uncertainty,” said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo in Singapore, adding:
double quotation mark“His return restores strategic continuity at Nvidia and reduces the immediate risk of disruptions to its supply chain and technology roadmap.”

But while Wall Street recorded its best day since April 2025 (when Donald Trump paused his Liberation Day tariffs), doubts over the high valuations of AI companies, and questions over whether the industry will generate revenues to sustain their high spending on data centres, remain.
As does the political backlash against Huang’s return, and the role played by Donald Trump’s White House in pressing Nvidia to take its former CEO back.

Democrat senator Elizabeth Warren has called Huang’s restoration “reckless,” and warned that the banking committee she will head next year will be digging into whether Nvidia has complied with export controls.
She also said the Trump administration “needs to explain to Congress what ‘input’ was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement.”

Republican lawmakers also roundly criticized the Nvidia board’s decision to reinstate its chief executive, Jensen Huang, even after Donald Trump said he spoke “directly and indirectly” with board members and “convinced them” to bring him back.
Pete Ricketts, a US senator from Nebraska, wrote on X that Huang’s “behavior does not support reinstatement”, a reminder of his alleged affair with a Chinese spy.
The agenda

items: 9am GMT: IFO survey of German business confidence
11am GMT: CBI Distributive Trades survey of UK retail
2pm GMT: US house price data

items: 14m agoIs AI too big to fail?

blocks.text: Is AI too big to fail?
Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, despite concerns over his conduct and the supply of AI chips to China, may show that AI – and Huang himself – are ‘too big to fail’.
That phrase was on everyone’s lips almost 20 years ago when the Global Financial Crisis struck, and several major banks were bailed out.
Roger Lee, head of equity strategy at investment bank Cavendish, explains:

double quotation markGiven Nvidia’s pivotal role in the AI capex rollout, the implications of Huang’s reinstatement could be profound. Borrowing from the GFC, are some technology CEOs now so systemically important to the future of AI and US leadership in the latest technology revolution that they cannot be fired? Questions around the scale of financing required and future monetisation remain, and the dependence on Huang for the future success of AI may paradoxically heighten those concerns especially given Anthropic fell despite yesterday’s broad market rally.
How Trump lobbied for Huang's return
Yohannes Lowe
A day before Nvidia announced Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as its CEO, the US president, Donald Trump, dialed into the AI giant’s Sunday board meeting to argue for his return, Semafor reports.

According to the NY Times, over the weekend, Trump also asked the vice-president, JD Vance, to work with the board to assure them that Huang, who was forced to resign over a reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy, was not a national security risk.

By Monday morning, Nvidia announced Huang’s return despite its chair previously stating they did not intend to reinstate him because his personal behaviour was inconsistent with the company’s “code of conduct, standards and cultural norms”.

Reflecting a wave of anger among lawmakers at the decision, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, Robert Garcia, said in a statement on Monday that Trump’s “direct involvement” in the matter raised “serious national security and corruption questions”:

double quotation mark“We must investigate these actions. No president who has invested in a private company should be involved in their board decisions. Congress must come together in swift bipartisan action and demand answers immediately.”

Trump’s holdings of Nvidia stock rose in value by as much as $15m (£11.5m) on Monday as the share price surged after news of Huang’s reinstatement broke, the FT notes. The US president owns between $11m (£8.4m) and $55m (£42.1m) in Nvidia stock, according to a Reuters review of his 2025 annual financial disclosure and 2026 share trading disclosures.
Chinese state media have warned that Jensen Huang’s reinstatement won’t end tensions between Beijing and Washington, or restrictions on AI chip exports.
China’s Global Times newspaper published a commentary urging China to “remain vigilant” today, saying:
double quotation mark“It is foreseeable that the malicious attempts to sow discord in China-US relations will not automatically disappear simply because Huang has been reinstated.”
The article also predicted a new round of “witch hunts” could include investigation letters, delays in export licenses and congressional hearings, Bloomberg reports.
London stock market dips in early trading
London’s stock market has opened, with more of a whimper than a bang.
The FTSE 100 share index has dipped by 5 points, or 0.05%, to 10,475 points.

Why no Jensen bounce? Because European markets rallied yesterday when Huang’s return to Nvidia was announced, lifting tech companies across the continent. That pushed the FTSE 100 up by 1.3% on Monday.
Plus, as Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote, explains, his return won’t ease the broader risks facing AI:

double quotation markThere’s the massive spending needed to build AI infrastructure, the pressure on free cash flow at hyperscalers — Nvidia’s biggest clients — and the need for these companies to raise money through equity or bond issuance. Then there are rising borrowing costs as inflation stays elevated and credit spreads widen, and of course the political hurdles with Democrats set to take control of Congress.
Video: Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia yesterday

blocks.caption: A display showing Asian stock markets in Taipei on November 24, 2026. Photograph: I-Hwa Cheng/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The surge in stock markets since Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia was announced shows that investors are “willing to re-engage with the AI theme when uncertainty recedes”, says Christian Stocker, lead equity strategist for UniCredit Munich.

But… Stocker argues that the rally reflected relief that the AI supply chain and investment cycle are unlikely to be abruptly disrupted, rather than renewed conviction that all concerns have disappeared.
He told clients this morning:

double quotation markQuestions about financing structures, profitability and the ultimate returns on AI spending remain largely unresolved. In other words, the debate has shifted. Investors are no longer asking whether AI investment will continue. They are increasingly asking whether the path from investment to monetisation will be slower, more uneven and more dependent on favourable financing conditions than previously assumed. Recent market volatility suggests that the AI narrative remains intact, but the market is becoming less willing to assume a straight-line path to future earnings growth.
Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia’s CEO could, perhaps surprisingly, be painful for US borrowers.
That’s because America’s central bank is more likely to raise interest rates if they’re not facing a bursting AI bubble.
Jim Reid of Deutsche Bank explains:

double quotation markWith fears of an AI slowdown receding, it also led markets to price back in a more hawkish path for the Federal Reserve over the months ahead. So for the next meeting in December, markets are once again fully pricing in a 25bp hike, with 26.1bps priced in for that decision (+3.1bps on the day). Then looking further out, 70bps of hikes are now priced in by the September 2027 meeting, up +6.6bps relative to Friday
US adds Megaspeed, AI firm at center of Nvidia scandal, to trade blacklist
In another significant development in the Nvidia story, Megaspeed International has been placed on a US trade blacklist that bars it from buying advanced AI chips.
In a filing on Monday, the Commerce Department moved to formally add the company to its entity list. This means Megaspeed will now need approval from the commerce department to obtain US exports.
This move revelations that Jensen Huang had a ⁠relationship with Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman alleged to be a spy for Beijing – a claim China has said is “groundless”.
Nvidia rejoices at Jensen Huang’s second coming
Dara Kerr
Jensen Huang made his return to Nvidia’s headquarters with a hero’s welcome yesterday.

Hours earlier he’d been reinstated as the CEO of the world’s most valuable chip company, following a whiplash series of events that involved a romantic affair with a suspected Chinese spy, a drastic plummet in the stock market, and an intervention from Donald Trump.
As Huang entered the company’s Silicon Valley office, wearing his signature dark-colored uniform, crowds of employees rushed to greet him clapping, hollering and chanting: “Jensen, Jensen, Jensen!”
“I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around,” Huang told employees, according to several verified videos posted to social media. The crowd went wild – it was Huang’s second coming.
