articles.title: King Charles and Elton John pay tribute to Australian music legend Molly Meldrum
articles.summary: The promoter and broadcaster helped define the music tastes of Australians for decades.

blocks.text: King Charles and Elton John have paid tribute to Australian music industry legend Molly Meldrum, who died aged 83 after a long illness.
Meldrum's family said he "passed away peacefully" at a hospital in Melbourne in the early hours of Monday morning.
The music promoter and broadcaster, born Ian Alexander Meldrum, helped define the nation's music tastes for decades, championing local artists like INXS and Kylie Minogue and global acts like Abba.
Known for his chaotic demeanour and trademark Stetson hat, he interviewed an array of stars, with the king on Monday calling him "a true giant of the music industry".

Born in Victoria in 1943, Meldrum displayed a love of music from an early age and went on to host the Australian Broadcasting Corporation's music television programme Countdown, and later a segment on variety show Hey Hey, It's Saturday.
Meldrum in 2014 became the first person who was not a recording artist to be inducted into the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria) Hall of Fame.
Meldrum lived with an acquired brain injury after falling from a ladder in 2011.
"Affectionately dubbed 'the Guru', Molly was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music," a statement from Meldrum's family said.
Among his most famous interviews was a 1977 sit-down with King Charles, in which Meldrum could not calm his jitters.
He stumbled over his lines, declaring: "Your Royal Highness... Oh, oh, I'm sweating like a pig".

King Charles reflected on the infamous interview for Countdown's 40th anniversary special, saying: "There is an old showbusiness saying which warns never to work with animals or children. But nobody prepared me for Molly Meldrum".
On Monday, an aide to the King said he had been "deeply saddened" to hear of Meldrum's death.

"His Majesty's interview with Molly is a moment he and many others will never forget - he hopes that interview will once again raise a few smiles as Australians honour Molly's legacy as a true giant of the music industry."
Elton John - a friend and regular interviewee - paid tribute to him as "an Australian legend and an institution", while pop star Kylie Minogue said she would be turning up the music in his honour.
"As a kid, I watched Molly Meldrum on Countdown every single weekend, in awe of the show and the magic it brought to our little TV in the lounge room."
"He championed so many Aussie artists and welcomed international artists to Australia in his own wonderful and inimitable way. I'm so grateful for his unwavering love and support."

Australia's Arts Minister Tony Burke said the country had lost an icon: "One of his greatest legacies will be the generations of Australians who grew up with his unmistakable enthusiasm and love of music."

articles.title: Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African police
articles.summary: South African communities tell the BBC of measures they're taking to keep women safe after a wave of horrific killings.
articles.byline: Nomsa Maseko, Thuthuka Zondi, Eleanor Smallwood

blocks.text: Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African police

blocks.caption: Image caption, Okuhle's body was found dumped near a river in August. She had two children, aged three and nine, and was a civil engineering student

blocks.text: Image source, Family handout
Okuhle's body was found dumped near a river in August. She had two children, aged three and nine, and was a civil engineering student
ByNomsa MasekoThuthuka Zondi and Eleanor Smallwood BBC World ServiceReporting fromEkurhuleni
Tuku Nkosiyaphantsi found out his daughter had been killed from a post on Facebook.
It was August and he hadn't been able to reach 27-year-old Okuhle for days, although it wasn't unusual for her to drop out of contact from time to time.

Then one Saturday, two of Tuku's neighbours called him to say that they had seen that Okuhle had been reported missing by police on Facebook. They had also seen a photo of what appeared to be Okuhle injured.
"When I looked at this photo, I saw that the person in it was dead, and when I looked closer I realised it was Okuhle," says Tuku, 50.

After seeing the image, Tuku phoned a police officer he knew. The policeman confirmed the woman in the picture had been killed and her body dumped near a river in Kokstad, an agricultural hub in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province, in the east of the country.
But because the morgue was closed for the weekend, it wasn't until Monday morning that Tuku was able to identify Okuhle's body.
When he did, Tuku saw she had been mutilated and her face badly beaten.
"It was very painful, so much that I cannot accept it."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Okuhle's father, Tuku, says he feels "ignored and unseen" by the government after his daughter's death

blocks.text: Image source, Thuthuka Zondi/BBC
Okuhle's father, Tuku, says he feels "ignored and unseen" by the government after his daughter's death
Okuhle had two children, aged nine and three, and was a civil engineering student.
She is among 581 women who were killed in the country between July and September, according to the South African Police Service.
Overall, there were 5,590 murders - 204 fewer than in the same period last year.
It is the first time police have broken down murders by gender, so it is unclear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease on previous years.

There has been a renewed national outcry this year about the scale of violence against women after the partially naked and bruised bodies of 12 women were found dumped in public areas in Ekurhuleni, a district to the east of Johannesburg, this summer.
South Africa has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and femicide - the intentional killing of a woman or girl - in the world.
Am I Next? Fear and Survival in South Africa
The BBC World Service visits communities struggling to confront widespread violence against women

In response to this summer's killings, President Cyril Ramaphosa promised safety audits across every municipality to identify and address dangerous spaces for women, as well as an increased police presence in the worst-affected areas.
But in places like Kokstad and Kempton Park, both in Ekurhuleni, the BBC World Service saw people taking the protection of women into their own hands.
For Tuku, that means investigating his daughter's killing himself.
Months after she was killed, he says no-one has been arrested.
"It was just silent after we buried Okuhle - there was nothing at all. I so wish the police would stand up and investigate."

He believes police failed to review CCTV footage from a local government building in the town that may have shown who his daughter was with on the day she disappeared. The footage is wiped every seven days, he says.
The BBC approached the South African Police Service for comment but at the time of publication, no response had been received.

The police service has previously acknowledged shortcomings in its overall response to gender-based violence and femicide, adding that it was continuing to invest in addressing these challenges. Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has said there needs to be "greater efforts" to prevent violence against women and children.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The killing of women this summer sparked widespread protests across South Africa

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
The killing of women this summer sparked widespread protests across South Africa
According to a 2024 report by the South African Medical Research Council, the number of unsolved cases of femicide was growing.
This year, Amnesty International said South Africa's police service was "under-resourced, poorly equipped, and insufficiently trained to respond effectively and sensitively to gender-based violence".
Tuku says he is now searching for CCTV footage and seeking out people who knew his daughter in the hope of finding leads.
Despite Ramaphosa's promises, he has little faith anything will change.
"I listened to Ramaphosa. The government acts only when something happened. We in Kokstad, we feel like we are ignored and unseen. The government does not care for us."

Asked earlier this month by the BBC what progress South Africa had made to keep women safe, Ramaphosa said the government would be allocating extra money in February's budget to deal with gender-based violence.

Speaking as he cast his vote in local elections, Ramaphosa added that the government had increased police numbers in the last three years "and we will continue to do so, so that there can be more visible policing".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Kokstad residents have started night-time patrols and are maintaining a curfew that advises children to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00

blocks.text: Kokstad residents have started night-time patrols and are maintaining a curfew that advises children to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00
Okuhle is not the only woman to be killed this year in Kokstad.
Between January and October this year, the bodies of five women and three very young children were found in the town, with arrests only taking place in two of the cases.
In response, this summer, the community set up street patrols and a curfew for women and children.
Since June, children have been told to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00.

Kamvalethu Cetywayo, 34, from a local neighbourhood watch group, leads a group of around 15 men who patrol crime hotspots in the town at night, including areas where bodies have been found or trouble has been reported to them.
The patrols tend to take place between Thursday and Sunday because this is when people drink alcohol most heavily, says Kamvalethu.
Most of the patrollers carry sticks, whips and torches, but Kamvalethu has a licensed gun. He says the group will call police when they need back-up.
Asked how he feels about restricting the freedoms of women and children, Kamvalethu says the curfew helps keep them safe, is voluntary, and a temporary measure until police arrest the killers.
"With the resolution we made with the community, we get to assist them with this, but if people are refusing there's nothing we can do."
Even so, not all victims are attacked at night or on the streets.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Kgothatso says she was taking a taxi to work when the driver attempted to kidnap her

blocks.text: Kgothatso says she was taking a taxi to work when the driver attempted to kidnap her
Kgothatso Mojela was kidnapped on her way to work in 2018 in Kempton Park.
She was in a taxi when the driver locked the doors and started driving in the wrong direction.
When Kgothatso told him he had missed the turn, she says he started punching and slapping her.
"Immediately, I just knew my life was in danger," says Kgothatso, who is now 35.

Kgothatso says she forced the passenger door open and threw herself out of the moving taxi, badly injuring her knee and causing nerve damage to her eyes. Two security guards, who were nearby, came to her aid.
She says her attacker was later jailed for a number of crimes, including what he did to her, but was released last year. Kgothatso says she now fears for her life.
Yet while Kgothatso was attacked by a stranger, according to the South African Medical Research Council, 60% of women murdered in the country between 2020-21 were killed by an intimate partner.
In the wake of her attack, Kgothatso has made changes to how she lives, including buying an imitation gun to scare off would-be attackers.
She has also stopped running alone, and insists on someone accompanying her if she goes to meet a client she hasn't met before at work.
Such precautions are all too familiar to many women in South Africa.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Zama says her running group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles

blocks.text: Zama says her running group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles
In September police urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone, "particularly in isolated areas" - after the killing of 38-year-old mother Elizabeth Moselakgomo.
She vanished on 9 September while out running. Her badly bruised, partially clothed body was found dumped near a busy motorway in Kempton Park three days later.

It was a killing that resonated deeply within South Africa's running community, including sisters Zonke and Zama Mthethwa. They started The Pack, a women's running group in Johannesburg nine years ago. Elizabeth would sometimes attend The Pack events.
Runners across the city joined the search efforts following Elizabeth's disappearance, and took part in protests calling for violence against women to end.

Zonke and Zama's group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles. They also get cars to follow them and have started offering self-defence coaching to the women in their running group.
"We need to try and rally and create safe spaces for women to show up authentically and to do what they love doing," says Zama, 37.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at a prayer march to remember women who have been killed

blocks.text: Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at a prayer march to remember women who have been killed
Following her ordeal, Kgothatso moved from Kempton Park and now lives closer to her parents in another part of the country.
Her mother, a community activist, recently organised a prayer march to remember women who have been killed.
Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at the march.
Wiping away tears, she said: "To a survivor listening right now, I want to say you are not dirty, you are not broken beyond repair. You are not to blame and you are not alone."

articles.title: Butt of the joke: Trump impersonator mocks president at Canada press dinner
articles.summary:
Carney watches on as comedian lampoons US leader and his interest in men’s backsides at correspondents’ event Ottawa

Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, was joined on stage in Ottawa by a…

blocks.text: Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, was joined on stage in Ottawa by a Donald Trump impersonator who mocked the US president to raucous laughter from a crowd of politicians and journalists at a parliamentary press gallery dinner on Saturday.

With coiffed hair and an ill-fitting suit, comedian Mark Critch – who portrays the president on the sketch show This Hour Has 22 Minutes – danced on to the stage and lampooned the trade war Trump started as well as the president’s threats to annex Canada.
“We’re going to have a great deal,” Critch said, channeling Trump’s distinct mannerisms. “There’s only one thing standing in the way: me, because I’m crazy.”
The fake Trump continued that he was “so popular we just had a big, blue wave”, a reference to the Democratic rout of Republicans in this month’s US midterm elections.

He also mocked Trump’s frequent mentions of other men’s physiques, saying of the comedian Mark McKinney, who was portraying Carney, that he had “a great ass – doesn’t he? What a beautiful ass, he’s got such an incredible ass.”

He earned the most laughter of his short appearance for saying of Carney: “I don’t call him the governor to his face, because I’m a coward”. The real Trump has frequently attempted to insult Canada’s leaders by calling them governor, not prime minister, suggesting Canada is a US state.
The annual dinner, attended by media, political leaders and lobbyists, is often defined by carefully written jokes by the staff of party leaders.
Throughout his own 16-minute set, Carney poked fun at his political rivals, the media and the US president.
At one point, he remarked: “Damn, this is a tough room, and I’ve been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator.”
Clips of the dinner, including the crowd laughing at the president, have circulated widely on US media.
The newly appointed governor general, Louise Arbour, also gave a speech, including a nod to the prime minister’s decision to travel extensively around the globe.

“Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he’s supposed to be,” she said.
The Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, also used the evening to poke fun at his own reputation.

“Some say that Mark has a controlling leadership style. There’s been reports that he yells and micromanages his staff. He acts like a miserable prick to journalists,” he said. “And when I hear things like that, I say once again, he’s stealing all my ideas.”

He attracted a stunned silence, however, for alluding to Justin Trudeau’s relationship with Katy Perry, saying, “Trudeau is running around the world doing to a faded pop princess what he did to Canada” while prime minister, a remark that was widely criticised as demeaning to the pop star.

The New Democratic party leader, Avi Lewis, who has not yet won a seat in parliament, took a shot at Carney’s early exit from the event, as well his own party’s dismal standings. “I do not have a seat in the House of Commons, but when I am given one at dinner, I stay there all night long,” he said.

articles.title: Gisèle Pelicot 'humiliated' after nude photos sent to media to promote book
articles.summary: The publisher of an essay on coercive control apologises for "an unfortunate and inappropriate communication".

blocks.text: Gisèle Pelicot has said she has been "once again humiliated" after nude images of her were sent to the media to promote a book about coercive control.
The 73-year-old told French broadcaster BFM TV she would take legal action against the publisher and author of the essay.

Pelicot made headlines across the world when she waived her right to anonymity in the trial of her then-husband Dominique, who was jailed for 20 years for drugging and raping her, as well as allowing other men to rape her while she was unconscious.
The publisher apologised, saying it would no longer print or promote the work after "an unfortunate and inappropriate communication".
Pelicot told BFM: "I am deeply shocked that images from the most intimate part of my private life are being displayed and exploited for commercial purposes."
"Today I find myself once again humiliated, exposed and hurt, as if the ordeal of the trial had not been enough," she said.
The essay was written by Sabine Prokhoris, a philosopher and psychoanalyst, who has previously criticised the Me Too movement.
French media reported that Tinbad, a small Paris publishing house, emailed nude photos of Pelicot taken by her ex-husband to some media outlets in order to promote the essay.
In a statement on its website, Tinbad said that no further print runs of the book would be produced beyond the 280 copies already in circulation.
"We offer our sincerest apologies to Ms Gisèle Pelicot," it said. The company also apologised to the author.
Tinbad said "no images of rape or pornographic videos" were sent to the media.
French news agency AFP quoted the blurb of the book as saying coercive control was "a cornerstone of #MeToo orthodoxy".
"These psychological situations, fundamentally ambiguous in nature, involve each of the parties in an equally responsible, though not symmetrical, way," it said.
Pelicot's lawyer Christophe Bigot told BFM the book "calls into question her status as a victim".
Prokhoris told AFP that she placed "full responsibility" for the "inappropriate" promotional campaign on her publisher.
Fifty men were convicted alongside Pelicot's ex-husband in 2024, in a case that made her a global feminist icon.

After her husband was arrested for secretly filming underneath women's skirts in a supermarket, she discovered she had been repeatedly raped by dozens of men, including her husband, while unconscious, over a period of nearly a decade.
Pelicot said she decided to waive her right to anonymity to show how "shame has to change sides" from victims to perpetrators.
If you have been affected by the issues in this story help and support can be found at BBC Action Line.

articles.title: Iranian singer and four others receive lashes after performance without hijab
articles.summary:
Western governments and human rights groups have criticised flogging as torture and a violation of international law

An Iranian singer and four members of her production team ⁠have each…

blocks.text: An Iranian singer and four members of her production team ⁠have each received 74 lashes after being sentenced for “offending public decency by producing and ⁠publishing obscene and ⁠immoral ​content online”, an Iranian news website said on Monday.
Parastoo Ahmadi and the four ⁠others were also handed two-year bans on artistic and musical activities and travel, the Emtedad website ⁠quoted lawyer Mostafa Nili as saying.

The case followed the ​release of a ‌video on YouTube ‌in December 2024 showing Ahmadi performing without the mandatory hijab alongside ‌male musicians in Qom, south of the capital Tehran, Norway-based human rights group Hengaw said.

Western governments and human rights groups have criticised flogging as torture and a violation of international law. Iran rejects accusations over ‌its human rights record, saying western countries should focus on their own human rights ​problems.

Rules requiring women to wear the hijab were a flashpoint during protests in 2022 after the ⁠death in custody of Kurdish Iranian woman Mahsa Amini, ​who was ​arrested for allegedly violating ​the dress code.
The rules have increasingly been ​flouted on ‌the streets of Tehran ​and ​beyond, and enforcement of the rules has also become more selective.

articles.title: What strike on Russian ship in Libya says about spread of Ukraine war
articles.summary: Ukraine's sinking of a Russian battleship at a port in Libya raises the stakes of the war a notch, writes Frank Gardner.

blocks.text: Anchored up in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.

The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi, co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?
The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.
Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes, has called it "a dangerous escalation".
It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.
Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.

Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks – what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" – have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.

The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.

And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses.
It's not just Russia that will be alarmed by this latest Ukrainian operation in Benghazi harbour. The United Nations mission in Libya has already expressed its "deep concern".

Libyan officials point out that their country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war, although the Merkury and an accompanying cargo ship that was also hit were berthed in the eastern part of Libya controlled by the pro-Moscow warlord and self-styled "Field Marshal" Khalifa Haftar.

articles.title: Israel seeks to jail Palestinian student activist without trial after dorm arrest
articles.summary:
Mahdi Tounsi appeared with visible bruising after being interrogated by police on his association with Israeli-Palestinian organisations

Israeli professors, students and rights activists are…

blocks.text: Israeli professors, students and rights activists are calling for the immediate release of Mahdi Tounsi, a sociology student at Jerusalem’s Hebrew University who has been held without charge for more than two weeks after he was seized from his dorm room.

The detention comes amid a racist campaign of delegitimisation against Palestinian citizens of Israel, whose votes were critical to stripping Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition of its majority in elections last month.
Police took Tounsi, 26, a criminology and sociology student from East Jerusalem who is active in Jewish-Palestinian campaign groups, from his dorm room on 8 November.
When he appeared by video link at a court hearing on 19 November he had visible bruises on his face, did not have the glasses he needs to see properly, and his hair and beard had been shaved.

Tounsi told his lawyer that police beat him in the dorm, in the patrol car and at the police station, Israeli media reported. Interrogators questioned him about his activism with Israeli-Palestinian organisations Standing Together and Ir Amim.
Both groups called for his immediate release and warned against using security agencies to silence political activity and critical speech.

“[This] could happen to any student and any one of us, especially in a month when the government is persecuting Arab citizens, from [journalist] Abed Abu Shehadeh to the leaders of Arab political parties,” Standing Together said in a statement, calling on the university to intervene to ensure a fair judicial process.

Ir Amim described Tounsi as thoughtful, gentle and a valued partner “in movements bringing Palestinians and Israelis together”, in a statement that also warned of “serious concerns for his safety, wellbeing, and right to due process”.

blocks.caption: Demonstrators call for the release of Mahdi Tounsi outside the Jerusalem district court. Photograph: Jess Flom/JNA/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: After losing the election, Netanyahu and his allies weaponised false accusations of mass fraud – Israel’s election commission validated the results – in an attempt to hold on to power by delegitimising the votes of Palestinian citizens of Israel.
The prime minister has also been accused of politicising security institutions in his campaign against Palestinian-led parties, and fostering a rise in racist rhetoric.

When police powers to hold Tounsi under the original arrest warrant expired last week, they submitted an order to hold him without trial in administrative detention, signed by the defence minister, Israel Katz.

The administrative detention law allows Israel to hold individuals for up to six months without charging them or allowing them to see evidence against them, although it has to be presented in a closed court.
Because the Shin Bet security force did not send a representative to the hearing on Tounsi’s detention last week, it was postponed until Tuesday.

Ahead of the court hearing, Jewish and Palestinian students demonstrated at universities across the country, including Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, with signs including “Free Mahdi” and “Kidnapping Palestinians will not silence justice”.
The university authorities did not inform his family, and his detention only came to light after concerned friends reported him missing.

Hebrew University said in a statement that it was notified about the arrest shortly before police seized Tounsi, that no university representatives were present when he was detained and police afterwards said the arrest took place “without unusual incidents”.
It did not directly address the allegations of police violence, his visible bruising, the shaving of his head and beard, removal of his glasses or the shifting legal framework.

“The university is not a party to the legal proceedings involving the student, and we do not have information that would allow us to comment on the circumstances leading to the arrest or on the ongoing legal proceedings,” the statement said.
“We are concerned for his wellbeing,” the statement added, saying the university hoped “that his rights will be fully respected throughout the process”.
Israeli police did not respond to requests for comment about Tounsi’s detention.

Tounsi is a resident of East Jerusalem, not a Palestinian citizen of Israel. Palestinians holding that status can move freely inside Israel and Jerusalem but are stateless and can not vote in Israeli national elections.

articles.title: Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say
articles.summary: Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were reportedly given 74 lashes in Qom.

blocks.text: A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.
Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.
Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.
This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.
In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.
At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.

There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.
On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom.
"We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said.
"The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately."
Pro-reform daily Etemad cited another defence lawyer, Mostafa Nili, as identifying the four men flogged alongside Ahmadi as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari.

"Parastoo Ahmadi's flogging for singing and dressing as she chooses is a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights and a chilling demonstration of the Iranian authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms and to violently punish anyone who dares to challenge their discriminatory laws and policies," said Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).

Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.

In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".

Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.

Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.

In January this year, thousands of people were killed and tens of thousands were arrested when security forces crushed another wave of mass anti-establishment protests, this time sparked by the country's economic crisis.
Since the start of Iran's war with the US and Israel in late February, authorities have intensified their use of the death penalty against protesters.

According to the Norway-based group Iran Human Rights, at least 39 men convicted over January's protests and two convicted over the 2022 unrest have been executed, along with 16 people allegedly affiliated with banned opposition groups and 17 others convicted of espionage or collaborating with foreign states.
Another 121 protesters detained in January, including six women and five juvenile offenders, have been sentenced to death and are at imminent risk of execution, it says.

articles.title: Comedian impersonates Trump's dance moves, mocks trade talks at Canada press dinner
articles.summary: The impersonator, Canadian comedian Mark Critch, poked fun at the US president's search for a new press secretary and US-Canada trade talks.

blocks.text: Prime Minister Mark Carney brought a Donald Trump impersonator on stage at Ottawa's annual press gallery dinner, where he poked fun at strained US-Canada relations and on-again, off-again trade talks.
The impersonator, played by comedian Mark Critch of the sketch comedy show This Hour Has 22 Minutes, came out after Carney jokingly pressed an "emergency comedy button" during his speech.
Critch appeared alongside another actor impersonating Carney, played by Canadian sketch comedian Mark McKinney.
"We've got two Carneys here, it's a disaster," the Trump impersonator said after he walked on stage.

Using some of Trump's signature mannerisms, like his dance moves and his slightly hunched posture, he joked about the latest US midterm elections, which led to Trump's Republican Party losing control in Congress.
"I'm so popular we just had a big BLUE WAVE in the states," the impersonator said at the Saturday press gala.
He also took aim at ongoing US-Canada trade negotiations, saying,"We're going to have a great deal. There's only one thing standing in the way: me, because I'm crazy."
There were also jabs at Trump's search for a new White House press secretary following Katie Zacharia's exit, and at US ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra, who is unpopular among Canadians.
"I said 'find somebody who is less likeable than me,' and we got one," the Trump impersonator joked about Hoekstra.

Carney stood behind him occasionally laughing. The prime minister also delivered his own zingers, saying at one point: "This is a tough room. And I've been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator."

Both Critch and McKinney - the two impersonators - are fixtures of This Hour Has 22 Minutes, a long-standing Canadian sketch comedy show that has recently enjoyed viral internet fame for its timely skits mocking the Trump administration.
The skits, published directly on Tik Tok and YouTube, have depicted Zacharia's quick ouster, external and poked fun at rapper Nicki Minaj's, external support for Trump.
They have garnered millions of views, and even captured the attention of major US media., external

Critch and McKinney's appearance at Saturday's dinner is part of an evening of traditionally light-hearted humour, where Canadian politicians poke fun at one another at a gala hosted by the Canadian Parliamentary Press Gallery.
In a separate speech, Canada's governor general, Louise Arbour, joked about Carney's popularity and frequent global travel.

"Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he's supposed to be," Arbour said.

articles.title: Barbados town’s three-year deal with Bristol ‘part of the reparative process’
articles.summary:
Island’s labour minister, Tony Dyer, says agreement acknowledges links between Speightstown and UK city are rooted in slave trade

A town in Barbados known as “Little Bristol” has signed a…

blocks.text: A town in Barbados known as “Little Bristol” has signed a “twinning’” agreement with the UK city, marking a new chapter in a centuries-long relationship rooted in the transatlantic slave trade.
Barbados says the new partnership between Speightstown and Bristol is part of its wider push for reparatory justice, built in small steps rather than around a multi-trillion-pound claim.
Colin Jordan, the island’s labour minister, signed a three-year memorandum of understanding (MOU) with the Bristol city council leader, Tony Dyer, at City Hall on Friday.

Speightstown is the second-largest town in Barbados. In the 17th and 18th centuries its port shipped sugar, produced by enslaved African people, to Bristol. A bar bearing the name is still a popular venue within the island, Jordan said.

blocks.caption: Colin Jordan, seated right, at the signing at Bristol’s City Hall on Friday. Photograph: Bristol city council

blocks.text: In an interview after the ceremony, Jordan said the agreement sat firmly within the island nation’s wider push for reparations, led by the prime minister, Mia Mottley.
“I see the MOU as part of the reparative process,” he said. “It is doing it in a complementary way because it is focused on the relationships between two towns, two cities, two peoples.”

He was careful with his language. “People get emotive about reparations,” said the politician, who is also MP for St Peter, the parish where Speightstown sits. “The word reparations comes from the word repair.”
Defensiveness, he continued, had threatened progress around the conversation. “The walls go up, and then it’s difficult for the message to get through.”
The agreement has no money attached to it and Bristol city council confirmed there was no dedicated funding for major projects involved.
However, it does set out a framework for cooperation on heritage, education, tourism, culture and the creative economy. The exact terms are to be determined through a series of discussions.

blocks.caption: View of Cobblers beach, Speightstown, St Peter’s, Barbados. Photograph: Richard Blunt/Alamy

blocks.text: Jordan said the money question was settled. “There is not going to be some grand $4tn something somewhere,” he said. “It’s going to be building block by building block.”
He offered a Barbadian proverb to make the point that steady progress was better than extravagant windfalls: “A sheep head a day is better than a cow head a year.”
The MOU recognises that the relationship began in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans. “Acknowledging that, we believe, is probably half of the repair,” he said.

He described a relationship that ran one way for roughly two centuries. “Bristol and the UK benefited from the extraction of wealth from Barbados and Speightstown,” he said. The aim now was one that was “mutually beneficial, inclusive”.
Jordan expected exchanges between schools and universities, and between cricket and football bodies – and also pointed to trade.

Repair, he argued, was not only financial. “Value is not just currency,” he said. He gave the example of a Speightstown schoolchild whose parents might be unable to afford a school bag, who could be helped through a link with a Bristol school. He also suggested the relationship could offer “psychological repair” to Bristolians uneasy about their ancestors’ part in slavery.
‘Not a shelf document’

The MOU runs to November 2029. Jordan has said it “will not become a ‘shelf’ document” but will serve as “a roadmap, as well as our motivation”. He was already looking to 2030, the 400th anniversary of Speightstown’s founding, for a successor agreement.
after newsletter promotion

Dyer said the deal was “firmly about the future” but should be honest about the past. At the ceremony, he said much of the work lay ahead and warned against signing the agreement and “putting it in the cupboard”.

“Bristol and Speightstown have a long and complex shared history, and signing this agreement is an important opportunity both to recognise that past and to decide together how we can build on our relationship.

“Our connections were shaped by the transatlantic trafficking and enslavement of African people and the sugar trade. It is important that we are open and honest about that history, while working with communities in Bristol and Barbados to deepen our understanding of it.”
Bristol is pursuing the same model elsewhere. A parallel MOU with Odesa, in Ukraine, covers the same period.
Beyond Bristol

Edmund Hinkson, Barbados’s high commissioner to the UK, who witnessed the signing, placed the deal within a longer history. Barbados’s 1650 slave code, he noted, defined Black people as chattel, and was later copied across the Caribbean and the Americas.
Hinkson said Barbados was not looking for the trillions of pounds that economists, including the Brattle Group, have estimated is owed for two centuries of unpaid labour.
“We know that the UK is not going to pay that,” he said, although he noted that British taxpayers, including Caribbean ones, serviced the debt used to compensate 46,000 enslavers in 1834, until 2015.

The high commissioner commended Bristol’s “maturity” in recognising the historical link between Barbados and the city’s role in the transatlantic trafficking of Africans into the Caribbean, including Barbados.
He said he believed that the Black Lives Matter’ protests in 2020, which included the toppling of the statue of enslaver Edward Colston, had propelled that recognition and education of Bristolians.

When asked to expand on the point afterwards, Hinkson said the Black Lives Matter movement did not drive Barbados’s reparations stance, but reiterated his belief that it had shaped the UK response. He pointed to the recent Commonwealth summit in Antigua where, he said, a British prime minister recognised the need for “structured and respectful dialogue” over a formal apology for Britain’s role in enslavement.
Speightstown also has a twinning-style MOU with Reading, formally signed in 2003, and Charleston, South Carolina, part of the Gullah Geechee corridor, in the US.
The signing with Bristol comes days before Barbados marks 60 years of independence on 30 November, and five years as a republic.

articles.title: Lucy Powell to visit China to promote UK education weeks after MI5 warning
articles.summary:
Delegation of 50 to accompany minister, with trip criticised after universities were warned about Chinese interference

The education secretary, Lucy Powell, is travelling to Beijing this…

blocks.text: The education secretary, Lucy Powell, is travelling to Beijing this week to promote UK education, weeks after MI5 issued a rare public warning to universities about Chinese interference in UK academia.

A 50-strong UK delegation, including 18 university leaders, will accompany the minister when she attends the first UK-China education summit in nine years, aimed at opening up new opportunities for universities, colleges and education businesses.

The visit prompted criticism, as it comes two months after UK universities were warned by MI5 that China’s intelligence services were using a front company to pay for research by UK academics and steal secrets from hi-tech projects.
One critic described Powell’s visit, which begins on Tuesday, as “mind-blowingly shortsighted”, while the Conservatives said the education secretary’s priorities were “all wrong”.

Discussions in China are expected to cover higher education, technical and vocational education, schools, English language teaching, digital education and education technology, the Department for Education (DfE) said

“The freedom and independence of our academic institutions is sacrosanct,” a DfE spokesperson said. “We will not accept collaborations which compromise our national security or attempt to benefit covertly from research done in partnership with UK universities.”

Successive British governments have welcomed Chinese investment and encouraged academic cooperation between the two countries. About 150,000 Chinese students currently study at UK universities, contributing £7bn to the UK economy every year. Concerns have been growing in recent years, however, about the potential risks of such close collaboration.

On 30 September, MI5 warned vice-chancellors that a Chinese state-owned conglomerate called the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI) had funded 100 or more academics in return for access to research which found its way back to China’s intelligence service.

The claim was denied by the Chinese embassy. Before that there was outcry when it emerged Sheffield Hallam University had complied with a demand from Beijing to halt research about human rights abuses in China.

Condemning the trip to China, the shadow education secretary, Laura Trott, said Powell’s priorities were all wrong. “Instead of seeking closer ties to China, Powell should clamp down on CCP [Chinese Communist party] attempts to influence our own universities & its treatment of those who criticise it,” she posted on X.
Luke de Pulford, the executive director of the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China, wrote on X: “Mind-blowingly shortsighted in policy terms.”
“What might seem to the uninitiated like an economic opportunity, or short-term hope to plug a gap in finances may actually be the government signing UK high education’s death warrant.
“If the balance tips too far towards dependence; if Beijing gets enough leverage, these institutions will cease to operate freely, and continue to leak IP and sensitive research to an adversary.”
after newsletter promotion

Sam Dunning, the director of UK-China Transparency, said the UK was in unprecedented territory. “British universities have never been so financially dependent on foreign students as they are today on Chinese students,” he said.
“Nor have there ever been more foreign nationals from any one country than British nationals studying Stem at an elite level in our top institutions, as is the case with China today.
“We are in unprecedented territory and on perilous terrain. The public interest demands careful, long-term thinking about these issues, and not continued short-termism.”

The summit forms part of government plans to grow education exports to £40bn a year by 2030. “British education is one of our country’s greatest strengths,” said Powell. “Expanding that internationally is a massive opportunity for our economy and wider society.

“Education builds lasting relationships and creates opportunities, but it also gives us the relationships and channels we need to have open and honest conversations. That is why we are putting education at the heart of clear-eyed engagement with China, using Britain’s world-class reputation to support growth, strengthen our global standing and stand up for what matters to Britain.”

articles.title: US and UK to host Women's World Cups in 2031 and 2035
articles.summary: FIFA has confirmed the United States, alongside Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, will host the 2031 Women's World Cup — the first to feature 48 teams. The UK will stage the 2035 edition, its first…

image.caption: Spain are the defending champions going into Brazil in 2027Image: Frank Fife/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: FIFA have confirmed the hosts for the 2031 and 2035 Women's World Cup.

The United States, along with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, was the only candidate to host in 2031, the first tournament that will feature 48 teams — as is the case with the men — for the first time. The US has hosted the tournamnent twice before, in 2003 and 1999, and is also the most successful country in World Cup history having won it four times.

After FIFA announced its revenue for the 2026 men's World Cup that finished just last summer was around $15 billionn (€13.7 billion), it is clear that US Soccer feels empowered that hosting the women's tournament is the next move forward. With the women's domestic league (NWSL) considered the strongest in the world and the US national team so strong, it is clear that securing the tournament in 2031 is a further sign of the US' committment to women's football.
"We expect and plan for the 2031 Women’s World Cup to be the largest women’s sporting event in history," Emily Cosler, US Soccer’s vice-president of strategy told The Guardian.
Two tournaments in seven years for the UK

The 2035 tournament was also awarded to the sole bidders, England, Scotland, Northern Ireland and Wales. This sees the World Cup return to the United Kingdom for the first time since 1966, the only time England's men's team won the competition. The women lost the 2023 final to Spain. It also means that the UK will host two major tournaments in relatively quick succession, with the men's 2028 European Championships also set to be held in England, Scotland and Wales and the Republic of Ireland.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the tournament would bring "visitors, investment and jobs to every part of the country."

Given that FIFA President Gianni Infantino had revealed last year that both bids were unchallenged, this news comes as little surprise. Nevertheless, with the hosts now official, a 48-team tournament marks a remarkable growth for the women's game. For reference, the 2011 World Cup in Germany had just 16 teams.
The next World Cup will be in Brazil next year. Eighteen of the 32 teams have already secured qualification, including Germany, for the tournament, which runs from June 24 to July 25.

articles.title: The rise and fall and rise again of Jensen Huang
articles.summary: Days after resigning while mired in scandal of extra-marital affairs, Nvidia's Jensen Huang is making a remarkable return.
articles.byline: Michael Race, Peter Hoskins, Lucy Hooker

blocks.text: It's being called a comeback for the ages.
For a long time it seemed that Jensen Huang, the leather jacket-clad founder of Nvidia, dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech", could do no wrong.
Then came allegations of two affairs - one with a businesswoman suspected of being a Chinese spy - that rocked the world of tech and the global stock market. Huang resigned.
Now, just 11 days later, he's been reinstated by the board, who says it believes he is the right person to lead the company.
So what do we know about the man who is once again at the head of Nvidia, a linchpin in the US's race for technology leadership with China?
Huang may not be a household name on the same level as Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg.

But his role in the tech industry, especially in relation to the explosion of artificial intelligence in the last three years, may prove more consequential. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips that are used to power the new technology.
The company is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses.
Huang enjoyed access to the seats of political power on an unrivalled scale, being courted by both US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping.

His remarkable rise to the top of his profession saw him amass an estimated fortune of close to $200bn earlier this year, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, though that has since dropped to around $105bn.

Despite always donning his trademark all-black outfits and taking a playful approach to investor presentations, Huang has worked for years to present himself as a family man, someone who exemplified the American Dream.

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to the west coast of the US when he was nine years old. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a Master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.
It was at college where he met his wife, Lori Mills. The pair were lab partners and married in 1985, eight years before Huang founded Nvidia.
They have two children, Madison and Spencer, who now both work in senior roles at Nvidia.

The company became a key provider of the computer chips and circuits used for gaming before it expanded in a new direction. It now creates the key processing chips used to power the growing AI technology.

Huang has hailed AI as a "new industrial revolution" that is on a par with the advent of electricity. Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company and its customers include the biggest firms on the planet, Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic, all spending big on its products.

So it is no surprise that at a recent AI summit at the White House, Huang was picked out from a group of 42 to flank the president, alongside Elon Musk, both men with whom Trump has famously close relationships.

"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Jensen Huang, told the BBC, referring to the late boss of Apple. He added that Huang was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.
He described him as a "demanding" boss, who "really pushes his people to the limit".
But while Huang is "very brilliant" and a "world-class computer scientist", there's also "a level of arrogance" and "a level of self-deception as well", he said.
Huang had gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, he added, something that was "very important to him".

First reports emerged on 29 October in the New York Times that Huang had conducted a relationship with Alice Huang, no relation. US officials allege the businesswoman associated with Singapore-based firm Megaspeed is a Chinese intelligence asset.
Huang admitted to having been unfaithful to his wife and apologised for hurting their family.

But the reporting of a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, vice president of healthcare who has worked at Nvidia for 18 years, prompted a board meeting, followed by an announcement that Huang was stepping down.
He'd barely been gone, however, before a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign was launched, reportedly by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters.
The man himself said he would be "honoured" to return, should the board ask him.
Although initially showing no interest in reinstating him, the board has now done just that, saying his return was "in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".

articles.title: Gukesh to defend chess crown against rising star Sindarov
articles.summary: As the World Chess championship gets underway, it's no coincidence that the titleholder, Gukesh Dommaraju, and his challenger, Jakhovir Sindarov, are both from Asia.

image.caption: Although he is the challenger, Javokhir Sindarov may be the favorite to beat title holder Gukesh Dommaraju Image: Salvatore Di Nolfi/KEYSTONE/picture alliance

blocks.text: When India's world chess champion, Dommaraju Gukesh, faced reporters at the pre-tournament press conference in Geneva on Sunday, there was no sign of the youthful, carefree energy one might expect from a 20-year-old.
"I don't think I'm here to defend anything—I'm here to win it all over again," he said.
Starting November 24, Gukesh will be facing challenger Jakhovir Sindarov of Uzbekistan for a purse of $2.5 million (€2.3m) in the World Chess Championship.

Gukesh captured the title in 2024, making him the youngest-ever world champion at just 18. Since then, however, things have not as gone well for the player known for his exceptional calculation skills and a penchant for risky moves. He currently languishes in 26th place in the FIDE world rankings.
The challenger as the favorite
Sindarov, who has climbed to number four in the world, told reporters that he only began training "seriously" last year and has learned a lot from observing the reigning world champion.
"He has a very good strength in typical positions, his calculation is very good, and Gukesh can fight until the end," Sindarov said.
Former world champion Viswanathan Anand, who was also one of the world's best players as a teenager, is not completely surprised by Gukesh's lack of form over the past two years.
"He became the world champion (very young). So suddenly the responsibility is shifted onto you and even expectations," Anand told DW.
"Clearly he has deficiencies in his chess as is normal for someone who's 20, he's not had time to experience a lot."
By the time he became India's first world champion, Anand was 37 – ancient by the age-standards of today's top players.
The computer generation
"With powerful chess software and global connectivity, it is easier for young players today to reach the top level," Jan Gustafsson, coach of Germany's national chess team, told DW.
"Online chess provides many more learning opportunities for talented players," added Gustafsson, who sees the recent movement at the top of the rankings as a "generational shift."

blocks.caption: Former world champion Magnus Carlsen now rarely competes in classical chessImage: Carina Johansen/NTB/IMAGO

blocks.text: While Norway's Magnus Carlsen, long considered the greatest player of all time, remains number one in the world rankings, he rarely plays classical chess anymore and gave up his world championship title after declining to defend it in 2023.

Now, young players—particularly from Asia—are pushing to the forefront. Alongside Gukesh and Sindarov, players such as Rameshbabu Praggnanandhaa from India and Nodirbek Abdusattorov of Uzbekistan—an emerging chess powerhouse—are considered contenders to win a world championship in the not-too-distant future.
"Broad social acceptance and state support ensure that children can focus on chess at a very early stage," Gustafsson said.

Another contender is Germany's Vincent Keymer, who at 22 is number nine in the world and well established among the world's elite. Most recently, Keymer and his teammates won a bronze medal at the World Team Championship, often referred to as the "Chess Olympiad."
Additional reporting by: Thomas Lemmer
